name: Kedarkantha
description: India's most beloved winter trek. Starting from the quiet village of Sankri, the trail winds through deodar and rhododendron forests to the frozen Juda Ka Talab lake and up to a 360° summit view of Swargarohini, Bandarpoonch, Black Peak, and the Gangotri ranges. Perfect for first-time Himalayan trekkers. Summit day begins at 4 AM in sub-zero temperatures — absolutely magical.

overview.location: Kedarkantha (3,810m) sits at the head of the Supin River valley in Govind Pashu Vihar National Park and Wildlife Sanctuary, Uttarkashi district, western Garhwal. The base village of Sankri (1,920m) is 210 km northeast of Dehradun via Purola and Mori. The mountain is flanked by Swargarohini (6,252m) to the north and the Bandarpoonch massif (6,316m) to the west. The Tons River — Uttarakhand's widest and one of its most powerful — drains the valley below.
overview.history: Kedarkantha is named for Shiva — 'Kedar' his high-Himalayan domain, 'Kantha' his throat — and the peak is sacred in local Garhwali tradition. The shepherding and Jaunsari communities who graze their flocks in these meadows every summer have followed the same seasonal routes for centuries. The frozen Juda Ka Talab lake on the ascent is considered a sacred offering pool in local belief. The trail was popularised as a winter trekking destination from the early 2000s and is now India's single most popular snow trek.
overview.length: The standard circuit covers 20 km over 5–6 days, Sankri to Sankri. Total elevation gain from Sankri (1,920m) to summit (3,810m) is 1,890m. Summit day begins at 4 AM, covers 11 km with approximately 1,200m of ascent and descent back to Sankri in a single long day of 8–9 hours. The approach days to Juda Ka Talab and base camp are each 4–5 km.
overview.temperature: Winter (Dec–Mar): –10°C to –20°C at camp; –25°C near summit. Heavy snowfall creates a white landscape ideal for winter trekking, but demanding on gear. Spring (Apr–May): –2°C to 10°C; snowmelt reveals wildflowers. Summer (Jun–Aug): 5°C to 20°C; lush meadows, fewer trekkers. Autumn (Sep–Nov): 0°C to 15°C; clearest skies and best photography. The recommended season for first-timers is December–February for the full winter experience, or October for clearest views.
overview.fitness: Suitable for fit beginners with no prior Himalayan experience. You should be able to walk 8–12 km per day on uneven terrain while carrying a 6–10 kg daypack. Summit day demands mental resilience as much as physical fitness — a 4 AM start in sub-zero darkness is the primary challenge. Recommended preparation: 4–6 weeks of daily cardio including stair climbing, treadmill at incline, and brisk 5–8 km walks. Lower-body strength training helps significantly on the steep final sections.

permitInfo.type: Govind Pashu Vihar NP/WLS Forest Entry Permit
permitInfo.where: Sankri check-post / DFO Purola, Uttarkashi Forest Division
permitInfo.fee: ₹150/day Indian nationals; ₹600/day foreigners. Carry fee receipts — trail posts verify them.
permitInfo.note: Sankri check-post issues permits on arrival; online registration + medical certificate introduced in 2018 — expect similar paperwork in peak season (Oct–Jan). Uttarkashi district practice: insurance required. Bugyal camping ban (HC order) applies — camp at designated off-meadow sites only. No drones inside NP. Carry 2 printed sets of all documents.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to all nationalities with standard forest entry permit.

itinerary.title: Arrival at Sankri Base Village
itinerary.desc: Drive from Dehradun via Mussoorie, Nainbagh, Purola, Naitwar, and Mori along the Yamuna and Tons rivers to reach Sankri — a compact mountain settlement of slate-roofed wooden homes set against pine ridges. Collect permits, sort gear, acclimatize with a sunset stroll, and fill up on hot dal and rice.

itinerary.title: Sankri to Juda Ka Talab
itinerary.desc: The trail threads upward through stands of deodar and oak. Snow bridges the roots in winter. A clearing reveals Juda Ka Talab — a small oval lake that freezes into a perfect mirror of ice between December and February. Pitch tents under the pines.

itinerary.title: Juda Ka Talab to Kedarkantha Base Camp
itinerary.desc: Trees thin quickly as the path climbs into high meadows draped in snow. Kedarkantha's summit pyramid appears directly above. Rest, hydrate, and watch the alpenglow paint the peaks in the late afternoon.

itinerary.title: Summit Push, Descent to Sankri
itinerary.camp: Return to Sankri or drive out
itinerary.desc: Torches on at 3–4 AM for the two-hour climb on packed snow. Sunrise at 3,810m delivers an unbroken ring of high peaks — Swargarohini, Bandarpoonch, Black Peak, the Gangotri massif. Then a full descent back to base, back through the forest, back to Sankri by afternoon.

itinerary.title: Return to Dehradun
itinerary.desc: Morning departure from Sankri down the Tons Valley. The drive reverses the approach route through Mori, Naitwar, Purola, and Mussoorie hills back to Dehradun city. Total return journey roughly 7–8 hours by shared jeep or private vehicle.

name: Kashmir Great Lakes
description: Widely considered the most beautiful trek in India. The trail passes through six glacial lakes — Vishansar, Krishansar, Gadsar, Satsar, Nundkol, Gangabal — and crosses three high mountain passes. Rolling meadows, turquoise alpine lakes, snow-fed icebergs floating in summer, and the backdrop of the Harmukh massif create an IMAX experience of Indian mountain landscapes.

overview.location: The Kashmir Great Lakes circuit traverses the Sind Valley watershed in Ganderbal and Bandipora districts of Jammu & Kashmir, threading through seven glacial lakes — Vishansar (3,770m), Krishansar (3,801m), Gadsar (3,600m), Satsar (3,600m), Gangabal (3,572m), and Nundkol (3,520m). The horseshoe-shaped route crosses the Harmukh range backdrop, with the Gadsar Pass (4,200m) as the highest point. Sonamarg (2,800m) is the most common starting town.
overview.history: Gangabal Lake is one of the most sacred pilgrimage sites in Kashmir — a major destination for the Harmukh Gangabal Yatra, a religious walk held in the month of Bhadra (August–September). The twin lakes at Gangabal are associated with Shiva and Parvati in Kashmiri Shaivite tradition. The Harmukh peak (5,142m) looming above is considered the 'Kailash of Kashmir.' The route follows ancient shepherd paths used by Gujjar and Bakarwal herders who bring their flocks to these high meadows every summer.
overview.length: The full circuit covers 70–75 km over 7–9 days, typically walked Sonamarg to Naranag (or reverse) as a one-way traverse needing a vehicle shuttle. The highest point is the Gadsar Pass at 4,200m. Total elevation gain across the traverse is approximately 3,800m. Daily distances range from 10–18 km. Some operators offer a compressed 6-day variant using longer days.
overview.temperature: July–Aug: 10°C–22°C at valley camps; 0°C–8°C at high passes. Afternoon cloud builds daily; expect some rain. September: Clearest month — 2°C–15°C, brilliant blue skies, lake reflections at their most vivid. Snow on passes possible from late September. Access: The route is inaccessible October–June due to snow blocking the Gadsar and other passes. The trekking window is July–September.
overview.fitness: Moderate to hard. Requires prior experience of multi-day trekking — at least 2–3 shorter treks beforehand. You should be comfortable walking 14–18 km per day with a loaded pack and managing pass altitudes of 4,200m without significant distress. A minimum of 8 weeks of cardio and loaded hiking preparation is recommended. Altitude awareness is essential — the route has no built-in acclimatisation day, so pace management on the high passes is critical.

permitInfo.type: Forest / Wildlife Sanctuary Entry Permit (J&K)
permitInfo.where: DFO Sonamarg or Srinagar Tourist Office at Sonmarg; permit may also be arranged through licensed local operators in Srinagar
permitInfo.fee: ₹200–400 per day Indian; ₹600–800 foreigner (confirm current J&K forest rates)
permitInfo.note: The route passes through Sindh Wildlife Sanctuary and forests managed by J&K Forest Department. Permits are obtained at the Sonamarg/Naranag ranger offices. A licensed local guide from Jammu & Kashmir is mandatory. Carry multiple ID copies — Army/CRPF checkposts at several points on this route. No camping at restricted zones. Sensitive border region — register with local police/CRPF post at Sonamarg.
permitInfo.foreigners: Foreign nationals permitted with forest entry permit and licensed J&K guide. Some internal zones may need additional DM clearance — confirm with J&K Tourism before travel.

itinerary.title: Srinagar to Sonamarg — Trek to Nichnai
itinerary.desc: Drive out of Srinagar along the Sindh River to Sonamarg at 2,800m — a broad alpine meadow backed by glacier peaks. Lace up and head into the hills, climbing steadily alongside the Nichnai Nala through meadows of wild iris to the first campsite by a clear stream.

itinerary.title: Nichnai to Vishansar Lake
itinerary.desc: Gain the Nichnai Pass at 4,100m — the first high crossing. Below opens the jewel-blue Vishansar Lake, dotted with floating icebergs in July. Camp on the grass beside the water with Vishansar Peak filling the sky above.

itinerary.title: Vishansar — Krishansar — Gadsar Pass — Gadsar Lake
itinerary.desc: Walk the short ridge to twin Krishansar, then tackle the highest point of the route — Gadsar Pass at 4,206m. The view from the top with both Kashmir lakes behind you and Gadsar Lake below is one of the great panoramas on this trek. Steady descent to camp beside the deep-blue Gadsar.

itinerary.title: Gadsar to Satsar Lakes
itinerary.desc: Follow the Gadsar Valley past wandering Gujjar flocks to Satsar — a chain of seven small linked lakes cupped in a wildflower meadow. This section sees far fewer trekkers; the peace here is complete.

itinerary.title: Satsar to Gangabal — Nundkol Lakes
itinerary.desc: Cross Zajibal Pass (4,080m) and drop into the Gangabal-Nundkol basin — the largest lake complex on the trek. The great Harmukh massif (5,142m) towers above the water. Catch the last light turning the lake surface gold.

itinerary.title: Gangabal to Naranag — Drive to Srinagar
itinerary.desc: A sharp descent through birch and pine forest leads to the ancient Naranag temple ruins. A vehicle picks up here for the roughly 2.5-hour drive back to Srinagar through the Sindh Valley. Total return from trailhead to city is around 7–8 hours combined.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Imad Clicks on Pexels

name: Roopkund
description: India's most intriguing high-altitude trek, leading to the mysterious Skeleton Lake at 15,700 ft where 9th-century human skeletons are still visible beneath the ice. The trail traverses alpine forests, the vast Bedni and Ali Bugyal meadows, and offers stunning views of Mt. Trishul (7,120m) and Nanda Ghunti. The final snow climb to the lake edge is unforgettable.

overview.location: Roopkund is a glacial mystery lake at 5,029m in Chamoli district, Uttarakhand, within the Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve buffer zone. It sits in a steep rocky basin between Trishul massif (7,120m) to the northwest and Nanda Ghunti (6,309m) to the north. The approach is from Lohajung village (2,270m) in the Wan valley, via the vast Ali-Bedni Bugyal alpine meadows. Rishikesh, 250 km west, is the nearest major hub.
overview.history: Roopkund became internationally famous after hundreds of human skeletal remains were found around the lake during a 1942 forest survey. DNA analysis has since identified at least two distinct groups — one South Asian (likely Indian pilgrims on the ancient Nanda Devi Raj Jat route) and one of Mediterranean genetic origin, both dating to around 800–1000 CE. The Raj Jat Yatra — held once every 12 years and one of India's largest religious processions — follows this exact route from Nauti village to the lake, carrying a four-horned ram as Shiva's messenger.
overview.length: The standard trek covers 53 km over 8–9 days, Lohajung to Lohajung. Total elevation gain is approximately 2,760m. The route crosses the Ali Bugyal (3,350m) and Bedni Bugyal (3,354m) meadows before climbing to Bhagwabasa (4,400m) base camp, then a steep final 2.5 km push to the lake. Note: the Uttarakhand High Court bugyal camping ban has modified the classic itinerary — overnight camps must now be staged below or above the meadows, not on them.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–18°C at meadows; –5°C to 5°C at Bhagwabasa. Trail accessible but lake may be under snow. Sep–Oct: –10°C to 8°C at Bhagwabasa; lake is clearest and most dramatic. July–Aug: Monsoon season — the meadows turn lush and green but paths become muddy. Winter: Completely inaccessible under deep snow. October is widely considered the best month for the full Roopkund experience.
overview.fitness: Moderate to hard. Prior experience on at least two multi-day treks is required. The Junargali ridge above Bhagwabasa (3 km over loose rock and potential snow) demands sure-footedness. Altitude of 5,029m requires the body to acclimatise properly — rushing this trek causes acute mountain sickness. Preparation: 10–12 weeks of cardio and strength training. Trekking pole experience is strongly recommended.

permitInfo: Forest entry/trek ticket from Lohajung or Wan check-post. No overnight camping on Aali-Bedni-Bagzi bugyals (HC order, WPPIL 123/2014) — classic itinerary substantially changed. Medical certificate and trek insurance required. Camps must be off-meadow.

itinerary.title: Kathgodam / Haridwar to Lohajung
itinerary.desc: A long mountain drive through Almora and Gwaldam to reach Lohajung — a small hilltop village of old houses and wide views. Sort permits in the evening, eat well, and sleep early before the trek proper begins.

itinerary.title: Lohajung to Didna
itinerary.desc: Drop to the Wan River crossing, then climb gently through oak and rhododendron forest and past terraced farm fields. Didna is a quiet Garhwali village where stone paths between wooden houses make for a fine warm-up day.

itinerary.title: Didna to Ali Bugyal
itinerary.desc: Push upward out of the treeline onto Ali Bugyal — a vast rolling grassland at 3,630m. Trishul (7,120m) and Nanda Ghunti materialize above the meadow's far edge. This is the first genuinely big view of the trek and it stops most people in their tracks.

itinerary.title: Ali Bugyal to Bedni Bugyal to Patar Nachauni
itinerary.desc: Stroll across the sacred Bedni Bugyal with its stone shrine and mountain lake, then gain the boulder-strewn plateau of Patar Nachauni at 3,780m. Trishul looms directly overhead — close enough to feel its cold shadow at dusk.

itinerary.title: Patar Nachauni to Bhagwabasa
itinerary.desc: Short but high — altitude now bites at 4,400m. The landscape turns austere and windswept. Sleep as early as possible; the summit bid starts before dawn.

itinerary.title: Roopkund Lake, Return to Bedni
itinerary.desc: Headlamps before 4 AM. A steep snow-slope leads to the shallow depression of Roopkund where the 9th-century skeletons remain visible through the ice. The rim at 5,029m frames Trishul in full. A long downhill run returns you to the gentle grasses of Bedni for the night.

itinerary.title: Bedni Bugyal to Lohajung — Return Drive
itinerary.desc: Descend through Wan village to Lohajung, then board the return vehicle to Kathgodam or Haridwar. The mountain road unfurls in reverse — Gwaldam, Almora, the plains — and you arrive back roughly 14–15 hours after leaving camp.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Saheb santanu on Pexels

name: Valley of Flowers
description: A UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the world's most ethereal trekking destinations. The valley blooms with over 500 species of rare Himalayan wildflowers during the monsoon, creating a riotous carpet of color beneath towering peaks. One of India's most iconic natural wonders.

overview.location: The Valley of Flowers National Park (87.5 sq km) lies in the upper Bhyundar Ganga valley, Chamoli district, within the Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve — a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005. The valley floor sits at 3,352m–3,658m at the base of the Bhyundar glacier, enclosed by Rataban (6,126m), Nilgiri Parvat (6,474m), and Gauri Parvat. Ghangaria village (3,048m) is the gateway, reached by a 14 km trail from Govindghat on the Badrinath highway.
overview.history: The valley was unknown outside Garhwal until 1931, when British mountaineer Frank Smythe stumbled upon it while descending from an attempt on Kamet (7,756m). Overwhelmed by the display of hundreds of wildflower species, he named it 'Valley of Flowers' and later wrote a celebrated book about it. Botanist Joan Margaret Legge, who returned with Smythe, died here in 1939 when she slipped on wet rock — her grave remains in the valley. The area has been locally sacred for far longer, associated with the Hanuman legend and the mythical Sanjivani herb that could raise the dead.
overview.length: The valley floor is 8 km long. A standard day visit from Ghangaria enters 3–4 km into the valley and returns. The approach walk from Govindghat to Ghangaria is 14 km — typically done as an overnight stay at Ghangaria. Total round-trip from Govindghat: 34 km over 2–3 days. Park regulations: no camping inside the valley, day visits only, gate opens 7 AM, last entry 2 PM, all visitors out by 6 PM.
overview.temperature: July–Aug: 10°C–20°C; peak wildflower season with 300+ species simultaneously in bloom — the only correct season for the full flower experience. Expect afternoon rain and mist daily (monsoon season). June and September: Drier conditions but the wildflower display is less peak. October onwards: Park closes due to snow. The valley is accessible only June through October.
overview.fitness: Moderate. The 14 km Govindghat–Ghangaria trail has 1,220m of elevation gain — manageable for reasonably fit trekkers who pace themselves. The valley floor itself is flat and easy walking. Suitable for older adults and families with children above 10 years. Ghangaria at 3,048m may cause mild altitude symptoms in those arriving from sea level — plan at least one night there before entering the valley.

permitInfo.type: Valley of Flowers National Park Permit (UNESCO World Heritage Site) — Day Entry Only
permitInfo.where: Ghangaria park gate counter (on site); also via official online portal: valleyofflower.uk.gov.in
permitInfo.fee: ₹150 Indian; ₹600 foreigner (per day entry; no camping fee since camping is banned inside)
permitInfo.note: STRICT day-entry only — no camping inside the park under any circumstances. Gate opens at 7 AM, last entry 2 PM, all visitors must exit by 6 PM. Joshimath district medical fitness practice applies at Govindghat for longer routes. Drones banned. Park open Jul–Oct only (closed Nov–Jun due to snow).
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to all nationalities. Foreign trekkers must present passport at gate. Online permit recommended to avoid queues.

itinerary.title: Haridwar to Govindghat
itinerary.desc: Follow the Alaknanda River upstream through Devprayag, Rudraprayag, Joshimath. Govindghat is where the road ends — a busy pilgrim junction and the trailhead for the Valley of Flowers. Organize the following day's permits and sleep early.

itinerary.title: Govindghat to Ghangaria via Pulna
itinerary.distance: 13 km (4 km road to Pulna + 9 km trail)
itinerary.desc: Drive 4 km from Govindghat to Pulna (motorable road), drive 4 km from Govindghat to Pulna village (motorable road), then begin the 9 km trek on a well-trodden path alongside the Pushpawati gorge, hemmed in by waterfalls cascading off the canyon walls. Mule traffic is heavy — step aside and enjoy the forest. Ghangaria at 3,048m is the only settlement in the area and your base for exploring the valley.

itinerary.title: Valley of Flowers Full Exploration Day
itinerary.desc: Step through the park gate (3 km from Ghangaria) into one of the Himalaya's most celebrated landscapes. In July–August the valley floor is an unbroken carpet of Himalayan blue poppies, brahmakamal, cobra lily, primulas, and anemones beneath a wall of snow peaks. Take your time — photography deserves hours. Return before the 4 PM gate closure.

itinerary.title: Ghangaria to Pulna — Drive to Govindghat
itinerary.desc: Trek back down from Ghangaria to Pulna (10 km), then take the 4 km motorable road back to Govindghat. Board the vehicle for the return drive down the Alaknanda — Joshimath, Rudraprayag, Devprayag — back to the plains.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Mario Vogt on Pexels

name: Har Ki Dun
description: Called the 'Valley of Gods,' Har Ki Dun is one of the most culturally rich treks in Uttarakhand. The trail winds through ancient villages of the Govind Wildlife Sanctuary, past terraced fields and pine forests, to a hanging valley surrounded by Swargarohini peak (6,252m) and the Jaundhar Glacier. The Pandavas are said to have ascended to heaven from this valley.

overview.location: Har Ki Dun — 'Valley of Gods' — is a hanging valley at 3,566m in Govind Pashu Vihar National Park, Uttarkashi district, western Garhwal. The valley is bounded by the Swargarohini group (highest peak 6,252m) and the Jaundhar Glacier to the north, and drains into the Tons River via the Supin tributary. The ancient villages of Osla and Seema sit on the valley floor and are among the most intact traditional settlements in the Garhwal Himalayas. Sankri (1,920m), 210 km from Dehradun, is the base.
overview.history: Har Ki Dun is steeped in Mahabharata legend — the Swargarohini peak above is traditionally identified as the 'Stairway to Heaven' climbed by the Pandavas on their final journey to Svarga (heaven). The Duryodhana temple in Osla village — one of only a handful of temples in India worshipping the Mahabharata's primary antagonist — reflects the valley's ancient and contrarian religious character. The Jaunsari-Garhwali communities here have maintained traditional wooden-frame architecture, polyandry customs, and local deity worship largely unchanged for centuries. British surveyor Richard Strachey documented the valley in 1848.
overview.length: Standard trek is 55 km over 6–7 days, Sankri return. Elevation gain from Sankri to valley floor: 1,646m. The trail passes through the villages of Taluka (motor road end), Gangar, and Osla before reaching the valley. Return is by the same route, with the option to vary via the Kalkatiyadhar ridge. A further 3 km from the valley floor reaches the Jaundhar Glacier snout.
overview.temperature: Apr–Jun: 5°C–20°C in the valley; rhododendron forests in full bloom below. Jul–Aug: 8°C–22°C; lush and green, with occasional afternoon showers in the lower forest sections. Sep–Oct: 0°C–15°C; clearest skies of the year; best for photography. Nov–Mar: –5°C to 5°C; the valley fills with snow and the glacier access closes, but a winter version of the lower trek is possible with guide.
overview.fitness: Easy to moderate. Suitable for fit beginners who can sustain 10–14 km per day of walking. The terrain is mostly gradual with no technical sections or steep scrambles. The altitude maximum of 3,566m is manageable for most trekkers who give themselves time to acclimatise. Preparation: 4–6 weeks of regular cardiovascular exercise and walking with a loaded pack of 6–8 kg is sufficient.

permitInfo.type: Govind Pashu Vihar National Park / Wildlife Sanctuary Entry Permit
permitInfo.where: Sankri check-post / DFO Purola, Uttarkashi Forest Division (also Taluka range office)
permitInfo.fee: ₹150/day Indian; ₹600/day foreigner
permitInfo.note: Entire Har Ki Dun valley falls inside Govind Pashu Vihar NP/WLS. Mandatory forest permit from Sankri. Bugyal camping ban applies: valley meadow floor may restrict overnight camping — verify legal sites with range staff at Sankri. HC order treats meadows as protected. Uttarkashi district practice: insurance and medical fitness increasingly verified. Carry 2 printed permit sets.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to all nationalities with NP forest permit. No ILP required on this specific route.

itinerary.title: Dehradun to Sankri
itinerary.desc: Drive the length of the Tons Valley — Mussoorie, Purola, Naitwar, Mori — to reach Sankri, which also serves Kedarkantha. This Uttarakhand valley road is itself beautiful, passing cliff-hanging villages and crashing rivers.

itinerary.title: Drive to Taluka, Trek to Seema
itinerary.distance: 12 km by road + 7 km on trail
itinerary.desc: Drive or walk 12 km down to the Taluka road-head. Then follow the Supin River on a broad stone-paved trail — ancient enough to predate written records — through forest and open valley to Seema.

itinerary.title: Seema to Osla Village
itinerary.desc: A leisurely morning walk to Osla, which harbours the Duryodhana temple — a 14th-century stone shrine where the Mahabharata villain is worshipped as a local deity. Stone lanes, carved wooden facades, and the smell of woodsmoke.

itinerary.title: Osla to Har Ki Dun Valley
itinerary.desc: The valley wall opens without warning onto the hanging cradle of Har Ki Dun. A flat meadow floor ringed by Swargarohini (6,252m), the Jaundhar Glacier, and unnamed snow ridges. Mythology says this is where the Pandavas ascended to heaven — standing here, that feels plausible.

itinerary.title: Rest Day — Glacier Exploration
itinerary.desc: A slow morning, a wander toward the Jaundhar snout or up to Maninda Tal. Watch high-altitude birds, photograph peaks, and rest sore muscles for the return.

itinerary.title: Valley to Sankri — Return Drive to Dehradun
itinerary.desc: Trek back to Sankri in a single long day through Osla and Seema, then board the vehicle for the Dehradun return. Combined travel is around 14 hours. Break the drive with a meal at Mori or Purola if needed.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Ranjeet Kumar Singh on Pexels

name: Kuari Pass (Curzon Trail)
description: Historically trekked by Lord Curzon in 1905, Kuari Pass offers one of the finest panoramic views in the Indian Himalayas — Nanda Devi (7,816m), Kamet, Dronagiri, Hathi Ghoda Parbat, and Mana Peak all visible in a single sweep. Oak forests, bugyals, and ridge walks define the trail. Considered one of the most rewarding beginner treks in the Indian Himalayas.

overview.location: Kuari Pass (3,640m) lies in Chamoli district, Garhwal Himalayas, connecting the Dhauli Ganga drainage with the Bireh Ganga. The trail traverses the edge of the Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve buffer zone and is renowned for arguably the widest panorama of 7,000m peaks visible from any standard Himalayan trek: Nanda Devi (7,816m), Kamet (7,756m), Dronagiri (7,066m), Mana, Hathi, Ghori, Bethartoli, Changabang, and Dunagiri are visible simultaneously from the ridgeline. Joshimath (1,875m) is the gateway town.
overview.history: The trail is named the 'Curzon Trail' after Lord Curzon, Viceroy of India, who trekked this route in 1905 and wrote enthusiastically about the panorama in his official dispatches. The route was well-known to local shepherds and Garhwali pilgrims centuries before Curzon's visit — it connects sacred sites including Tapovan near Joshimath. British explorer Eric Shipton traversed these hills extensively in the 1930s, documenting the glacier systems and mapping approaches to the Nanda Devi sanctuary.
overview.length: The classic trek is 35–40 km over 5–7 days from Auli or Dhak village. Total elevation gain approximately 2,000m from Joshimath level. The pass crossing involves 700m of ascent on summit day. Can be walked as a one-way traverse Auli–Tapovan or as a loop. The ridge walk section above 3,000m — with uninterrupted peak views — covers approximately 15 km.
overview.temperature: Apr–Jun: 5°C–20°C; rhododendron forests in full bloom on the lower approach. Sep–Oct: 0°C–15°C; clearest Himalayan skies of the year; the recommended season for peak views. Dec–Mar: –10°C to 0°C; the trek can be done as a winter snowshoeing route with proper preparation — the ridge under snow is extraordinary. Joshimath district has an on-arrival medical fitness check practice in peak season.
overview.fitness: Moderate. Suitable for trekkers with at least one prior multi-day Himalayan trek. The panoramic ridge walk requires sustained uphill effort over multiple days but has no technical sections. Altitude of 3,640m is manageable for well-acclimatised trekkers. Preparation: 6–8 weeks of cardio, hiking with an 8 kg pack, and stair training recommended.

permitInfo.type: Forest Entry Permit (Chamoli Forest Division)
permitInfo.where: Joshimath Forest Range office or Dhak village check-post
permitInfo.fee: ₹150/day Indian; ₹600/day foreigner
permitInfo.note: Kuari Pass corridor managed by Chamoli Forest Division. Joshimath administration has required on-spot medical fitness checks at the Govt. hospital since summer 2024 (district practice). Insurance mandatory (Chamoli practice). Carry 2 printed ID/permit sets. Bugyal camping ban applies to meadow sections above Tali Top — use designated camp sites only.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to all nationalities. No ILP restriction on this route.

itinerary.title: Haridwar to Joshimath
itinerary.desc: The Alaknanda highway carries you past four sacred confluences — Devprayag, Rudraprayag, Karnprayag, Vishnuprayag — before depositing you at Joshimath, the gateway town for Nanda Devi and the Kuari Pass route. Settle in and acclimatize.

itinerary.title: Drive to Dhak, Trek to Gulling
itinerary.desc: A 12 km drive from Joshimath to Dhak village (the trek trailhead), then upward through stands of oak and rhododendron. Pass Tugasi village. The trees part occasionally to frame Hathi Ghoda Parbat and Dronagiri above the valley. Gulling is a generous campsite on an open slope at 2,900m.

itinerary.title: Gulling to Khullara
itinerary.desc: A steady climb through rhododendron and birch forest into the open meadow at Khullara (3,350m). The skyline broadens with each step — Nanda Devi, Dunagiri, Hathi Ghoda Parvat, and Dronagiri appear across the horizon. Khullara is an outstanding campsite with unobstructed peak views.

itinerary.title: Khullara to Kuari Pass and back to Tali
itinerary.desc: The summit day. Climb from Khullara to Kuari Pass (3,900m) — a 180° panorama of 14 Himalayan peaks including Nanda Devi (7,816m), Kamet (7,756m), Dronagiri, Chaukhamba, and Hathi Ghoda Parvat. Retrace to Khullara then continue to Tali Lake (3,550m), a beautiful alpine lake often frozen in winter.

itinerary.title: Tali to Auli via Gorson Bugyal — Drive to Joshimath
itinerary.desc: Descend from Tali through the sweeping Gorson Bugyal meadow (3,090m), one of the finest high-altitude meadows in Uttarakhand, then down to Auli — India's premier ski resort. Board a vehicle back to Joshimath (13 km), then onward to Haridwar or Rishikesh.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Balaji Srinivasan on Pexels

name: Brahmatal
description: A winter gem in Uttarakhand that stands apart for its extraordinary views. From the Brahmatal ridge, you get simultaneous close-up views of Mt. Trishul (7,120m) and Nanda Ghunti (6,309m) — so close they seem touchable. The trek also passes two mountain lakes, Bekaltal and Brahmatal, and gives a bird's-eye view of the entire Roopkund trail laid out below.

overview.location: Brahmatal (3,454m) is a high-altitude frozen lake perched on an open ridge in Chamoli district, approached from Lohajung village (1,680m) in the Wan valley of the Nanda Devi buffer zone. The lake sits directly below the Ali-Bedni Bugyal plateau and offers wide views of Trishul (7,120m), Mt. Kamet (7,756m), and Nanda Ghunti (6,309m) from the surrounding ridge. It is the premier winter trekking destination in Uttarakhand for those seeking snow without the extreme cold of Kedarkantha's summit push.
overview.history: Brahmatal — 'Lake of Brahma' — is sacred in Hindu tradition: the creator-god Brahma is said to have meditated here. The surrounding meadows have been seasonal grazing grounds for local Garhwali shepherd communities for centuries. The trek rose to prominence as a winter destination after the 2014 Uttarakhand High Court bugyal camping ban restricted the classic Roopkund and Bedni Bugyal itineraries, requiring route modifications that made the Brahmatal ridge approach more distinct.
overview.length: Standard trek is 35 km over 6 days, Lohajung return. Total elevation gain approximately 1,774m. The trail passes through the forest zone and the Bedni Bugyal meadow area before climbing to the Brahmatal Lake ridge at 3,454m. The summit of Brahmatal peak (3,593m) is accessible as a short day extension from the lake camp.
overview.temperature: Dec–Mar: –10°C to –5°C at lake camp; the lake is fully frozen, the meadows deep in snow — the most dramatic and recommended season. Apr–Jun: 0°C–15°C; snowmelt reveals wildflowers. Sep–Nov: –2°C to 12°C; clear autumn skies. Jul–Aug: Lush monsoon greens but rainy. Winter (December–February) is by far the best season for this trek.
overview.fitness: Easy to moderate. An excellent first winter Himalayan trek for reasonably fit individuals who are comfortable in cold temperatures. No technical terrain, but deep snow in winter requires gaiters and warm layering. Prepare for sustained cold: thermal base layers, insulated mid-layers, waterproof outer shell, and quality gloves are essential. 4–6 weeks of regular cardiovascular exercise is sufficient preparation.

permitInfo.type: Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve Buffer Zone Entry + Forest Entry Permit
permitInfo.where: Lohajung check-post (Chamoli Forest Division)
permitInfo.fee: ₹150/day Indian; ₹600/day foreigner
permitInfo.note: Same permit hub as Roopkund (Lohajung). Bugyal camping ban applies — overnight on meadows is illegal. Chamoli district practice: medical fitness + insurance increasingly verified. Brahmatal lake and ridge are within the biosphere buffer zone. Permits issued at the Lohajung check-post on arrival; carry multiple ID copies.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to all nationalities with standard forest permit.

itinerary.title: Kathgodam to Lohajung
itinerary.desc: Drive through Almora and Gwaldam to Lohajung — the same starting village as the Roopkund trek, though Brahmatal takes a very different path. Check permits and gear in the evening.

itinerary.title: Lohajung to Bekaltal
itinerary.desc: A forest walk to the lesser-known Bekaltal lake — a quiet oval of water among the trees. In winter months it carries a skin of ice. A gentle opener that builds appetite for the days ahead.

itinerary.title: Bekaltal to Brahmatal Lake via Tilandi
itinerary.desc: The gradient sharpens as the trail leaves the forest behind. Above the treeline, snowfields spread in every direction through winter. Brahmatal lake sits in a hollow at 3,600m — turquoise when open, a white disc when frozen. Trishul materializes above the far ridge.

itinerary.title: Brahmatal Top Summit and Descent to Lohajung
itinerary.desc: Start early at 5–6 AM for the summit push. From Brahmatal lake, ascend through rhododendron forest and across two ridges — Chota Jhandidar and Bada Jhandidar — to the Brahmatal Top (3,734m). The panorama is extraordinary: Trishul (7,120m) and Nanda Ghunti (6,309m) dominate the foreground, with Kamet, Neelkanth, Chaukhamba, and Mana visible behind. Looking east you can map the entire Roopkund trail — Ali Bugyal, Bedni Bugyal, and the lake rim — laid out below. Descend via the same ridge to Daldum clearing and continue down to Lohajung.

itinerary.title: Drive from Lohajung to Kathgodam / Rishikesh
itinerary.desc: Retrace the descent through forest to Lohajung, then board the return vehicle through Gwaldam and Almora back to the plains at Kathgodam. Total return journey is roughly 12 hours.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Pawan Sehgal on Pexels

name: Tarsar Marsar
description: A twin-lake trek in the heart of the Kashmir Himalayas, connecting the turquoise Tarsar and Marsar lakes through stunning meadows and passes. The trail passes through dense conifer forests, flower-laden valleys, and pastoral meadows used by Gujjar shepherds. A more demanding and less crowded alternative to the Kashmir Great Lakes — ideal for experienced trekkers seeking solitude.

overview.location: Tarsar and Marsar are twin alpine lakes above the Aru Valley in Anantnag district, Jammu & Kashmir, south of the main Sindh Valley. Tarsar Lake (3,840m) is a vivid blue glacial lake beneath Tarsar peak; Marsar Lake (3,900m) sits higher and more hidden, beyond a ridge. The Kolahoi Glacier (the summer water source of the Jhelum River) and Kolahoi peak (5,425m) dominate the upper approaches. Pahalgam (2,130m) or Aru (2,414m) are the base towns.
overview.history: The lakes have been important to the Kashmiri pastoral communities — particularly the Gujjar and Bakarwal herders — who bring their flocks to these high meadows every summer. The Kolahoi area was surveyed in early British-era Kashmir records and became a trekking destination in the mid-20th century. The route passes through the broader Kolahoi Glacier landscape, whose retreat is one of the most closely monitored climate indicators in the western Himalayas.
overview.length: Standard circuit: 55 km over 7 days from Aru village (2,414m). The trail crosses a high camp above Tarsar (4,100m) before descending to Marsar, then returns via Sekiwas. Total elevation gain approximately 2,800m with multiple ridge crossings. Some operators run compressed 5-day versions.
overview.temperature: July–Aug: 8°C–22°C at valley camps; 0°C–5°C at high ridge. Afternoon clouds build daily in July–August; expect some rain and occasional snow on the passes even in August. September: 2°C–15°C; the clearest and most photographically rewarding month; lake reflections are at their best. The route is inaccessible outside July–September.
overview.fitness: Moderate to hard. Prior trekking experience on multi-day routes is required. The ridge crossings demand sure-footedness and a reasonable head for heights. Altitude at the high camp (4,100m) requires proper acclimatisation pacing. Physical preparation: 8 weeks of hiking and cardio with a loaded pack. Guide and licensed operator required (J&K regulation).

permitInfo.type: Sindh Wildlife Sanctuary / J&K Forest Department Entry Permit
permitInfo.where: Aru village ranger office or via licensed J&K operator (Pahalgam)
permitInfo.fee: ₹200–400/day Indian; ₹600–800/day foreigner (current J&K forest rates)
permitInfo.note: Route passes through the Sindh Wildlife Sanctuary and upper Lidder Valley forests under J&K Forest Department jurisdiction. Licensed local guide from J&K mandatory. Army/CRPF checkposts along the route require group registration and ID verification. Sensitive zone — register with local police in Aru village before departure. No camping at restricted meadow zones.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to foreigners with forest permit and licensed J&K guide. Some upper valley zones near Marsar may need additional DFO clearance.

itinerary.title: Srinagar to Aru Valley
itinerary.desc: A swift drive through Pahalgam to the broad, green Aru Valley near the Lidder River. Aru is the jumping-off point for several Kashmir treks. Gather permits, meet the guide, and acclimatize with a valley walk in the afternoon.

itinerary.title: Aru to Lidderwat
itinerary.desc: Follow the Lidder stream upward through a corridor of conifers, their canopy filtering the light. The valley opens at Lidderwat into a wide grazing meadow flanked by high ridges. Gujjar shepherd families camp here through summer.

itinerary.title: Lidderwat to Tarsar Lake
itinerary.desc: A sustained climb over the Tarsar ridge brings the first glimpse of the lake from above — an intense cobalt-blue set in a bowl of snow-dusted cliffs. The descent to the shoreline is short. Camp right beside the water. Sunset here is exceptional.

itinerary.title: Tarsar to Marsar Lake
itinerary.desc: Cross the ridge separating the two lakes — the toughest section of the trek. Views back to Tarsar and forward to Marsar are superb from the top. Marsar sits higher, wilder, and in far greater solitude. Virtually no other trekkers reach here.

itinerary.title: Marsar to Sumbal Village
itinerary.desc: A long descent from the high lakes through open alpine grassland into the Sindh Valley forests. The trail loses altitude steadily, ending at the road village of Sumbal or Wangath.

itinerary.title: Sumbal to Srinagar — Return
itinerary.desc: Drive back through the Sindh Valley and Sonamarg to Srinagar in about 2.5 hours. The return journey is entirely by road.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Imad Clicks on Pexels

name: Hampta Pass
description: One of India's most dramatic crossover treks, connecting the lush Kullu Valley to the stark, rain-shadow Spiti Valley via the 4,270m Hampta Pass. The transition is extraordinary — green meadows and streams on one side, lunar desert on the other. The trek is optionally extended to the otherworldly Chandratal Lake ('Moon Lake'), one of the most beautiful high-altitude lakes in India.

overview.location: Hampta Pass (4,270m) connects the lush, forested Kullu Valley of Himachal Pradesh with the stark, arid Lahaul Valley on its rain-shadow northern side. The approach starts from Jobra village (3,180m) above Manali; the descent reaches Chatru (3,360m) in the Chandra Valley and usually continues to Chandra Tal Lake (4,270m) — a separate jewel of a high-altitude lake. The dramatic landscape contrast between the green Kullu side and the lunar Spiti terrain is one of the most visceral geographical transitions in the Himalayas.
overview.history: Hampta Pass has been used for centuries as a trade route between the Kullu Valley's temperate forest communities and the high-altitude Lahaul grazing grounds, where yak herders and Lahauli farmers came to exchange wool, grain, and mountain produce. The pass appears in British Survey of India maps from the 1870s. The route gained trekking popularity in the 1980s–90s when Manali developed as a major backpacker hub.
overview.length: Trek is 26–35 km over 4–5 days from Jobra. Elevation gain from Jobra to pass: approximately 1,090m. Most groups continue past the pass to Chatru (3,360m) and then arrange a jeep to Chandra Tal Lake for an additional breathtaking high-altitude experience before driving back to Manali. The full crossing pass day is typically 6–7 hours of walking.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–22°C on the Kullu side; 0°C–15°C on the Lahaul side; the pass may retain significant snow in May. Jul–Aug: 10°C–25°C; warmest season; green and lush on the Manali side. Sep–Oct: 0°C–18°C; clearest skies; best season. Pass closes under snow November–April.
overview.fitness: Easy to moderate. An excellent trek for first-timers seeking a genuine pass crossing. No technical sections; the trail is well-worn and straightforward. Altitude of 4,270m is manageable with gradual approach from Manali (2,050m). Preparation: 4–6 weeks of regular exercise including hill walking. Spending the first night in Manali for altitude acclimatisation before heading to Jobra is strongly recommended.

permitInfo.type: Forest Entry Permit (Kullu Forest Division, Himachal Pradesh)
permitInfo.where: Jagatsukh / Jobra trailhead check-post, Manali Forest Range
permitInfo.fee: ₹100–150/day Indian; ₹300–500/day foreigner (HP forest rates)
permitInfo.note: Himachal Pradesh route managed by Kullu Forest Division. Permit at Jagatsukh check-post. For Chandratal extension (Spiti side): Lahaul and Spiti District — foreigners may need Protected Area Permit (PAP) for certain inner Spiti zones (confirm with DC Kaza). No restrictions for Indian nationals in open areas. Drones banned in protected zones.
permitInfo.foreigners: Mostly open; foreigners should verify PAP requirements for Spiti Valley sections with DC Kaza/Reckong Peo before travel.

itinerary.title: Manali to Jobra — Acclimatization
itinerary.desc: Drive 18 km from Manali up the Kullu Valley to Jobra (3,060m / 10,040ft) — the starting point of the Hampta Pass trek. Spend the afternoon walking the meadows around camp and letting the body begin adjusting to altitude. The first views of the Pir Panjal peaks that guard the pass appear above the valley walls.

itinerary.title: Jobra to Chika (Chikha)
itinerary.desc: The trail follows the Rani Nallah stream between walls of maple and birch, crossing a wooden bridge over the river. Everything is lush and green — the 'heaven' side of this crossover trek. Chika (3,078m / 10,100ft) is a charming camp beside the stream, surrounded by conifers and the first high meadows.

itinerary.title: Chika to Balu Ka Ghera
itinerary.desc: A long gradual ascent through the wide Hampta Valley, crossing the river twice and passing the wildflower meadows of Jwara — sometimes called the 'Valley of Flowers of Himachal'. Balu Ka Ghera (3,600m / 11,800ft) means 'sandy arena' — a flat, open basin formed by river sediment and glacial deposits. The Hampta Pass wall rises directly ahead. Camp here for the crossing.

itinerary.title: Hampta Pass Crossing to Shea Goru
itinerary.desc: The crux day. Early start from Balu Ka Ghera — the climb to Hampta Pass (4,270m / 14,010ft) is steep on snow and loose rock. At the pass the world switches completely: behind you, lush green Kullu Valley; ahead, the stark grey-brown rain-shadow of Lahaul. A geological transformation in a single step. The descent to Shea Goru (3,900m) on the arid Lahaul side is steep and requires careful footing. Total ascent/descent makes this the hardest day of the trek.

itinerary.title: Shea Goru to Chatru — Optional Chandratal
itinerary.desc: Drive from Chatru through the Spiti Valley. An overnight at the crescent-shaped Chandratal lake (Moon Lake) at 4,250m is unmissable — under clear Spiti skies the Milky Way reflects in the still water.

itinerary.title: Return to Manali from Kaza or Chatru
itinerary.distance: 120–230 km by road depending on route
itinerary.desc: Return to Manali either via the Rohtang Pass route (when open) or the Atal Tunnel. From Chatru the drive takes about 5 hours; from Kaza it takes 7–8 hours over the Kunzum Pass. Arrive in Manali by evening.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Jayant Bhatt on Pexels

name: Pin Bhaba Pass
description: One of Himachal Pradesh's finest crossover treks connecting the Kinnaur and Spiti valleys. Starting from Kafnu in the Bhaba Valley, the trail ascends through mountain pastures before a gruelling summit crossing of the 5,319m Bhaba Pass. The descent leads into the alien landscape of Spiti Valley, ending in the town of Kaza.

overview.location: Pin Bhaba Pass (5,319m) is a high glacier crossing linking the Bhaba Valley of Kinnaur district, Himachal Pradesh, with the Pin Valley of Spiti. The Bhaba approach starts at Kafnu village (2,615m) in a lush, forested side valley of the Sutlej. The Spiti descent ends at Mudh village in the arid, Tibetan-influenced Pin Valley National Park — a dramatically different world in terms of landscape, vegetation, and culture.
overview.history: The Pin Bhaba route has been used for centuries by Kinnauri traders and shepherds crossing to Spiti for wool, grain, and salt exchange. The Pin Valley's ancient Tibetan Buddhist monasteries reflect centuries of cultural exchange across these high passes. The pass was surveyed by the British in the late 19th century. Commercial trekking on this route began in the 1990s when Himachal Pradesh opened its previously restricted inner valleys.
overview.length: 50 km over 6–7 days. Elevation gain from Kafnu to pass: approximately 2,704m. The most demanding section is the final approach over the glacier to the pass (5,319m), requiring crampons and ice axe in early season. Descent on the Spiti side is steep rocky terrain with a 1,800m drop to Mudh village.
overview.temperature: May: Heavy snow at pass; technically most serious crossing. Jun: Snow softens; 0°C at pass, 10°C–20°C at lower camps. Jul–Aug: 5°C–22°C at camps; pass becomes non-technical but still cold. Sep–Oct: 0°C–15°C; clearest and most stable season; recommended for experienced trekkers. Pass closes October–May.
overview.fitness: Hard. Requires experience on multi-day high-altitude treks. The glacier section demands crampons, ice axe, and ideally prior scrambling or glacier experience. Altitude of 5,319m is serious — proper acclimatisation days are essential and must not be skipped. A licensed guide is strongly recommended. Preparation: 10–12 weeks of strenuous hiking and strength training.

permitInfo.type: Forest Entry Permit (Kinnaur/Shimla Forest Division) + No permit required for Himachal-only section
permitInfo.where: Kafnu village check-post (Kinnaur Forest Division, HP); ITBP registration at upper checkpoints
permitInfo.fee: ₹100–150/day Indian; ₹300–500/day foreigner
permitInfo.note: Kafnu trailhead in Kinnaur district requires forest entry. Upper sections approach sensitive LAC border zone — ITBP checkposts verify documents. Kinnaur district: some zones require Inner Line Permit (ILP) for foreigners (PAP regime). Verify with DC Reckong Peo before travel. Guide strongly recommended. Insurance required in practice.
permitInfo.foreigners: Kinnaur district has Protected Area Permit (PAP) requirements for foreigners in specific zones. Verify with DC Reckong Peo or HP Tourism before booking.

itinerary.title: Shimla / Reckong Peo to Kafnu Village
itinerary.distance: 200 km from Shimla / 90 km from Reckong Peo
itinerary.desc: Drive from Shimla (or Reckong Peo) along the Sutlej gorge on NH-5 (Hindustan–Tibet Highway) past Wangtu Bridge to Kafnu village (2,450m / 8,000ft) in the Bhaba tributary valley. Kafnu is a charming Kinnauri village of apple orchards, wooden balconies, and traditional stone houses. Check equipment and receive trekking permits. India's first underground hydroelectric dam is visible at the trailhead.

itinerary.title: Kafnu to Mulling
itinerary.desc: The trek's first day is the longest. From Kafnu (2,450m) the trail climbs through dense kail, pine, silver birch, and oak forest alongside the Bhaba River. Cross a bridge to the left bank 2 km in, passing India's first underground dam. The forest deepens before bursting suddenly into the vast open grasslands of Mulling (3,200m / 10,700ft) — a spectacular meadow camp with the first panoramic mountain views of the trip.

itinerary.title: Mulling to Kara (Karah)
itinerary.desc: A moderate day ascending from Mulling through rocky terrain and open meadows. A mystical subterranean river section — where water flows underground audibly but invisibly — is one of the trail's talking points. Cross several icy streams (expect to wade barefoot). Kara (3,550m / 11,700ft) is a beautiful open camp near a glacial stream, offering first views of the Tari Khango and Nimish Khango peaks that flank the pass above.

itinerary.title: Kara to Phutsirang (Base Camp)
itinerary.desc: A short but steep ascent from Kara to Phutsirang (4,100m / 13,500ft) — the final base camp before the pass. Cross a tributary of the Bhaba River. The landscape shifts from meadows to rocky moraine. From Phutsirang a natural amphitheatre opens up with three passes visible: Tari Khango, Nimish Khango, and Pin Bhaba Pass. Sleep early — pass day begins at 2–3 AM.

itinerary.title: Phutsirang — Pin Bhaba Pass — Mangrungse
itinerary.desc: Depart at 2–3 AM for the crossing of Pin Bhaba Pass (4,865m / 15,960ft). The final 3.5 km to the pass is a steep climb on snow, scree, and moraine. At the saddle, Spiti's vast Tibetan-desert landscape stretches below — a complete transformation from the green Bhaba Valley behind. The descent on the Spiti side is long and demanding through moraine and scree to Mangrungse (4,150m / 13,600ft) — the first camp in Pin Valley.

itinerary.title: Mangrungse to Mudh — Drive to Kaza
itinerary.desc: 17 km descent from Mangrungse through the barren, beautiful Pin Valley to Mudh village (3,750m / 12,300ft) — the last village before the wilderness. The landscape is polar opposite to the Bhaba side: bare brown rock, brilliant blue sky, geometric terraced fields, and Buddhist prayer flags. Drive 50 km to Kaza (3,800m) for overnight. Explore Key Monastery or Pin Valley National Park.

itinerary.title: Kaza to Shimla / Manali — Return Drive
itinerary.desc: Long drive back to Manali over Kunzum Pass and Rohtang, or to Shimla via Spiti and Kinnaur. Both routes offer spectacular Himalayan scenery. Plan for a full day of travel.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Jayant Bhatt on Pexels

name: Markha Valley
description: The definitive Ladakh trek — a journey through the 'Land of High Passes' that packs an extraordinary range of experiences into one week. The trail follows the Markha River through ancient monasteries, remote Ladakhi farming villages, and canyons before ascending to Kongmaru La (5,260m). The high-altitude Nimaling plateau, backdrop of Kang Yatze (6,400m), is one of the most dramatic campsites in India.

overview.location: The Markha Valley trek crosses Ladakh's high desert plateau between the Indus Valley and the Zanskar Range, traversing Hemis National Park — the largest national park in South Asia. The trail begins near Chilling (3,260m) on the Indus and follows the Markha River valley through ancient villages — Skiu, Markha, Hankar — to the high camp at Nimaling (4,700m) before crossing Kongmaru La (5,100m) and descending to Hemis or Martselang.
overview.history: The Markha Valley has been inhabited by Ladakhi farming and pastoral communities for over a thousand years. The villages contain gompas (Buddhist monasteries) and chortens from the 10th–15th centuries. Hemis Gompa — one endpoint of the route — holds the largest monastic festival in Ladakh. The valley was part of the historical trade network connecting the Indus Valley with Zanskar and the Tibetan plateau. Ladakh was an independent Buddhist kingdom from the 10th century until absorbed into Jammu & Kashmir in 1834.
overview.length: Classic traverse: 80 km over 7–9 days. The Kongmaru La crossing (5,100m) is the high point. Total elevation gain approximately 4,200m across the full route. Can be shortened or extended with side trips to Kang Yatse base camp or by starting from Spituk rather than Chilling.
overview.temperature: Jun–Jul: 10°C–25°C in valley; –2°C to 5°C at Nimaling. Aug: Similar to July; highest chance of afternoon cloud. Sep: 5°C–20°C; excellent — clear skies and fewer trekkers. Oct: 0°C–15°C; colder nights at high camps; very clear. Thermal layers always needed above 4,000m regardless of season.
overview.fitness: Moderate to hard. Best suited to trekkers with prior high-altitude experience. Kongmaru La at 5,100m is serious altitude — acclimatise in Leh (3,524m) for a minimum of 2 nights before starting. Daily distances of 15–18 km in thin air at 4,000m+ are physically demanding. Preparation: 10–12 weeks of intensive cardio and loaded hiking, with prior experience above 3,500m preferred.

permitInfo.type: Hemis National Park Entry Permit + Inner Line Permit (ILP) for non-Indian nationals
permitInfo.where: Hemis NP entry fee at Chilling trailhead; ILP from DC Leh office or via authorised tour operator
permitInfo.fee: ₹25/day Indian nationals (Hemis NP); foreigners: ILP fees apply. Camera fee ₹100.
permitInfo.note: The Markha Valley passes through Hemis National Park. Indian nationals pay the NP fee at the trail start. Foreigners require an ILP issued by DC Leh — apply minimum 1–2 days before. Shang Sumdo exit side may have ITBP checkpoint. No camping in the national park without designated-site clearance. Environmentally sensitive zone.
permitInfo.foreigners: ILP mandatory for all foreign nationals. Apply at DC Leh at least 1–2 working days before trek. Can also be arranged through registered Leh tour operators.

itinerary.title: Leh to Chilling — Trek to Skiu
itinerary.distance: 75 km by road + 10 km on trail
itinerary.desc: Drive from Leh along the Zanskar River road to the Chilling crossing. Step onto the trail where the canyon narrows and the Markha River takes over. Reach Skiu — a small Ladakhi hamlet with a crumbling fort perched on the cliff above.

itinerary.title: Skiu to Markha Village
itinerary.desc: The canyon trek in earnest. Rock walls hundreds of metres high on both sides. Multiple knee-deep river crossings in July. Pass the settlements of Chalak and Sara before reaching Markha — a proper village with a monastery, a ruined fort, and local homestays serving butter tea and tsampa.

itinerary.title: Markha to Thachungtse
itinerary.desc: The valley gradually opens. Pass Hankar with its dramatically sited monastery. Kang Yatze (6,400m) appears ahead for the first time — a pyramid of snow dominating the upper valley.

itinerary.title: Thachungtse to Nimaling Plateau
itinerary.desc: A short but high climb to the Nimaling plateau — one of the most dramatically beautiful camps in Indian trekking. Flat grassland at 4,700m, Kang Yatze directly overhead, yaks grazing at the tent edges. The stars here at night are astonishing.

itinerary.title: Kongmaru La Pass — Descent to Chogdo
itinerary.desc: The highest point of the trek. Kongmaru La at 5,260m opens a panorama across the Ladakh and Zanskar ranges. A steep descent on shale and gravel leads to the Indus Valley. Vehicles are available from Shang Sumdo.

itinerary.title: Drive Back to Leh — Return Journey
itinerary.desc: Board a vehicle at Shang Sumdo for the 45-km drive back to Leh along the Indus River highway. Arrival in Leh in roughly 2 hours. Rest day recommended before onward travel due to lingering altitude effects.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Shashank Kumawat on Pexels

name: Chadar — Frozen River
description: One of the world's most unique and exhilarating treks — walking on the frozen Zanskar River in the depths of winter. With temperatures plunging to -25°C, trekkers walk on a naturally formed ice sheet through dramatic gorges that are impassable by any other means. Chadar means 'sheet' — referring to the ice sheet that forms each January-February in the Zanskar canyon.

overview.location: The Chadar trek follows the frozen surface of the Zanskar River through a gorge up to 100m deep between Chilling (3,250m) and the caves of Nirak or Tibb in Zanskar district, Ladakh. The canyon walls of sheer rock and hanging ice are one of the most extraordinary natural spectacles in India. In winter, the frozen river is the only passage connecting Zanskar to the outside world — a tunnel road is now being constructed to end this isolation.
overview.history: For centuries, the frozen Zanskar River was the Zanskari people's only winter road to Leh for trade, medicine, and schooling for their children. They called it their 'chadar' — a blanket of ice laid over the river. The tradition of walking the frozen river is likely thousands of years old. The trek gained outside attention in the 1980s when Ladakh opened to foreign visitors, and became globally famous through documentary films in the 2000s.
overview.length: 65–105 km over 8–10 days depending on conditions and turnaround point. The typical target is the caves at Nirak (~30 km from Chilling) or Tibb, returning by the same route. Conditions vary dramatically year to year — warm spells can make sections impassable and the route is often shortened at short notice.
overview.temperature: January–February: –15°C to –30°C in the gorge; wind chill can drop to –40°C. This extreme cold is not incidental — it is the defining characteristic of the trek. Daytime on the ice: –10°C to –20°C. Nights inside rock caves or tented camps: brutal without proper four-season sleeping systems. This is one of the coldest inhabited trekking environments on Earth.
overview.fitness: Moderate physically, extreme in terms of cold tolerance. Walking on ice is essentially flat but requires constant attention for cracks, open water, and unstable sections. The primary challenge is cold endurance, not altitude (maximum ~3,500m). Prior cold-weather camping experience is strongly recommended. A high pain threshold, excellent cold-weather gear, and mental resilience are the essential requirements.

permitInfo.type: Hemis National Park Entry Permit + ILP for foreigners + Zanskar Valley Travel Permit
permitInfo.where: Permits at DC Leh office; NP fee at Chilling trailhead; ITBP registration en route
permitInfo.fee: ₹25/day Indian (Hemis NP); foreigners: ILP fees + NP fee
permitInfo.note: Chadar is the most restricted and regulated trek in Ladakh. Zanskar Valley is a sensitive border zone — all trekkers must be registered. Foreigners need ILP from DC Leh (minimum 2 days processing). ITBP checkpoints at multiple points on the river — carry all documents in waterproof case. Jan–Feb season only: check river conditions annually as route varies. Mandatory experienced local Zanskari guide.
permitInfo.foreigners: ILP mandatory — apply at DC Leh minimum 2 working days before departure. Route closure possible without notice due to security or weather — build buffer days.

itinerary.title: Leh — Full Rest and Gear Check
itinerary.desc: Mandatory acclimatization in Leh. Altitude sickness at -15°C is life-threatening. Confirm every layer of cold-weather gear: sleeping bag rated to -20°C, insulated mountaineering boots, multiple base layers, balaclava, and pogies for the trekking poles.

itinerary.title: Drive to Chilling — First Steps on the Ice
itinerary.distance: 75 km drive + 2 km walk to river
itinerary.desc: Drive to Chilling at the Zanskar River confluence, then descend to the frozen surface. The first contact with the Chadar is a shock — translucent blue ice over black river water, hemmed in by 200m canyon walls. Guides chip and test each section before crossing.

itinerary.title: Shingra Koma to Tibb Cave
itinerary.desc: A full day on the Chadar. The canyon walls close in as the gorge narrows. Frozen waterfalls cling to the rock faces in blue and white curtains. Ice thickness and texture change constantly — transparent, milky, ridged, cracked. Camp in caves that Zanskari traders have used for centuries.

itinerary.title: Tibb to Nerak Waterfall
itinerary.desc: The deepest and most dramatic section. Canyon walls narrowest here. Temperatures at night can reach -30°C in the valley depths. The frozen Nerak waterfall — 50m of solid blue ice — is the visual highlight of the entire Chadar.

itinerary.title: Nerak — Rest or Exploration
itinerary.desc: A rest day beside the frozen waterfall. Explore further into the canyon if conditions allow, or visit the cliff-perched Nerak village. Tea with Zanskari families offers a window into winter life in the world's most remote inhabited valley.

itinerary.title: Nerak to Tibb Cave (Return Walk)
itinerary.desc: The return journey begins. The same ice feels completely different walking the opposite direction — new cracks, new pressure ridges, different light on the canyon walls. Guides pick the safest lines daily.

itinerary.title: Tibb to Shingra Koma
itinerary.desc: Long final day on the river. Weather deteriorates fastest in the afternoon — stick close to the canyon wall and follow guide instructions without hesitation.

itinerary.title: Shingra Koma to Leh — Return Journey
itinerary.desc: Step off the ice for the last time and board the vehicle at Chilling for the 75-km drive back to Leh. Arrive in roughly 2 hours. A hot shower and warm meal in Leh will be the finest thing you have ever experienced.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Sakshi Patwa on Pexels

name: Goechala
description: The Goechala trek is the crown jewel of Sikkim — a journey to one of the closest frontal views of Mt. Kanchenjunga (8,586m), the world's third highest mountain. The trail winds through Khangchendzonga National Park (UNESCO World Heritage), past rhododendron forests, glacial lakes, and the stunning Samiti Lake, culminating at the Goechala viewpoints from 4,940m.

overview.location: Goechala Pass (4,940m) is a high viewpoint in Khangchendzonga National Park and Biosphere Reserve, West Sikkim, offering what many consider the world's most dramatic accessible close view of Khangchendzonga (8,586m) — the third-highest mountain on Earth. The approach is from Yuksom (1,780m) via the Prek Chu River valley, ascending through subtropical forest, rhododendron zones, the high camp at Zemathang, and the sacred Samiti Lake before the final viewpoint.
overview.history: Yuksom, the starting town, was the first capital of Sikkim (1642 CE) where the first Chogyal (King of Sikkim) was crowned by three Buddhist lamas. The entire route passes through one of the oldest pilgrimage circuits in the eastern Himalayas. Khangchendzonga is the sacred guardian deity of Sikkim, worshipped by the Lepcha people as the 'Demon of the Snows.' By local agreement with the Sikkim government, climbers never stand on the exact summit — it remains forever untrodden out of respect.
overview.length: Standard trek is 90 km over 10–12 days, Yuksom return. Total elevation gain approximately 3,160m. The trail crosses multiple vegetation zones — subtropical, temperate, sub-alpine, and alpine. Goechala viewpoint is split into Zone A (4,940m, standard) and Zone B (5,100m, requiring extra permit and early start). Mandatory rest days for acclimatisation are built into the standard itinerary.
overview.temperature: April–May: 5°C–20°C at camps; rhododendron forests in spectacular bloom; views can be partially obscured by afternoon haze. October–November: 0°C–15°C; the clearest month for Khangchendzonga views — the recommended season. Dec–Mar: –10°C to 5°C; cold but beautiful. Jun–Sep: Monsoon — heavy rain, leeches in the forest sections, but the vegetation is lush and extraordinary.
overview.fitness: Hard. Multiple consecutive days above 4,000m. Prior experience on multi-day high-altitude treks is essential. The long daily distances (12–18 km) at altitude require sustained cardiovascular fitness over 10+ days. Preparation: 10–12 weeks of intensive hiking and cardio. A registered guide and licensed Sikkim tour operator is mandatory by law.

permitInfo: Khangchendzonga National Park permit (₹200/day Indian, ₹1500/day foreign). PAP (Protected Area Permit) required for foreigners trekking near Sikkim borders. Obtain from Sikkim Tourism/District Collector Gangtok. Registered local guide mandatory. No camping in core NP zones.

itinerary.title: NJP / Bagdogra to Yuksom
itinerary.desc: Drive from the NJP railhead or Bagdogra airport through rolling Sikkim hills to Yuksom — the ancient first capital of Sikkim, where the coronation site of the first Chogyal king still stands. A place of quiet power.

itinerary.title: Yuksom to Sachen
itinerary.desc: Enter Khangchendzonga National Park through dense subtropical forest alive with birdsong and orchids. Cross the Prek Chu river on a suspension bridge. Arrive at Sachen in a clearing where fireflies appear at dusk.

itinerary.title: Sachen to Tshoka
itinerary.desc: Climb through rhododendron forest — a tunnel of scarlet and pink blooms in April. Tshoka is a small Lepcha settlement with a Buddhist gompa and views that hint at what is still ahead. The air at 3,050m already feels thinner.

itinerary.title: Tshoka to Dzongri Plateau
itinerary.desc: Break above the treeline onto the Dzongri plateau — a sweeping highland ringed by snow peaks. Kangchenjunga, Kabru, Pandim, and Rathong are all visible. The pre-dawn Dzongri sunrise on a clear morning is one of the finest mountain views in Sikkim.

itinerary.title: Acclimatization — Dzongri Top Hike
itinerary.desc: Hike to Dzongri Top at 4,400m for the full Kangchenjunga panorama. The afternoon must be spent resting at altitude before the high push of the next two days.

itinerary.title: Dzongri to Thansing
itinerary.desc: Descend into the Prechetak Valley then regain height to the rocky Thansing basin. Kangchenjunga's southwestern glaciers are now close enough to hear on warm afternoons.

itinerary.title: Thansing to Samiti Lake to Lamuney
itinerary.desc: Reach the stunning Samiti Lake — a glacial tarn that perfectly mirrors Kangchenjunga (8,586m) in still morning conditions. Continue to Lamuney camp for the summit bid.

itinerary.title: Goechala Viewpoints, Return to Thansing
itinerary.desc: Set out before dawn for Viewpoint 1 and Viewpoint 2 at 4,940m — one of the closest accessible vantage points of Kangchenjunga's southwest face on Earth. The mountain fills the entire field of view. Return to Thansing for lunch and rest.

itinerary.title: Thansing to Yuksom — Return to NJP
itinerary.desc: Descend through Dzongri and Tshoka back to Yuksom over two comfortable days, then drive to NJP or Bagdogra (4–5 hours). Total return from Yuksom to the railhead is roughly half a day by road.

coverImageCredit: Photo via Brave Search

name: Sandakphu–Phalut
description: A trek along the Indo-Nepal border ridge, Sandakphu is the highest peak in West Bengal (3,636m). On a clear day the summit offers what is called the 'Sleeping Buddha' view — the silhouette of four of the world's five highest peaks (Everest, Kangchenjunga, Lhotse, Makalu) forming the shape of a reclining figure. Trekkers stay in rustic homestays through the Singalila National Park.

overview.location: The Sandakphu–Phalut ridge walk traverses the Singalila Ridge on the India–Nepal border in Darjeeling district, West Bengal, within Singalila National Park. Sandakphu (3,636m) is the highest point in West Bengal; Phalut (3,595m) marks the confluence of four states. The ridge offers the only viewpoint in the world where four of the five highest mountains — Everest (8,849m), Kangchenjunga (8,586m), Lhotse (8,516m), and Makalu (8,485m) — are visible simultaneously.
overview.history: The Singalila Ridge formed the boundary between the Sikkim Kingdom, Nepal, and British India and was mapped by Survey of India teams in the 1860s–70s. The teahouses (trekkers' huts) along the route have operated for generations, serving trekkers, traders, and pilgrims. The Buddhist and Hindu traditions of the Gurkha and Lepcha communities are present throughout. The rhododendron forests here — some of the finest in the Himalayas — have been protected since Singalila National Park was established in 1986.
overview.length: One-way traverse: 57 km over 6–7 days, Manebhanjang to Rimbik. If returning via the same ridge: 114 km over 10+ days. The terrain is a continuous high ridge walk between 2,500m and 3,636m. Total elevation gain one-way approximately 2,200m. The trail follows a mix of paths and 4WD tracks, with teahouse accommodation at each camp.
overview.temperature: March–May: 0°C–15°C; rhododendron bloom in April is spectacular — the hillsides turn red, pink, and white. October–November: –2°C to 12°C; clearest views of the four 8,000m peaks. Dec–Feb: –10°C to 5°C; snowfall possible; views excellent when clear. Jun–Sep: Monsoon season — views obscured by daily clouds; heavy rain.
overview.fitness: Moderate. Suitable for trekkers with some prior multi-day experience. The ridge walk is sustained but not technically difficult, and the teahouse accommodation removes the need for carrying camping equipment. Altitude maximum of 3,636m is manageable. Preparation: 6–8 weeks of regular hiking and cardio recommended.

permitInfo.type: Singalila National Park Entry Permit (West Bengal) + Trekkers Hut Booking
permitInfo.where: Manebhanjang check-post (DFO Darjeeling, West Bengal Forest Department); trekkers huts booked through DGHC (Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council)
permitInfo.fee: ₹100/day Indian; ₹200/day foreigner (Singalila NP); trekkers hut: ₹200–500/night
permitInfo.note: Route lies within Singalila National Park. Permit at Manebhanjang check-post. Trekkers huts along the route (Tonglu, Kalipokhri, Sandakphu, Phalut, Gorkhey) must be booked in advance through DGHC — peak season (Apr–May, Oct–Nov) books out months ahead. The route crosses into Nepal at several points — carry passport. Anti-poaching checkposts verify permits along the ridge.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to all nationalities. Foreign nationals must carry passport (Nepal crossings along ridge). NP permit mandatory.

itinerary.title: NJP / Bagdogra to Manebhanjang
itinerary.desc: Drive through Darjeeling town to Manebhanjang — the official start of the Singalila Ridge trek and a busy border market straddling the India-Nepal line. Collect permits for the Singalila National Park.

itinerary.title: Manebhanjang to Tonglu
itinerary.desc: The ridge rises immediately through rhododendron and magnolia forest — a blaze of red, pink, and white in March and April. Nepal stretches away on the left, India on the right. Kangchenjunga shows itself on clear mornings.

itinerary.title: Tonglu to Kalipokhri
itinerary.desc: Walk the classic Singalila ridge through Chitrey and Lamey Dhura with the Himalayan panorama expanding with every hour. Kalipokhri has a sacred dark lake ringed by rhododendrons — 'kali' for dark, 'pokhri' for lake.

itinerary.title: Kalipokhri to Sandakphu Summit
itinerary.desc: Arrive at Sandakphu — the highest point in West Bengal. On a clear dawn the Sleeping Buddha takes shape across the horizon: Everest (8,849m), Lhotse, Makalu, and Kangchenjunga in one sweeping silhouette. One of the most celebrated mountain views on Earth.

itinerary.title: Sandakphu to Phalut
itinerary.desc: A long but glorious ridge walk to Phalut at the junction of Nepal, Sikkim, and West Bengal. Sparse trees, open sky, and 270° of Himalayan views. The trekkers hut at Phalut is the most remote overnight on this route.

itinerary.title: Phalut to Gorkhey
itinerary.desc: Descend steeply into the deep Sirikhola forests on the Nepal side of the ridge — bamboo groves, giant ferns, and the sound of waterfalls. Gorkhey is a beautiful village with warm homestays.

itinerary.title: Gorkhey to Rimbick — Return to NJP
itinerary.desc: Trek out to Rimbick village, then drive back through the Darjeeling hills to NJP or Bagdogra. Total return from Rimbick to railhead is roughly 3 hours by road.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Getty Images via Brave Search

name: Nag Tibba
description: The highest peak in the lower Himalayan range of Uttarakhand, Nag Tibba (Serpent's Peak) is the ideal first Himalayan summit. Starting from Pantwari village, the trail passes through dense oak and rhododendron forests to a ridge that opens stunning views of Bandarpoonch, Kedarnath, Gangotri, Swargarohini and the Doon Valley. An all-season trek perfect for beginners and families.

overview.location: Nag Tibba — 'Serpent's Peak' (3,022m) — is the highest summit of the lesser Himalayan range in Tehri district, Uttarakhand, situated 60 km northeast of Dehradun and 20 km from Mussoorie. The trek begins at Pantwari village (2,270m), reached by road from Mussoorie (30 km) or Dehradun (70 km). On a clear day the summit offers views of Bandarpoonch (6,316m), Kedarnath Dome (6,831m), Gangotri Group, and Chaukhamba (7,138m).
overview.history: Nag Tibba is a sacred peak in Garhwali tradition — 'Nag' refers to the serpent deity (Nagas) who hold an important place in both Hindu and local animistic belief systems. A Nag Devta temple at the summit is the focus of local pilgrimage. The peak is worshipped as a protector of the crops and villages below. The trek has grown significantly in popularity since the 2000s as an accessible weekend destination from Delhi and Dehradun, making it one of India's most-trodden beginner snow treks.
overview.length: 16 km round-trip over 2 days from Pantwari village. Total elevation gain approximately 752m from Pantwari to summit. Day 1: 8 km trail to a forest campsite (4–5 hours). Day 2: 3 km optional extension to a snow viewpoint, then return to Pantwari (3 hours). A very compact and accessible schedule, making it ideal for a weekend escape from Delhi.
overview.temperature: Dec–Mar: –5°C to 5°C; the summit trail is under snow — the most popular season for the winter experience. Apr–Jun: 5°C–18°C; pleasant and green with wildflowers. Sep–Nov: 2°C–15°C; clearest views of the Himalayan horizon. Monsoon (Jul–Aug): Lush but rainy and cloudy.
overview.fitness: Easy. The best first Himalayan trek for complete beginners. The trail is gradual with no technical sections or exposed scrambling. The 752m elevation gain over 8 km is manageable for most adults with basic fitness. Suitable for teenagers, families, and older adults. No special preparation required beyond regular walking. This trek is often the first point at which city-dwellers experience Himalayan snow.

permitInfo.type: No formal permit required
permitInfo.where: No permit office — walk-in
permitInfo.fee: No fee
permitInfo.note: Forest land — no entry permit. Carry government ID. Pantwari to Nag Tibba falls within Tehri Garhwal district forest; no national park or sanctuary entry. Free and open year-round.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to all nationalities

itinerary.title: Leh to Chilling (Chadar start)
itinerary.camp: Chilling — first night camp on the frozen river
itinerary.desc: Drive from Leh to Chilling (35 km). The Zanskar river freezes completely from late January to mid-February, creating the 'Chadar' (flat sheet of ice) that monks and villagers have used for centuries. Walk 8–10 km on Day 1 to the first campsite. Temperature at night: -20°C to -30°C. Total Chadar distance: 105 km round trip over 8–9 days.

itinerary.title: Day 2 on Chadar — Tibb Cave
itinerary.desc: 12 km walk on the frozen Zanskar. The ice is constantly shifting — blue in some sections, white and rough in others. Tibb cave has a large overhang that serves as a natural shelter. Campfires critical for survival at night.

itinerary.title: Tibb to Naerak
itinerary.desc: 18 km deepest penetration day into the Zanskar gorge to Naerak village (3,400m) — the furthest most Chadar treks reach. A Zanskari village cut off from road access in winter. The canyon walls rise to 1,000m on both sides.

itinerary.title: Naerak to Tibb — Return Journey Begins
itinerary.desc: Return 18 km from Naerak to Tibb along the same frozen river. The ice surface changes each day as new sections freeze and others break.

itinerary.title: Tibb to Chilling — Drive to Leh
itinerary.desc: Final 20 km on the Chadar back to Chilling. Drive 35 km to Leh. Total Chadar trek: approximately 80–100 km on ice over the full itinerary, January–February only.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Jędrzej Koralewski on Pexels

name: Dayara Bugyal
description: One of the most beautiful alpine meadows in the Himalayas, Dayara Bugyal sits at 3,408m in the Uttarkashi district — a vast, undulating grassland stretching for kilometres with an unbroken view of Bandarpoonch (6,316m), Black Peak (Kalanag), Srikanth, and the Gangotri peaks. An all-season trek: lush green in monsoon, golden in autumn, snow-blanketed in winter. Base camp is Raithal village (2,286m) near Bhatwari, 183 km from Dehradun.

overview.location: Dayara Bugyal (3,408m) is one of the largest and most accessible alpine meadows in Uttarakhand, situated in Uttarkashi district at the head of the Bhagirathi valley. The rolling plateau extends over 28 sq km above the treeline, covered in wildflowers from May to June. Base village is Raithal (2,286m) near Bhatwari, 180 km northeast of Dehradun. The Bandarpoonch massif (6,316m) and Black Peak (Kalanag, 6,387m) dominate the northern skyline.
overview.history: Dayara Bugyal is part of the ancient shepherd grazing circuits of the Garhwal Himalayas. Van Gujjar and local Garhwali communities have brought their flocks to these meadows for centuries during summer transhumance. The 2014 Uttarakhand High Court order WPPIL 123/2014 specifically protects these bugyals — overnight camping is banned on the meadow surface to protect the fragile alpine grassland. The bugyal is also the venue of the annual Butter Festival (Makhan Holi / Andhuri Utsav) every August, where villagers from Raithal, Barsu, and surrounding areas celebrate with traditional Garhwali music and the ritual smearing of butter and curd.
