overview.length: 21 km round trip over 5 days from Raithal base camp. Route: Raithal (2,286m) → Gui (2,935m, 5 km) → Dayara Top (3,750m, 8 km) → back to Gui → Raithal (5 km). Total elevation gain from Raithal to Dayara Top: 1,464m. Single campsite at Gui (forest clearing, peak views). Summit day is a long 13 km round trip from Gui — start early.
overview.temperature: Apr–Jun: 5°C–18°C; wildflower season — Primula, Potentilla, and orchid species carpet the meadow. Sep–Oct: 0°C–12°C; clear skies and golden light. Nov–Mar: –5°C to 2°C; the bugyal fills with snow — beautiful in winter. Monsoon (Jul–Aug): Lush but overcast.
overview.fitness: Easy to moderate. Suitable for beginners with basic fitness. The elevation gain is gradual through forested trails and well-maintained paths. No technical terrain anywhere on the route. Altitude of 3,408m is manageable for most trekkers without significant acclimatisation concerns. Children above 8 years can generally complete this trek with proper pacing.

permitInfo.type: Forest Entry Permit
permitInfo.where: Raithal village check-post or Uttarkashi Forest Range office
permitInfo.fee: ₹150–250 per person per day (Indian nationals); ₹600 per day (foreigners)
permitInfo.note: Falls within Uttarkashi Forest Division. Entry permit issued at village check-post on arrival. Bugyal camping ban (Uttarakhand HC order) applies — camp at designated sites off-meadow at Gui or Chilapada. Insurance and medical fitness increasingly required (Uttarkashi district practice).
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to all nationalities with forest permit

itinerary.title: Dehradun to Raithal Village
itinerary.desc: Drive from Dehradun via Mussoorie, Suwakholi, Moryana Top, Uttarkashi, and Bhatwari to Raithal village (2,286m) — the base camp for Dayara Bugyal. 183 km, 7–8 hours. The drive follows the Bhagirathi river from Uttarkashi onward; the Gangotri range appears near Moryana Top. Raithal is a traditional Garhwali village with basic guesthouses and homestays. This is the last point with ATM access — Uttarkashi town. Evening briefing with your trek leader. Acclimatise overnight.

itinerary.title: Raithal to Gui Campsite
itinerary.desc: Trek begins at the Raithal entry gate. The 5 km trail climbs steadily through oak (kharsu), maple, rhododendron, and Himalayan cherry forest. You pass the Nag Devta temple and a small water point on the way up. Above a clearing called Ubaru ki Darali, the forest deepens and the trail narrows. Gui campsite (2,935m) sits in a grassy clearing surrounded by dense forest — views of Srikanth peak, and the Gangotri I, II, and III peaks are visible from the thatch. Sunset at Gui is exceptional. Afternoon side trip option: Gui Lake, a small frozen lake near the campsite worth exploring.

itinerary.title: Gui → Dayara Bugyal → Dayara Top → Gui
itinerary.desc: The summit day. Start early from Gui. The trail climbs steeply through dense oak and rhododendron forest, passing through Chilapada (3,094m) — a rain shelter at the treeline edge. Within 90 minutes the forest opens completely and the vast meadow of Dayara Bugyal (3,408m) unfolds before you. Shepherd huts (chaanis) dot the meadow edge; in summer wildflowers carpet the ground, in winter it is a vast snowfield. Trek across the full length of the meadow to Dayara Top (3,750m) — a steep final push to the highest viewpoint with a sweeping 360° panorama of Bandarpoonch (6,316m), Black Peak / Kalanag (6,387m), Srikanth, Jaonli, Draupadi Ka Danda I & II, and the entire Gangotri massif. Optional: descend the far side to Barnala Tal, a glacial lake set in the open bugyal. Return to Gui campsite for the night.

itinerary.title: Gui to Raithal — Drive to Dehradun
itinerary.desc: Early breakfast and morning descent from Gui campsite back to Raithal (5 km, 3–4 hours) through the oak and rhododendron forest. Arrive Raithal by late morning. Drive 183 km from Raithal to Dehradun via Bhatwari, Uttarkashi, Chinyalisaur, and Mussoorie. Lunch stop in Uttarkashi. Reach Dehradun by 7:30–8:00 pm.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Ankit Lakhiwal on Pexels

name: Dodital Trek
description: A forest and lake trek to Dodital — a pristine high-altitude lake at 3,024m believed to be the birthplace of Lord Ganesha. The lake is home to the rare Himalayan brown trout and surrounded by dense oak, rhododendron, and maple forest. The optional extension to Darwa Pass (4,150m) opens panoramic views of the Gangotri and Bandarpoonch peaks. Rich in birdlife and mythology.

overview.location: Dodital (3,310m) is a serene alpine lake in a dense mixed forest in Uttarkashi district, Uttarakhand. 'Dodi' refers to the golden mahseer fish (Tor putitora) that inhabit the lake — considered sacred and protected. The lake is surrounded by oak, deodar, and rhododendron forest with views of Darwa Top (4,120m) above. The approach is from Agoda or Sangamchatti village (1,800m) on the Assi Ganga river, 24 km from Uttarkashi. The route continues beyond to Darwa Top, from which Bandarpoonch and Swargarohini are visible.
overview.history: Dodital is traditionally the birthplace of Ganesha — the elephant-headed son of Shiva and Parvati — an unusual and locally significant legend. A Ganesha temple on the lakeshore is the spiritual focus of the site. The mahseer fish in the lake are considered sacred and must not be harmed — villagers regard them as divine guardians. The surrounding forest has been a pilgrimage corridor from the Ganges plains to Yamunotri and Gangotri for centuries.
overview.length: 22 km over 3–4 days, Sangamchatti return. Total elevation gain approximately 1,510m. The trail is continuous through enchanting forest all the way to the lake. Optional extension to Darwa Top (4,120m) adds 5 km and 810m of elevation gain with a sweeping Himalayan panorama. Agoda village above the lake is a final inhabited settlement before the high forest.
overview.temperature: Mar–Jun: 5°C–20°C; the best season — wildflowers below and clear skies. Sep–Nov: 0°C–15°C; clear and dry with autumn colours in the forest. Monsoon (Jul–Aug): Lush and green but rainy. Winter: –5°C to 5°C; trail icy but accessible with caution.
overview.fitness: Easy to moderate. The forest trail is well-marked and continuously interesting. No technical terrain. Suitable for families with children above 10 years for the lake. The Darwa Top extension substantially increases the physical demand. 4 weeks of regular walking is sufficient preparation for the lake objective.

permitInfo.type: Forest Entry Permit + Sanctuary Entry
permitInfo.where: Agora/Sangamchatti check-post (Uttarkashi Forest Range)
permitInfo.fee: ₹150–200 per person (Indian); ₹600 (foreigner) per day
permitInfo.note: The Dodital route falls within the Assi Ganga wildlife zone under Uttarkashi Forest Division. Permit issued at Sangamchatti or Agora check-post at trailhead. Bugyal camping rules apply at higher elevations. Uttarkashi district practice: insurance and medical fitness increasingly verified. Carry multiple ID sets.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to all nationalities with standard forest permit

itinerary.title: Rishikesh / Dehradun to Uttarkashi
itinerary.desc: Drive from Rishikesh to Uttarkashi (165 km, 5–6 hours) along the Bhagirathi gorge — one of Uttarakhand's most scenic highways. Uttarkashi is a major Garhwal town and the pilgrim hub for Gangotri. Stock up on supplies.

itinerary.title: Uttarkashi to Sangamchatti — Trek to Agoda
itinerary.desc: Drive 22 km from Uttarkashi to Sangamchatti (1,700m) — the road end and official trek start. Trek 6 km to Agoda village (2,400m) through terraced fields and oak forest along the Assi Ganga stream.

itinerary.title: Agoda to Dodital Lake
itinerary.desc: 8 km from Agoda through dense mixed forest of oak, maple, and rhododendron to Dodital lake (3,310m / 10,860 ft). Dodital is a high-altitude lake famous as the mythological birthplace of Lord Ganesha and home to the rare Himalayan golden mahseer fish. The GMVN rest house and forest campsite are on the lake shore.

itinerary.title: Dodital — Darwa Pass Exploration
itinerary.distance: 8 km round trip to Darwa Pass
itinerary.desc: Optional day hike 4 km to Darwa Pass (4,150m / 13,615 ft) — an open ridge with sweeping views of Bandarpoonch (6,316m), Kalanag (Black Peak, 6,387m), and Gangotri peaks. Return to Dodital.

itinerary.title: Dodital to Sangamchatti — Drive to Rishikesh
itinerary.distance: 14 km descent + 22 km drive + 165 km road
itinerary.desc: Descend 14 km from Dodital to Sangamchatti (8 km to Agoda + 6 km to Sangamchatti). Drive 22 km to Uttarkashi, then 165 km to Rishikesh.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Pawan Sehgal on Pexels

name: Deoriatal Chandrashila
description: A double-summit showcase that begins at the fairy-tale Deoriatal lake — its surface perfectly reflecting the Chaukhamba massif — before ascending through Chopta meadows to Tungnath (3,680m), the world's highest Shiva temple, and culminating at the Chandrashila summit (4,090m) with one of the broadest Himalayan panoramas in Uttarakhand. Nanda Devi, Trishul, Kedarnath, Bandarpoonch all visible in a single sweep.

overview.location: This two-part trek connects Deoriatal (2,438m) — a mountain lake sacred in the Mahabharata, famous for its reflections of the Chaukhamba massif — with Chandrashila summit (4,000m) above Chopta, both in Rudraprayag district, Uttarakhand. Deoriatal sits above Sari village on the edge of the Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary; Chandrashila rises above Chopta meadow (2,680m) and the ancient Tungnath temple. The two sites are 15 km apart by road.
overview.history: Deoriatal is mentioned in the Mahabharata — it is the lake where the Yaksha (a nature spirit) posed his famous moral riddles to the Pandavas. The name 'Devaria Tal' means 'divine lake' in Garhwali. Chandrashila ('Moon Rock') above Tungnath is named for its luminous appearance under moonlight. Tungnath itself is one of the Panch Kedars — five sacred manifestations of Shiva built by the Pandavas — and is attributed to be over 1,000 years old.
overview.length: Deoriatal: 5 km round-trip from Sari village (1.5–2 hours). Chandrashila: 9 km from Chopta via Tungnath (5–6 hours round-trip). Combined as a 3–4 day trip including transfers: approximately 25 km trekking total. Total elevation gain across both sections: approximately 2,100m. Separately, each section is a highly rewarding half-day to day outing.
overview.temperature: Mar–Apr: Rhododendron bloom; –2°C to 15°C; possible snow near summit. May–Jun: 5°C–20°C; pleasant at all altitudes. Sep–Nov: 0°C–12°C; the clearest reflections at Deoriatal; best summit views from Chandrashila. Dec–Feb: –5°C to 5°C; snow on both sections; Chopta road may be closed — call ahead.
overview.fitness: Easy to moderate. Deoriatal is accessible for most adults and children above 8 years. Chandrashila summit gains 1,320m over 5 km from Chopta — manageable for fit trekkers but demanding for those unacclimatised to 4,000m. Suitable as a combined trip for moderately fit families. The 360° summit panorama (Kedarnath, Trishul, Nanda Devi, Chaukhamba, Bandarpoonch) makes every step worthwhile.

permitInfo.type: Forest Entry Permit + Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary Entry
permitInfo.where: Sari village check-post (Deoriatal gate) and Chopta Forest Range
permitInfo.fee: ₹150 per person (Indian); ₹600 (foreigner). Tungnath temple: ₹50 puja donation
permitInfo.note: Deoriatal is within Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary. Day-use permit at Sari gate. Chopta is a buffer zone — camping at designated Chopta sites only (bugyal camping ban applies above Tungnath). Uttarkashi/Chamoli district practice: medical fitness verified for Chandrashila summit. Temple timings: Tungnath opens May–Nov.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to all nationalities; sanctuary permit required

itinerary.title: Rishikesh to Sari Village
itinerary.desc: Drive from Rishikesh (pick up 7 AM) to Sari village (1,997m) via Devprayag, Rudraprayag, and Ukhimath. 190 km, 7–8 hours. Sari is the gateway to Deoriatal lake. Registration, health screening, and document verification begins at 4 PM.

itinerary.title: Sari to Deoriatal Lake
itinerary.desc: 4.1 km climb from Sari (2,000m) to Deoriatal lake (2,438m). A short but steep trail through dense rhododendron and oak forest. Altitude gain: 1,450 ft. Deoriatal is a serene high-altitude lake with perfect reflections of the Chaukhamba massif on clear mornings — one of the most photographed lake views in Uttarakhand.

itinerary.title: Deoriatal to Chopta via Rohini Bugyal
itinerary.desc: 9.1 km trail from Deoriatal (2,438m) to Chopta (2,680m / 8,792 ft) via a rocky forest path. Altitude loss then gain. The route briefly passes through Rohini Bugyal. Chopta is a small meadow hamlet — India's mini Switzerland — with a cluster of dhabas and the famous Tungnath temple above.

itinerary.title: Summit Day — Chopta to Chandrashila via Tungnath, Descent to Ukhimath
itinerary.distance: 13 km (5.4 km ascent + 7.6 km descent to Ukhimath)
itinerary.time: 7–8 hrs trek + 1.5 hrs drive to Rishikesh
itinerary.desc: Pre-dawn start from Chopta. 3.5 km steep paved trail to Tungnath temple (3,680m / 12,073 ft) — the highest Shiva temple in the world, 3rd of the Panch Kedar. Then 1.9 km to Chandrashila summit (3,672m / 12,083 ft) — 360° panorama of Kedarnath (6,940m), Chaukhamba (7,138m), Neelkanth (6,596m), and Nanda Devi (7,816m). Descend 7.6 km via Baniyakund trail to Ukhimath. Drive 21 km from Ukhimath, then 190 km to Rishikesh. Total trek: 13 km.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Naveen Rawat on Pexels

name: Gaumukh Tapovan
description: A spiritual and visually staggering trek to the source of the Ganges. The Gaumukh glacier snout, where the sacred river emerges from an ice cave, sits at 3,892m. Above it, a steep moraine climb leads to the Tapovan meadow (4,463m) — a grassy shelf suspended beneath the vertical walls of Mt. Shivling (6,543m), Meru (6,660m), and the Bhagirathi peaks. One of India's most iconic trekking destinations.

overview.location: Gaumukh (3,892m) — 'Cow's Mouth' — is the glacier snout of the Gangotri Glacier and the primary source of the Bhagirathi River (upper Ganga) in Uttarkashi district. Tapovan (4,463m) is a hanging meadow suspended 2.5 hours above the glacier, directly at the base of Mt. Shivling (6,543m), Meru (6,660m), and the three Bhagirathi peaks. Both sites are within Gangotri National Park, 18–28 km from Gangotri town (3,048m).
overview.history: Gaumukh is among the holiest sites in Hinduism — the Ganga goddess is worshipped here at her source, and pilgrims have been making the journey since at least the 7th century CE when Adi Shankaracharya documented his visit. The Gangotri glacier has retreated over 20 km in the past 200 years due to climate change — when the Gangotri temple was built in the 18th century, the glacier extended to the town. Tapovan has been a base for yogis and sadhus meditating in isolation for centuries, and gained global fame when Conrad Anker, Jimmy Chin, and Renan Ozturk filmed their 2011 Meru Shark's Fin ascent here.
overview.length: Gangotri to Gaumukh and back: 18 km over 2 days. Gangotri to Tapovan: 28 km over 4–5 days (includes a steep 2.5-hour moraine scramble above the glacier). Total elevation gain Gangotri–Tapovan: approximately 1,415m. Bhojbasa (3,792m) at 7 km from Gangotri is the natural overnight camp midway.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–18°C at Gaumukh; –2°C to 8°C at Tapovan. Sep–Oct: 0°C–12°C at Gaumukh; –5°C to 5°C at Tapovan; clearest skies. Night temperatures at Tapovan reach –15°C even in September — a four-season sleeping bag is non-negotiable. Gangotri NP closes November–April.
overview.fitness: Moderate (Gaumukh) to hard (Tapovan). The 9 km walk to Gaumukh is accessible to reasonably fit trekkers. The moraine scramble above the glacier to Tapovan is steep, loose, and demanding — requiring fitness and sure-footedness. High altitude of 4,463m at Tapovan requires proper acclimatisation. Preparation: 8–10 weeks of cardio and hill walking for Tapovan; 4–6 weeks sufficient for Gaumukh only.

permitInfo.type: Gangotri National Park Trekking Permit
permitInfo.where: Permit office above the bus stand in Gangotri town (DFO Uttarkashi / Gangotri NP range office)
permitInfo.fee: ₹150/day Indian; ₹600/day foreigner. Camera fee ₹200. Daily cap: 150 trekkers per day for Tapovan
permitInfo.note: Mandatory NP permit for both Gaumukh and Tapovan sections. Permits checked at the NP gate 4 km above Gangotri town. Uttarkashi district now requires trek insurance for all trekkers, and medical fitness certificate for Tapovan (4,463m+). Trekkers 50+ need medical certificate even for Gaumukh. Carry 2 sets of all documents. Drones banned inside national park. No camping inside core NP zone without forest dept clearance.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to foreigners with NP permit. Some inner corridors beyond Tapovan may require additional clearance.

itinerary.title: Rishikesh to Gangotri
itinerary.desc: Drive from Rishikesh via Tehri, Uttarkashi, and Harsil to Gangotri (3,048m). 250 km, 9–10 hours. Mandatory registration at Gangotri National Park entry gate. Maximum 150 trekkers/day permitted to Gaumukh–Tapovan (government regulation).

itinerary.title: Gangotri to Bhojbasa via Chirbasa
itinerary.distance: 14 km (9 km to Chirbasa + 5 km to Bhojbasa)
itinerary.desc: Trek starts at the Gangotri temple gate. 9 km on a well-trodden path along the Bhagirathi gorge to Chirbasa (3,600m / 11,811 ft) — so named for the chirr pine trees. Rest here. Then 5 km to Bhojbasa (3,790m), which sits at the end of the treeline (the last bhoj / birch trees). GMVN huts and a basic ashram available at Bhojbasa. Total: 14 km.

itinerary.title: Bhojbasa to Gaumukh Glacier — Climb to Tapovan
itinerary.distance: 8 km (4 km to Gaumukh + 4 km to Tapovan)
itinerary.desc: 4 km from Bhojbasa to Gaumukh glacier snout (3,892m) — the source of the Ganges, literally 'cow's mouth'. The glacier has receded significantly. Then a steep 4 km scramble up the lateral moraine and rocky flank to Tapovan meadow (4,460m) — a flat, green meadow at the base of Shivling peak (6,543m). Shivling's sheer granite faces rise directly from the meadow edge — an incomparable view.

itinerary.title: Tapovan Exploration / Acclimatisation
itinerary.desc: Rest day at Tapovan. Optional explorations: walk toward Meru Glacier base, or toward the Khara Patthar ridge for close views of Shivling, Meru (6,660m), and Bhagirathi peaks. This is base camp country for major Himalayan expeditions.

itinerary.title: Tapovan to Gangotri — Return Drive
itinerary.desc: Descend 22 km from Tapovan to Gangotri (4 km to Gaumukh + 4 km to Bhojbasa + 14 km to Gangotri). Drive 250 km back to Rishikesh. Long day — start Tapovan by 5 AM.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Rishu Bhosale on Pexels

name: Kedartal
description: A demanding high-altitude lake trek to the sacred Kedartal — the Lake of Shiva — at 4,750m, source of the Kedar Ganga River. The trail from Gangotri involves steep unstable terrain, boulder fields, and two dramatic cliff faces. The reward is a hidden glacial lake ringed by Thalay Sagar (6,904m), Jogin peaks, and Bhrigupanth — a jewel in a savage setting. Not for beginners.

overview.location: Kedartal (4,750m) — 'Lake of Shiva' — is a glacial lake in a steep rock basin northwest of Gangotri town in Uttarkashi district, within Gangotri National Park. The lake is the source of the Kedar Ganga, which joins the Bhagirathi at Gangotri. The lake is encircled by Thalay Sagar (6,904m) — one of the most technically demanding peaks in the world — and the Jogin group (6,465m–6,931m). The trail is widely regarded as the most technically demanding standard trek in Uttarakhand.
overview.history: Kedartal is sacred to Shiva — 'Kedar' is his high-Himalayan domain, and the lake is associated with his divine presence in the mountains. The Kedar Ganga joining the Bhagirathi at Gangotri makes this glacial lake an indirect source of the sacred Ganga. The lake was known to pilgrims long before mountaineers arrived. It gained wider attention when British and Japanese expeditions documented the extraordinary northwest face of Thalay Sagar in the 1970s–80s — now considered one of Asia's great technical climbs.
overview.length: 32 km round-trip over 5–6 days from Gangotri town. Total elevation gain approximately 1,702m. The trail is not a standard walking path — it crosses two cliff sections with fixed ropes, extensive boulder fields, and loose scree above 4,000m. The fixed rope sections require upper-body engagement and confidence at height. Not suitable for casual trekkers.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 0°C–12°C at the lake; trail open from May 1. Sep–Oct: –5°C to 8°C; best for visibility and stable conditions; lake may be partially frozen. Gangotri NP closes October–April. Night temperatures at the lake can reach –15°C in October.
overview.fitness: Hard. Considered the most physically and mentally demanding standard trek in Uttarakhand. The fixed rope sections require upper body strength and confidence. Boulder-field navigation demands sure-footedness, agility, and sustained concentration. Altitude of 4,750m is serious — proper acclimatisation at Gangotri required. Minimum prior experience: 5+ multi-day treks including at least one above 4,000m. Preparation: 12 weeks of intensive training including upper-body work.

permitInfo.type: Gangotri National Park Trekking Permit
permitInfo.where: Permit office in Gangotri town (same as Gaumukh office)
permitInfo.fee: ₹150/day Indian; ₹600/day foreigner
permitInfo.note: Kedartal falls within Gangotri National Park. Mandatory NP permit from Gangotri permit office; checks at the NP gate. Uttarkashi district requires insurance and medical fitness certificate for this route — enforced rigorously as the terrain is extremely hazardous (loose boulder trail with two steep cliff sections). Guide mandatory; solo trekking strongly discouraged. Carry 2 sets of all permits.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to foreigners with NP permit and guide

itinerary.title: Rishikesh to Gangotri
itinerary.desc: Drive from Rishikesh via Tehri, Uttarkashi, and Harsil to Gangotri (3,048m) — the sacred temple town and glacier gateway. 250 km, 9–10 hours. Gangotri temple is the spiritual source of the Ganges. Register at the forest office for the Kedartal trek permit.

itinerary.title: Gangotri to Bhojkharak
itinerary.desc: 8 km from Gangotri along the Kedar Ganga stream valley. A steep, relentless climb through mixed forest, then scrub and moraines to Bhojkharak (3,790m). The trail is rocky and demanding. Bhojkharak means 'birch plateau' — sparse birch trees at the treeline. The Jogin massif becomes visible.

itinerary.title: Bhojkharak to Kedartal
itinerary.desc: 7 km from Bhojkharak over boulder fields and moraines to Kedartal (4,750m) — a high-altitude glacial lake fed by the Thalaysagar (6,904m) and Jogin massif glaciers. The lake's waters are a brilliant turquoise-blue. The surrounding cirque of peaks includes Thalaysagar, Jogin I-III, Brigupanth, and Meru. This is one of the highest and most spectacular glacial lakes in Uttarakhand.

itinerary.title: Kedartal to Gangotri — Return Drive
itinerary.desc: Descend 15 km from Kedartal (7 km to Bhojkharak + 8 km to Gangotri). Drive 250 km back to Rishikesh via Harsil, Uttarkashi, Tehri.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Balaji Srinivasan on Pexels

name: Rupin Pass
description: One of India's most technically satisfying treks — a crossover from Uttarakhand to Himachal Pradesh via the dramatic Rupin Pass (4,650m). The trail passes through the cliff-perched village of Sarahan, a frozen waterfall section, the Rupin River gorge, and a final steep snow slope to the pass. The descent into Spiti-adjacent terrain from the Kinnauri side is a complete landscape transformation.

overview.location: Rupin Pass (4,650m) connects the Supin Valley of Uttarkashi, Uttarakhand with the Baspa Valley of Kinnaur, Himachal Pradesh — one of the most scenic crossover treks in the Indian Himalayas. The trail starts at Dhaula village (2,320m) on the Tons River and passes through a unique series of hanging waterfalls, 'upper waterfall' camp (a dramatically situated campsite beneath a 100m waterfall), and open snowfields before the pass crossing. The descent into Kinnaur reveals a completely different geological and cultural world.
overview.history: The Rupin Pass was historically a trade and movement corridor for the Kinnauri and Supin Valley communities. The Kinnauri culture on the Himachal side has deep Tibetan Buddhist influences — the Baspa Valley is dotted with ancient gompas and wooden temples. The pass appears in British-era Survey of India maps. The trek became one of India's most celebrated routes after trekking organizations began documenting its unusual landscape in the 2000s.
overview.length: 52 km over 8 days from Dhaula to Sangla (Himachal Pradesh). The trek is a one-way crossing requiring vehicle drop/pickup at both ends. Total elevation gain approximately 2,330m. The pass crossing day involves 5–6 hours of steep ascent on snow and scree — the single most demanding day of the trek.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 0°C–15°C; snow on the pass still significant — the waterfall sections are dramatic with snowmelt volume. Sep–Oct: –2°C to 10°C; best visibility and most stable conditions. Pass closes November–April under deep snow.
overview.fitness: Hard. One of the most technically demanding standard treks in Uttarakhand. Crampons and trekking poles are required for the snow sections near the pass. Prior experience on high-altitude crossover treks is essential. Altitude of 4,650m is serious. Preparation: 10–12 weeks of intensive training. Guide or organized operator is strongly recommended.

permitInfo.type: Forest Entry Permit (Uttarakhand side) + No formal permit (Himachal side for most sections)
permitInfo.where: Dhaula village check-post (start, Uttarkashi Forest Division); Himachal entry is open
permitInfo.fee: ₹150–200 per person per day (Indian) at Dhaula check-post
permitInfo.note: The Uttarkashi side requires a forest entry/trek permit from the Dhaula check-post before beginning. The Himachal Pradesh side (post-pass descent toward Sangla/Chitkul) is largely open except Kinnaur Inner Line zones — verify Kinnaur ILP status if your route continues beyond Sangla toward restricted zones. Uttarkashi district practice: insurance required. High risk pass — guided groups recommended.
permitInfo.foreigners: Foreigners open on Uttarakhand side with forest permit. Himachal/Kinnaur sections may have ILP requirements for foreigners.

itinerary.title: Shimla to Jiskun
itinerary.distance: 85 km from Rohru (total ~170 km from Shimla)
itinerary.time: 5 hrs drive from Rohru (pick up 8 AM Shimla)
itinerary.desc: Drive from Shimla to Rohru (115 km), then 85 km from Rohru to Jiskun over the spectacular Chainsheel Pass (3,350m). The drive itself is extraordinary — the Chainsheel valley road runs at 11,000 ft through vast grasslands. Jiskun (1,890m) is the base camp. Stepping out of the car you see Jhaka village hanging impossibly on the mountainside above.

itinerary.title: Jiskun to Jakha to Saruwas Thatch (Udaknal)
itinerary.distance: 5 km (Jiskun to Sewa / Jakha area) + 8.1 km to Udaknal
itinerary.camp: Saruwas Thatch / Udaknal meadow by river
itinerary.desc: Trek begins from Jiskun post office. 5 km through traditional Himachali villages of Jakha and Sewa (state border bridge between HP and Uttarakhand). Then 8.1 km along the Rupin river through ancient fir forest, past dwarf rhododendron meadows of Buras Kandi, arriving at Saruwas Thatch / Udaknal (3,140m). First thundering view of the Rupin Waterfall (1,500 ft drop). Total: ~13 km.

itinerary.title: Udaknal to Dhanderas Thatch (Lower Waterfall)
itinerary.desc: Short but spectacular 3.5 km day through small meadows bursting with wildflowers in summer. Trail culminates at Dhanderas Thatch (3,566m) — the iconic U-shaped glacial valley camp at the base of the roaring 1,500 ft Rupin Waterfall. Hundreds of waterfalls stream down the valley walls. Acclimatise here.

itinerary.title: Acclimatisation Day at Dhanderas Thatch
itinerary.desc: Rest day at the lower waterfall camp. Explore the valley, cross snow bridges over the Rupin, and mentally prepare for the steep days ahead. Mandatory for safe altitude adaptation.

itinerary.title: Dhanderas Thatch to Upper Waterfall Camp
itinerary.camp: Upper Waterfall Camp (large basin below pass)
itinerary.desc: 3 km of switchback climbs over three tiers of the Rupin Waterfall — on snow bridges and patches in summer. A series of steep zigzags brings you to the Upper Waterfall Camp (4,080m) — a vast mountain basin where icy flanks surround you and hundreds of snowmelt streams join to form the Rupin. First view of the intimidating Rupin Gully above.

itinerary.title: Upper Waterfall to Rupin Pass — Descent to Ronti Gad
itinerary.desc: The biggest day. From Upper Waterfall, traverse the vast snowfields of Rata Pheri (3–4 hrs). Then the notorious Rupin Gully — a steep snow couloir requiring care and poles/crampons. Crest the pass at 4,650m / 15,250 ft (not the often-cited 15,279 ft variant — both altitudes quoted). Then a long, multi-hour descent through Kinnaur meadows to Ronti Gad (4,003m) by the Sangla Kanda grasslands. Total: 10–11 hours.

itinerary.title: Ronti Gad to Sangla via Sangla Kanda
itinerary.desc: 8 km descent from Ronti Gad through the vast shepherd meadows of Sangla Kanda (3,480m) with commanding views of the Kinnaur Kailash range, then a long 1,000m drop to Sangla town (2,680m) in the Baspa valley. A jeep is arranged from Sangla to drive back to Shimla or Chandigarh.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Kunal Singh on Pexels

name: Phulara Ridge
description: An offbeat gem in the Sankri belt — the Phulara Ridge walk traverses a high ridge between the Rupin and Supin valleys, with continuous 270° views of the peaks including Swargarohini, Bandarpoonch, and the Black Peak (Kalanag). Unlike valley treks, most of the walking here is above the treeline on an open ridge. Far less crowded than the neighbouring Kedarkantha trail.

overview.location: Phulara Ridge (3,800m) is an elevated ridge walk above the Har Ki Dun valley in Govind Pashu Vihar National Park, Uttarkashi district. The ridge commands a panoramic view from Swargarohini (6,252m) and Bandarpoonch (6,316m) across to the Tons Valley and the Sangla peaks of Himachal Pradesh. The approach starts from Osla village in the Har Ki Dun valley, making it a natural extension or standalone alternative to the Har Ki Dun trek.
overview.history: Phulara Ridge is part of the high-altitude grazing ground above the ancient Jaunsari village of Osla. The name 'Phulara' likely derives from 'phool' (flower) — wildflower meadows carpet the ridge from May to June. Local shepherds have traversed this ridge for generations. The ridge connects minor summits above the Har Ki Dun hanging valley and was popularised as a distinct trekking objective in the 2010s.
overview.length: 45 km over 5–6 days from Sankri, passing through the Har Ki Dun approach. The ridge walk section covers approximately 12 km across the open plateau at 3,800m. Total elevation gain from Sankri approximately 1,880m. Can be combined with the Har Ki Dun valley trek as a circuit for a longer 8–9 day route.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–18°C; wildflower display at its finest. Sep–Oct: 0°C–12°C; clearest ridge views of the year. Winter: –10°C to 0°C; deep snow covers the ridge — possible with a guide. Monsoon: Lush but rainy and misty.
overview.fitness: Moderate. The approach via Har Ki Dun is gradual and well-maintained. The ridge itself requires sustained walking at 3,800m. No technical terrain. Prior experience on multi-day treks is recommended. Good cardiovascular fitness and comfort at altitude are the key requirements. Preparation: 6–8 weeks of cardio and hill walking.

permitInfo.type: Govind Pashu Vihar NP/WLS Forest Entry Permit
permitInfo.where: Sankri check-post / DFO Purola, Uttarkashi Forest Division
permitInfo.fee: ₹150 per day Indian; ₹600 foreigner
permitInfo.note: Falls within or adjacent to the Govind Wildlife Sanctuary buffer zone. Forest entry permit from Sankri check-post. Medical certificate increasingly required at Sankri (2018 precedent for online registration + medical). Bugyal camping ban: no overnight camps on open ridge meadow — use designated off-ridge sites.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to all nationalities

itinerary.title: Dehradun to Sankri
itinerary.desc: Drive from Dehradun (6:30 AM) to Kotgaon / Sankri (195 km, 10–11 hrs) via Mussoorie, Purola, and Mori. Sankri sits in the Govind Wildlife Sanctuary — same base as Kedarkantha. The Phulara Ridge was discovered and put on the map by Indiahikes.

itinerary.title: Sankri to Phulara Ridge
itinerary.desc: 7 km climb from Sankri through deodar and oak forest, then into rhododendron and birch before emerging on the Phulara Ridge (3,150m). This dramatic open ridge runs for kilometres — walking on it feels like being above the world. The ridge is covered in grass and wildflowers from May to October; in winter it is snow-covered. Views of Swargarohini, Bandarpoonch, and the Tons valley below.

itinerary.title: Phulara Ridge Walk — Kalkatti Ridge
itinerary.desc: 8 km walk along the spine of the ridge — undulating, open, and dramatic throughout. The trail alternates between meadow summits and saddles. Views are continuous and unobstructed. The ridge separates the Tons valley (Govind Sanctuary side) from the Supin valley (Har Ki Dun side).

itinerary.title: Ridge Descent to Osla — Trek to Taluka
itinerary.distance: 9 km descent to Osla + 4 km to Taluka / Sankri drive
itinerary.desc: 9 km descent from the ridge down to Osla village in the Har Ki Dun valley (2,590m / 8,500 ft). The descent is steep in places. From Osla, 4 km trek to Taluka road head. Drive to Sankri for the night.

itinerary.title: Sankri to Dehradun — Return Drive
itinerary.desc: Drive back from Sankri/Kotgaon to Dehradun (195 km, 10–11 hrs) via Mori and Mussoorie.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Feyruz Aslanov on Pexels

name: Bali Pass
description: A demanding crossover trek connecting Har Ki Dun valley to the Yamunotri region via Bali Pass (5,360m), one of the highest trekking passes in Uttarakhand. The trail traverses the Govind Wildlife Sanctuary past the sacred Ruinsara Tal lake and over a technical high snow pass with views of Bandarpoonch, Kalanag, Swargarohini, and the Yamuna watershed. Experienced trekkers only.

overview.location: Bali Pass (5,360m) is one of the highest regularly trekked passes in Uttarakhand, connecting the Har Ki Dun valley (Govind Wildlife Sanctuary, Uttarkashi) with the Yamunotri region. The trail crosses the sacred Ruinsara Tal lake (4,025m) before the technical pass ascent. Bandarpoonch (6,316m) and Kalanag (Black Peak, 6,387m) tower above the approach — two of the most majestic peaks in the western Garhwal Himalaya.
overview.history: Bali Pass was a traditional crossing route between the Tons River watershed and the Yamuna watershed, used by shepherds and pilgrims for centuries. Ruinsara Tal en route is held to be the abode of the five Pandavas (Mahabharata). The name 'Bali' is associated with the demon king Bali of Hindu mythology. The pass remains one of the most serious high-altitude trekking challenges in Uttarakhand and is attempted by only a small number of expedition-standard trekking teams each year.
overview.length: 57 km over 8–9 days from Sankri to Janki Chatti (Yamunotri side). The trek is a one-way crossing needing vehicle logistics at both ends. Total elevation gain approximately 3,440m. The pass day from Ruinsara involves 1,335m of steep ascent with technical sections — one of the hardest single days on any Uttarakhand trek.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: Snow on the pass; technically most challenging crossing. Sep: –5°C to 5°C at the pass; –10°C to 8°C at Ruinsara; best conditions. Crampons are needed from May through October. The window is narrow — mid-September to early October is optimal.
overview.fitness: Expert/hard. Crampons and ice axe are required for the pass crossing. Prior experience on technical high-altitude passes is essential. A guide is mandatory. The 5,360m altitude demands serious physiological conditioning and experience with altitude sickness management. Preparation: 12+ weeks of intensive training including scrambling and ideally prior glacier experience.

permitInfo.type: Govind Pashu Vihar National Park / Wildlife Sanctuary Permit
permitInfo.where: Sankri check-post / DFO Purola. Both entry and exit points need to be registered.
permitInfo.fee: ₹150/day Indian; ₹600/day foreigner. Camera fee applicable inside NP.
permitInfo.note: Bali Pass route falls entirely within Govind Pashu Vihar NP/WLS. Mandatory forest/NP permit from Sankri office. Dual registration needed — Har Ki Dun entry at Sankri and exit registration at Yamunotri side (Janki Chatti). Medical certificate mandatory given 5,360m pass elevation. Insurance required (Uttarkashi practice). Technical gear (crampons, poles) advised for pass day. Guide mandatory.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to foreigners with NP permit and registered guide. Inner sanctuary zones may require additional DFO clearance.

itinerary.title: Dehradun to Sankri
itinerary.desc: Drive from Dehradun (195 km, 10–11 hrs) to Kotgaon / Sankri. Same base as Kedarkantha and Har Ki Dun.

itinerary.title: Sankri to Taluka — Trek to Osla
itinerary.distance: 12 km drive to Taluka + 13 km trek to Osla
itinerary.desc: Drive 12 km from Sankri to Taluka. Trek 13 km along the Supin valley: 8.4 km to Kalkatiyadhar, then 5 km to Osla (or alternate via Gangaad: 2.6 km Dharkot–Gangaad descent, 8.4 km Gangaad–Kalkatiyadhar, 5 km to Osla). Osla is the last village on the Har Ki Dun trail.

itinerary.title: Osla to Ruinsara Lake
itinerary.desc: 10 km from Osla through increasingly barren terrain to Ruinsara Tal (3,530m) — a beautiful glacial lake in a high cirque at the base of the Bandarpoonch massif. The Swargarohini peaks (I–IV) surround the basin. The lake is sacred — 'Ruinsara' means 'sacred water from Lord Shiva'.

itinerary.title: Ruinsara to Bali Pass Base Camp
itinerary.desc: 5 km from Ruinsara up the glacier and moraines toward Bali Pass. Camp at ~4,200m in a boulder field or snowfield.

itinerary.title: Bali Pass Crossing — Descent to Yamunotri Side
itinerary.distance: 8 km (pass + descent to Seema or Janki Chatti direction)
itinerary.desc: The crossing day. Steep 3 km ascent to Bali Pass (4,850m / 15,912 ft). The pass gives panoramic views of Bandarpoonch, Swargarohini, Kala Nag (Black Peak), and toward Yamunotri. 5 km descent on the Yamunotri side — very steep, often snow-covered. Camp at upper meadow on Yamunotri side.

itinerary.title: Descent to Janki Chatti / Hanuman Chatti — Drive to Rishikesh
itinerary.desc: 12 km descent from the Yamunotri-side camp through Seema / Phulchatti to Janki Chatti or Hanuman Chatti road head on the Yamunotri Highway. Drive 250 km back to Rishikesh via Barkot and Dehradun.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Ashok J Kshetri on Pexels

name: Pindari Glacier
description: One of the most accessible glacier treks in the Kumaon Himalayas, Pindari Glacier is a 3-km expanse of ice at 3,660m that is the source of the Pindar River. The trail from Loharkhet passes through oak and rhododendron forest, the charming villages of Dhakuri and Khati, and the dramatic moraines of Dwali and Phurkia. Views of Nanda Devi, Nanda Kot, and the Nanda Devi East face accompany the final approach.

overview.location: Pindari Glacier (3,660m) is a 3-km-long glacier in the Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve, Bageshwar district, Kumaon Himalayas. The glacier is the source of the Pindar River, which eventually joins the Alaknanda. The trail from Loharkhet (2,132m) passes through the forest villages of Dhakuri and Khati — one of the most idyllic trailside communities in Kumaon. Nanda Devi (7,816m) and Nanda Kot (6,861m) are visible from the glacier approach. The nearest major town is Bageshwar, accessible from Kathgodam railhead (90 km).
overview.history: The Pindari Glacier was surveyed by the British Survey of India in the 1840s. Historical records show it extended 3 km further down the valley at that time than today — the retreat is a visible measure of Himalayan climate change. The Pindar Valley has been inhabited by the Bhotiya trading community for centuries — before the 1962 border closure they crossed the Traill's Pass to Tibet carrying wool, salt, and grain. The trek became accessible after road construction to Loharkhet in the 1970s and now has a well-developed KMVN (Kumaon Mandal Vikas Nigam) rest house network.
overview.length: 64 km over 7–8 days, Loharkhet to glacier and return. Total elevation gain approximately 1,528m — one of the most gradual and accessible glacier approaches in India. No technical sections. KMVN rest houses at each camp (Dhakuri, Khati, Dwali, Phurkia) mean camping gear is not required.
overview.temperature: Apr–Jun: 5°C–18°C; rhododendron forests in bloom in April — outstanding for flower photography. Sep–Nov: 0°C–15°C; stable, clear weather. Monsoon (Jul–Aug): Heavy rain and leeches. Winter: –5°C to 5°C; trail icy.
overview.fitness: Easy to moderate. One of the most accessible glacier treks in India and ideal for first-time Himalayan glacier visitors. The gradual trail and KMVN facilities make this suitable for families with children above 12 years, older adults with good basic fitness, and those wanting a first genuine Himalayan wilderness experience without technical demands. Preparation: 4–6 weeks of regular walking.

permitInfo.type: Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve Entry Permit + Forest Entry
permitInfo.where: Loharkhet check-post (Bageshwar Forest Division) and Khati village forest office
permitInfo.fee: ₹150/day Indian nationals; ₹600/day foreigners. Camera ₹200.
permitInfo.note: Pindari Glacier falls within the Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve buffer zone. Entry permit from Loharkhet check-post (Bageshwar Forest Division, Kathgodam/Bageshwar side). An additional inner zone clearance is required if going beyond Phurkia toward the Zero Point viewpoint. No permit required from Kathgodam up to Loharkhet. Guide strongly recommended. Family-friendly if all members are reasonably fit.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to all nationalities with standard biosphere reserve permit

itinerary.title: Kathgodam to Khati
itinerary.desc: Drive from Kathgodam via Almora and Bageshwar to Kharkia (225 km, 8 hrs) — the road terminus. Walk 3 km to Khati (2,200m), the last inhabited village and true start of the Pindari trek. Collect permits at Kharkia. Khati has GMVN rest houses and homestays with views of Nanda Kot and Lapsadhura.

itinerary.title: Khati to Dwali
itinerary.desc: 12 km from Khati along the Pindar river to Dwali (2,580m). Trail passes through a landslide zone with views into the Kafni Valley on the left. Dwali is the three-way junction — Kafni Glacier turns south, Sunderdhunga opens west, and Pindari continues east.

itinerary.title: Dwali to Phurkia
itinerary.desc: 8 km from Dwali to Phurkia (3,353m) through dense birch forest with the Pindar River roaring below. The valley narrows and Nanda Kot (6,861m) comes into view. GMVN rest house at Phurkia.

itinerary.title: Phurkia to Pindari Glacier Zero Point — Return to Dwali
itinerary.distance: 6 km to Zero Point + 11 km return
itinerary.desc: 3 km up to the Pindari Glacier Zero Point (3,660m / 12,300 ft) — the viewpoint overlooking the glacier snout below Nanda Kot (6,861m) and Nandakhan. The glacier pours down between sheer rock walls. Return 3 km to Phurkia then 8 km back to Dwali.

itinerary.title: Dwali to Kharkia — Return to Kathgodam
itinerary.desc: Walk 12 km from Dwali to Khati then 3 km to Kharkia. Drive 225 km to Kathgodam via Bageshwar and Almora. Arrive Kathgodam by evening for onward trains.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Prince lakra on Pexels

name: Milam Glacier
description: One of the most remote and rewarding glacier treks in India, following the ancient salt and trade route between India and Tibet along the Gori Ganga Valley. The trail passes through Munsiyari, climbs through the dramatic gorge sections above Rilkot, and opens onto the vast Milam Glacier — 16 km long and one of the largest in the Kumaon Himalayas. The abandoned villages of the upper valley bear testament to the Indo-China border closure of 1962.

overview.location: Milam Glacier (3,870m) is one of the largest glaciers in the Kumaon Himalayas and the source of the Gori Ganga river, in Pithoragarh district close to the Indo-China border. The trek passes through the Milam Valley — a former Bhotiya trade corridor — and the abandoned villages of Rilkot, Burfu, and Martoli, which were thriving settlements before the 1962 border closure. The surrounding peaks — Hardeol (7,151m), Rishi Pahar (6,992m), and Trishul (7,120m) — make this one of the most scenically and historically rich treks in India. Munsiyari (2,200m) is the base.
overview.history: The Milam Valley was the most important trade corridor between Kumaon and Tibet before the 1962 Indo-China war abruptly closed the border. The Bhotiya (Shauka/Rang) community had been trading wool, salt, borax, and grain across the Milam and Unta Dhura passes for centuries — a trade worth significant wealth in pre-modern terms. The 1962 war ended this overnight, and the valley's villages were abandoned as border security restrictions were imposed. The haunting, well-preserved ruins of Martoli are among the most atmospheric abandoned settlements in the Himalayas.
overview.length: 55–70 km over 8–9 days from Munsiyari. Inner Line Permit (ILP) from SDM Munsiyari and ITBP clearance required throughout. The glacier itself extends 16 km from its source — one of the longest accessible glaciers in Kumaon. Total elevation gain approximately 1,670m from Munsiyari.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–18°C at lower camps; 0°C at glacier. Sep–Oct: 0°C–12°C; best visibility and stable weather — the recommended season. Monsoon (Jul–Aug): Accessible but rainy in the lower valley. Winter: Inaccessible — permits restricted and snow closes the trail.
overview.fitness: Moderate to hard. The ILP requirement and remote nature demand self-sufficiency. Altitude reaches 3,870m at the glacier. Long daily distances. Prior multi-day Himalayan trek experience is recommended. Carry medical certificate and insurance documentation for the ITBP checkpoints.

permitInfo.type: Inner Line Permit (ILP) + Forest Entry Permit + ITBP Registration
permitInfo.where: SDM office at Munsiyari (Pithoragarh district) for ILP; Forest permit at Lilam check-post; ITBP registration at checkpoints en route
permitInfo.fee: ILP: nominal administrative fee; Forest permit ₹150/day Indian; ₹600 foreigner
permitInfo.note: Milam Glacier lies in a border-sensitive valley near the Line of Actual Control (LAC) with China. Indian nationals require ILP from SDM Munsiyari (apply in person or via district portal). Foreigners face restrictions on the upper valley sections — verify current rules with DM Pithoragarh before planning. ITBP posts check permits and document trekker groups along the route. Carry multiple sets of all documents. Medical fitness and insurance required in practice.
permitInfo.foreigners: Restricted — foreigners may be limited to sections up to specific checkpoints; DM Pithoragarh clearance required. Check current rules.

itinerary.title: Kathgodam to Munsiyari
itinerary.desc: Drive to the beautiful mountain town of Munsiyari — base for several Kumaon treks. Obtain ILP from the SDM office (open weekdays). Munsiyari has remarkable panoramic views of the Panchachuli massif (five summits).

itinerary.title: Munsiyari to Lilam
itinerary.desc: Trek begins down and then up the Gori Ganga gorge. Collect forest permits at the Lilam check-post.

itinerary.title: Lilam to Bugdiyar
itinerary.desc: Impressive gorge section — sheer rock walls and roaring river. The trail clings to the cliff face above the Gori Ganga in places.

itinerary.title: Bugdiyar to Rilkot
itinerary.desc: Enter the broader upper valley. Evidence of the old trade route becomes visible — stone-paved sections and porter shelters. ITBP checkpoint at Rilkot — document check.

itinerary.title: Rilkot to Milam Village
itinerary.desc: Arrive at Milam — a large stone-built village that was entirely abandoned after the 1962 border closure but is now partially resettled. The atmosphere is haunting and magnificent.

itinerary.title: Milam Village to Glacier Snout
itinerary.desc: Trek to the snout of Milam Glacier — 16 km long and framed by Hardeol (7,151m), Trishul, and the peaks of the upper Munsiyari basin. An extraordinary wilderness setting.

itinerary.title: Return to Munsiyari — Return to Kathgodam
itinerary.desc: Reverse the approach over 3 days back to Munsiyari, then drive to Kathgodam. Total return from Munsiyari to Kathgodam railhead is approximately 8–9 hours.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Prince lakra on Pexels

name: Pangarchulla Peak
description: The ultimate beginner peak climb in the Garhwal Himalayas — Pangarchulla (4,700m) is a trekking summit that extends the classic Kuari Pass route into a genuine peak conquest. The summit day involves a sustained snow climb to the top ridge from where Nanda Devi, Kamet, Dronagiri, Trishul, and the entire panorama of Kuari Pass is visible — all at once, from above. No technical mountaineering needed with the right conditions.

overview.location: Pangarchulla (3,912m) is a trekking summit above the Kuari Pass trail in Chamoli district, Uttarakhand. Reached from the same base as the Kuari Pass (Auli or Dhak village near Joshimath), it offers extraordinary close views of Dronagiri (7,066m), Kamet (7,756m), Nanda Ghunti, and the Nanda Devi massif. The peak sits on the rim of the Nanda Devi Biosphere buffer zone and provides a higher, more panoramic vantage than the Kuari Pass itself.
overview.history: Pangarchulla is not named in classical Himalayan mountaineering literature — it was identified and developed as a trekking peak in the 2000s–2010s as part of the growth of guided Himalayan trekking in Garhwal. The area has been part of the Garhwali pastoral circuit for centuries, with shepherds grazing flocks on the high meadows below the peak. The Joshimath area around it has deep religious significance as the winter seat of the Badrinath temple administration.
overview.length: 40–50 km over 6–7 days, Dhak village return. Total elevation gain from Joshimath level approximately 2,600m. The summit push from the high camp involves a 400m steep snow ascent requiring an early 4–5 AM start. The Kuari Pass section of the route can be combined for a longer circuit.
overview.temperature: Mar–Jun: 0°C to 15°C; snow on the summit approach — the most popular season. Sep–Oct: –5°C to 10°C; clearest views. Nov–Feb: –15°C to 0°C at camp; deep snow — winter route for experienced trekkers only. Joshimath medical check practice applies.
overview.fitness: Hard. Suitable for experienced trekkers who have completed similar routes (Kuari Pass or equivalent). Summit day involves steep snow climbing — crampons and trekking poles required. Altitude of 3,912m plus the technical approach demands good fitness and altitude experience. Preparation: 10–12 weeks of training including loaded hill walks.

permitInfo.type: Forest Entry Permit (same zone as Kuari Pass) + Local guide mandatory
permitInfo.where: Joshimath Forest Range office / Dhak village check-post
permitInfo.fee: ₹150/day Indian; ₹600/day foreigner
permitInfo.note: Follows the Kuari Pass/Dhak–Auli corridor. Joshimath administration has required on-spot medical fitness checks at the Government hospital for Pangarchulla-level treks since 2024 (district practice — confirm locally). Medical certificate and trek insurance mandatory in practice. Guide is essential for the summit push. Microspikes/crampons and trekking poles required on the summit day snow slope.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to all nationalities with forest permit and registered guide

itinerary.title: Rishikesh to Auli / Dhak
itinerary.desc: Drive from Rishikesh via Rudraprayag, Chamoli, and Joshimath to Auli or Dhak village (255 km, 9–10 hrs). Auli is the famous Garhwal ski resort; Dhak is the actual trek starting village, 5 km beyond Auli.

itinerary.title: Dhak to Gulling
itinerary.desc: 7 km trek from Dhak through oak forest to Gulling meadow (2,499m). The Kuari Pass trail and the Pangarchulla trail share this section. Easy gradient, good for acclimatisation.

itinerary.title: Gulling to Khulara
itinerary.desc: 4 km steep climb from Gulling to Khulara (3,590m) through Gorson Bugyal. Nanda Devi (7,816m), Dronagiri (7,066m), Kamet (7,756m), Hathi Ghoda peaks all appear. The Pangarchulla ridge is visible from camp.

itinerary.title: Summit Day — Khulara to Pangarchulla Peak, Descent to Tugasi
itinerary.desc: Pre-dawn start from Khulara. 5 km steep scramble to the Pangarchulla summit (4,700m / 15,419 ft). The route goes over loose shale, boulder fields, and a final snow/rock ridge. Summit views: Nanda Devi, Trishul, Kamet, Dronagiri, Mana, and Chaukhamba at extremely close range. Descend 6 km to Tugasi. Total: 11 km summit day.

itinerary.title: Tugasi to Rishikesh — Return Drive
itinerary.distance: 15 km road to Joshimath + 230 km to Rishikesh
itinerary.desc: Drive from Tugasi/Joshimath back to Rishikesh (245 km total, 9–10 hours).

coverImageCredit: Photo by INDU BIKASH SARKER on Pexels

name: Satopanth Tal
description: A glacial lake trek of exceptional spiritual and natural power, ascending from Badrinath through the valley of the Alaknanda's source to the triangular sacred lake of Satopanth Tal at 4,402m. The lake is believed to be the site of mediation of the Hindu Trinity — Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva — reflected in its three triangular corners. Above the lake rises the massive Chaukhamba massif (7,138m) and Balakun peak.

overview.location: Satopanth Tal (4,402m) is a sacred triangular glacial lake above Badrinath in Chamoli district. The lake's perfect equilateral triangle shape is traditionally associated with the Hindu Trinity — Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva — who are said to bathe in the three corners on auspicious occasions. Swargarohini (6,252m) and the Chaukhamba group tower above. The approach from Badrinath (3,133m) passes through Mana village — India's last inhabited village before the Tibetan border.
overview.history: Satopanth Tal has been a sacred pilgrimage site since at least the 8th century CE — Adi Shankaracharya, the philosopher who systematised Advaita Vedanta, is said to have meditated here during his Himalayan tour. 'Satopanth' means 'path of the virtuous' or 'true path' in Sanskrit. The lake features in multiple Puranic texts as a place of spiritual power. Mana village en route has its own extraordinary connections — the cave where Vyas dictated the Mahabharata to Ganesha is a sacred site here.
overview.length: 32 km over 4–5 days from Badrinath town. Total elevation gain from Badrinath (3,133m) approximately 1,269m. The trail passes through Mana village, the Laxmi Van campsite, and Chakratirtha before reaching the lake. The trail is well-defined as far as Chakratirtha; beyond, route-finding over boulder fields requires experience.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 0°C–10°C at lake; park opens May 1. Sep–Oct: –5°C to 8°C; best conditions for clarity and stable weather. The Badrinath NP closes by Diwali (October). Night temperatures at the lake can drop to –10°C in October. Joshimath medical check practice applies.
overview.fitness: Moderate to hard. The altitude of 4,402m and boulder-field approach demand proper fitness and acclimatisation. Minimum 2 nights at Badrinath before proceeding to Satopanth. The Joshimath district on-arrival medical fitness check is commonly applied to trekkers heading to this elevation.

permitInfo.type: Forest Entry Permit / Nanda Devi Biosphere Buffer Zone Permit
permitInfo.where: Badrinath Forest Range office / DFO Chamoli check-post at Mana Village
permitInfo.fee: ₹150/day Indian; ₹600 foreigner
permitInfo.note: The route passes through Mana village (last Indian village on the Badrinath–Tibet road) and enters the Satopanth glacial valley inside the Chamoli Forest Division. Permit from Mana check-post. Joshimath administration medical/fitness checks apply (Chamoli district). Insurance mandatory in practice. The upper section toward Satopanth Glacier (beyond the lake) requires additional DFO Chamoli clearance. High rescue risk — guide strongly recommended.
permitInfo.foreigners: Some sections near Mana (India-China border zone) may have restrictions. Verify DM Chamoli rules before travel.

itinerary.title: Haridwar to Badrinath
itinerary.desc: Drive up the Alaknanda to Badrinath — one of Hinduism's four sacred dhams. Acclimatize. Visit the Badrinath temple. Collect permits from the Mana forest office near the village check-post.

itinerary.title: Badrinath to Mana Village to Laxmivan
itinerary.desc: Walk through Mana — India's last inhabited village before the Tibetan border. Cross the Saraswati River on the famous boulder bridge. Trek through the valley below the massive Chaukhamba massif.

itinerary.title: Laxmivan to Chakrateertha
itinerary.desc: Enter the high glacial plateau. The landscape becomes stark and elemental — moraines, glacial ice, and the Chaukhamba above.

itinerary.title: Chakrateertha to Satopanth Tal
itinerary.desc: Arrive at the sacred triangular lake of Satopanth. The water is an impossibly deep blue-green. Chaukhamba (7,138m) reflects in the lake at dawn. The atmosphere is one of complete silence and sacredness.

itinerary.title: Satopanth to Badrinath — Return Drive
itinerary.desc: Descend back through Chakrateertha and Mana to Badrinath. Drive down to Haridwar via the Alaknanda — approximately 10–11 hours.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Siddhartha Sen on Pexels

name: Auden's Col
description: One of India's greatest and most demanding treks — Auden's Col (5,490m) connects Gangotri to Kedarnath through a complete wilderness crossing of the Gangotri and Kedarnath glacial systems. Named after British geologist John Bicknell Auden who first crossed it in 1939, the route traverses three high glaciers, involves roped travel on crevassed terrain, and delivers some of the most savage and beautiful mountain scenery in India. Expert mountaineers and seasoned expedition trekkers only.

overview.location: Auden's Col (5,490m) is one of India's most remote and technically challenging glacier passes, crossing from the Gangotri glacier (Uttarkashi) to the Kedarnath glacier (Rudraprayag) over the main Himalayan divide. The route traverses four glaciers and passes beneath Jogin (6,465m), Thalay Sagar (6,904m), and Kedarnath Peak (6,940m) in a continuous sequence of extraordinary glaciated terrain.
overview.history: The Col is named after John B. Auden, a geologist with the Geological Survey of India, who made the first crossing in 1935 during a survey of Himalayan glaciology — an extraordinary feat of exploration for its time. Auden later wrote a celebrated account describing it as one of the most arduous and spectacular crossings in the Himalayas. The route was rarely repeated for decades due to its extreme demands. In recent years it has been completed by small guided expedition teams as one of India's premier high-altitude 'super-trek' objectives.
overview.length: 140–160 km over 14–18 days, Gangotri to Kedarnath or reverse. The route requires dual permit clearance from Uttarkashi (Gangotri NP) and Chamoli/Rudraprayag (Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary), with identical dates on both permits. Four major glaciers must be crossed. Full mountaineering equipment is mandatory — this is an expedition, not a standard trek.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: Heavy snow at the Col; technically most serious. Sep: –10°C at the Col during the day; –20°C to –30°C at night at high glacier camps; the most stable and recommended season for experienced teams. May–September is the narrow operational window.
overview.fitness: Expert only. Full mountaineering team with ice axes, crampons, fixed ropes, and multi-day glacier travel experience is absolutely required. Not accessible to recreational trekkers under any circumstance. This is a serious mountaineering expedition requiring years of prior Himalayan climbing experience. IMF expedition permit is required for the glacier sections.

permitInfo.type: Dual NP Permits: Gangotri NP (Uttarkashi) + Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary (Rudraprayag), plus DFO Chamoli for Khatling Glacier section
permitInfo.where: Gangotri permit office + SDM Uttarkashi; Rudraprayag/Okhimath forest range office on exit
permitInfo.fee: ₹150/day per park (Indian); ₹600/day per park (foreigner). Multiple days in each zone.
permitInfo.note: Requires permits for both Gangotri NP (entry) and Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary (exit). Intermediate Khatling Glacier section requires DFO Chamoli clearance. Uttarkashi and Chamoli districts both require medical fitness certificates and full trek insurance. ITBP posts checked along the glacial sections. Guide with glacier travel experience and full technical kit (rope, crampons, ice axe) mandatory. Very serious route — multiple rescue evacuations reported. Not suitable for guided group tourism; expedition format required.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open with dual NP permits. Restricted zones may require additional clearances through expedition/IMF channels.

itinerary.title: Haridwar to Gangotri — Permit Collect
itinerary.desc: Drive to Gangotri. Collect Gangotri NP permits. Rest and acclimatize — the following days are unrelenting.

itinerary.title: Gangotri to Nala Camp (via Gaumukh approach)
itinerary.desc: Enter Gangotri NP and trek to the base of the Gangotri Glacier. Camp at the standard Nala site.

itinerary.title: Nala to Vasuki Tal Base
itinerary.desc: Leave the main Gaumukh route and turn west into the Gangotri Glacier's heart. Roped travel on crevassed sections. The terrain becomes raw and spectacular.

itinerary.title: Vasuki Tal to Auden's Col Base Camp
itinerary.desc: Gain the base of the col on steep moraine and snow. The Jogin peaks and Thalay Sagar visible above. Prepare equipment for the crossing.

itinerary.title: Auden's Col Crossing (5,490m)
itinerary.desc: The defining day. A sustained glacier ascent to the 5,490m col. At the top, the entire Kedarnath massif opens ahead. Descend carefully on the Khatling side — steep and crevassed.

itinerary.title: Khatling Glacier to Kedarnath Valley — Return to Haridwar
itinerary.desc: Descend through the Khatling Glacier system, exiting via Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary to Ukhimath/Chopta and then driving back to Haridwar. Total return from Ukhimath to Haridwar is approximately 7 hours.

coverImageCredit: Photo by INDU BIKASH SARKER on Pexels

name: Ali Bedni Bugyal
description: A meadow journey through two of the most celebrated bugyals (alpine grasslands) in the Garhwal Himalayas. Ali Bugyal and Bedni Bugyal form a continuous highland plateau at 3,500–3,700m framed by Trishul (7,120m), Nanda Ghunti (6,309m), and the Kedarnath peaks. The route from Wan village passes through dense forest before breaking into the vast open grasslands. Sacred Bedni Kund lake sits at the upper edge.

overview.location: Ali Bugyal (3,350m) and Bedni Bugyal (3,354m) together form one of the largest contiguous alpine meadow systems in Uttarakhand — a vast undulating grassland above the treeline in Chamoli district. The meadows lie within the Nanda Devi Biosphere buffer zone, with Trishul (7,120m) and Nanda Ghunti (6,309m) as a constant backdrop. The approach is from Lohajung village (2,270m) in the Wan valley, 270 km from Rishikesh.
overview.history: The Ali and Bedni Bugyals are part of the sacred route of the Nanda Devi Raj Jat Yatra — held once every 12 years, this is one of India's largest religious processions, involving thousands of pilgrims who walk from Nauti village to Roopkund Lake. The meadows have been seasonal grazing lands for millennia — a Bedni Kund (sacred pool) at Bedni is a significant religious site. The 2014 Uttarakhand High Court order (WPPIL 123/2014) specifically prohibits overnight camping on these meadow surfaces to protect the fragile alpine grassland ecosystem.
overview.length: 45 km over 5–6 days, Lohajung return. Total elevation gain from Lohajung approximately 1,084m to the bugyals. The meadows themselves extend 10–15 km across at altitude. This forms the first section of the Roopkund trek route — trekkers going to Roopkund continue beyond Bedni Bugyal to Bhagwabasa.
overview.temperature: Apr–Jun: Wildflower season; –2°C to 15°C. Sep–Oct: 0°C to 10°C; clear views of Trishul and Nanda Ghunti. Monsoon: Green and accessible but leeches present below treeline. Winter: Deep snow on the bugyals.
overview.fitness: Moderate. Suitable for trekkers with 1–2 prior multi-day treks. The gradual forest ascent to the meadows is well-maintained. No technical terrain. Beautiful for all skill levels as a meadow exploration. Guide knowledge is needed to stage camps legally off the protected meadow surface.

permitInfo.type: Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve Buffer Zone Forest Entry Permit
permitInfo.where: Wan village check-post / Lohajung range office (Chamoli Forest Division)
permitInfo.fee: ₹150/day Indian; ₹600/day foreigner
permitInfo.note: The Uttarakhand High Court order (WPPIL 123/2014) specifically names Aali-Bedini-Bagzi bugyals — no overnight camping on these meadows is permitted under any circumstances. Camps must be at designated off-meadow sites near Wan or Didna. Chamoli district practice: medical fitness and insurance increasingly required. Route is the approach to Roopkund — same permit zone.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to all nationalities with standard forest entry permit.

itinerary.title: Kathgodam / Haridwar to Lohajung
itinerary.desc: Drive from Kathgodam or Haridwar through Almora and Gwaldam to Lohajung. Collect forest permits at the check-post on arrival. This is the same base village as the Roopkund and Brahmatal treks.

itinerary.title: Lohajung to Wan — Trek to Didna
itinerary.desc: Drive or walk to Wan village, then begin the gradual climb through oak and rhododendron forest to Didna — a traditional Garhwali settlement with carved wooden houses and wide crop terraces.

itinerary.title: Didna to Ali Bugyal
itinerary.desc: Break out of the treeline onto Ali Bugyal — a vast rolling grassland that stretches for kilometres. Trishul materialises with sudden force above the meadow's far edge. Camp at the designated off-bugyal site at the forest boundary.

itinerary.title: Ali Bugyal to Bedni Bugyal — Bedni Kund
itinerary.desc: Walk across the continuous meadow plateau to Bedni Bugyal. The ancient stone shrine at Bedni and the sacred Bedni Kund lake sit at the upper edge of the plateau. Nanda Ghunti (6,309m) and Trishul are both visible simultaneously from here.

itinerary.title: Bedni Bugyal to Wan — Return to Kathgodam
itinerary.desc: Descend through forest back to Wan village and drive to Kathgodam. The return journey by road takes approximately 8–9 hours through Gwaldam and Almora.

coverImageCredit: Photo via Brave Search

name: Tapovan (Shivling Base Camp)
description: A shorter standalone version of the Gaumukh–Tapovan route focusing on reaching Tapovan meadow — the legendary grassy shelf at 4,463m beneath the vertical walls of Shivling (6,543m) and Meru (6,660m). The approach along the Bhagirathi from Gangotri, across the Gangotri Glacier, and up the moraines to Tapovan is one of India's most iconic mountain approaches. Spiritual, dramatic, and deeply satisfying.

overview.location: Tapovan (4,463m) is a hanging meadow suspended above the Gangotri glacier in Uttarkashi district, within Gangotri National Park. The camp sits directly at the base of Mt. Shivling (6,543m) — the 'Shiva's lingam' peak whose perfectly pointed profile makes it one of the most recognisable and photographed mountains in the world. Meru (6,660m), the three Bhagirathi peaks, and Kedarnath Dome are also visible from the meadow. The approach is 14 km from Gangotri town — 9 km to Gaumukh glacier snout, then a steep 5 km moraine scramble above.
overview.history: Tapovan ('forest of tapas/meditation') has been a retreat for sadhus and yogis for centuries, its isolation and beauty making it a natural place for spiritual practice. The site gained global mountaineering fame for its proximity to technically demanding routes on Shivling, the Shark's Fin on Meru, and the Bhagirathi group. The 2011 ascent of Meru's Shark's Fin by Conrad Anker, Jimmy Chin, and Renan Ozturk — filmed as the documentary Meru — brought Tapovan to a worldwide audience.
overview.length: 28 km over 4–5 days from Gangotri town. Total elevation gain approximately 1,415m. The moraine scramble above Gaumukh to Tapovan (2.5 hours, very steep) is the crux section. Expedition teams targeting peaks from Tapovan may remain for weeks. The standard trekking itinerary allows 1–2 nights at the meadow before returning.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 0°C–12°C at meadow; –5°C to –10°C at night. Sep–Oct: –5°C to 8°C; clearest skies and most stable; best season. Night temperatures at Tapovan drop to –15°C even in summer. A four-season sleeping bag is essential. Gangotri NP closes November–April.
overview.fitness: Hard. The moraine climb from Gaumukh to Tapovan is steep, loose, and physically demanding. Altitude of 4,463m requires proper acclimatisation (minimum 2 nights at Gangotri). No fixed ropes or technical climbing on the main trail, but scrambling ability and confidence on loose terrain essential. Preparation: 10 weeks of training. Experience with glacier moraine navigation is helpful.

permitInfo.type: Gangotri National Park Trekking Permit
permitInfo.where: Permit office above the bus stand in Gangotri town (DFO Uttarkashi / Gangotri NP)
permitInfo.fee: ₹150/day Indian; ₹600/day foreigner. Camera fee ₹200. Daily cap: 150 trekkers per day to Tapovan.
permitInfo.note: Mandatory NP permit from Gangotri permit office; checks at the NP gate 4 km above Gangotri town. Uttarkashi district now requires trek insurance for all trekkers and medical fitness certificate for Tapovan (4,463m+). Trekkers 50+ need medical certificate even for Gaumukh. Carry 2 sets of all documents. Drones banned inside national park. The glacier crossing is route-finding dependent — guide mandatory.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to foreigners with NP permit. Some inner corridors beyond Tapovan may require additional clearance.

itinerary.title: Haridwar to Gangotri
itinerary.desc: Drive the Bhagirathi gorge to Gangotri. Collect NP permits from the permit office above the bus stand. Acclimatize at Gangotri overnight — the altitude here is already 3,048m.

itinerary.title: Gangotri to Chirbasa
itinerary.desc: Enter Gangotri NP at the gate. Walk through Himalayan birch forest alongside the roaring Bhagirathi. First views of the Bhagirathi peaks above the treeline at Chirbasa.

itinerary.title: Chirbasa to Bhojbasa to Gaumukh Snout
itinerary.desc: Reach Bhojbasa then walk to Gaumukh — the glacier snout where the Ganga emerges from a vast ice cave. Rest and prepare for the next day's moraine climb.

itinerary.title: Gaumukh to Tapovan
itinerary.desc: The most dramatic section: cross the glacier surface and gain the steep moraine above Gaumukh. The meadow of Tapovan appears suddenly — a green oasis under Shivling's impossible-looking summit tower. Mountaineering expeditions camp here. The views are extraordinary.

itinerary.title: Tapovan to Gangotri — Return to Haridwar
itinerary.desc: Descend from Tapovan through Bhojbasa, Chirbasa back to Gangotri. Drive back to Haridwar down the Bhagirathi gorge — approximately 9–10 hours.

coverImageCredit: Photo by INDU BIKASH SARKER on Pexels

name: Sahastra Tal
description: One of Uttarakhand's most remote and least-visited lake treks — Sahastra Tal (the Lake of a Thousand) sits at 4,700m in a glacial basin above the Bhilangna Valley in the Uttarkashi district. The approach involves crossing the Dodi Tal route and then turning west into deep wilderness. The lake complex is surrounded by peaks above 5,000m and sees very few trekkers annually. For experienced wilderness trekkers only.

overview.location: Sahastra Tal (3,780m) is a remote sacred lake complex in the Bhilangana River watershed, Tehri district of Garhwal, Uttarakhand. 'Sahastra' means thousand — the area is said to contain a thousand sacred water bodies. The trek approaches from Reeh village (2,200m) near Ghuttu, following the river valley into pristine wilderness rarely visited by outside trekkers. The Jogin peaks and Kedarnath Dome are visible from the high camps.
overview.history: The Sahastra Tal lakes are mentioned in ancient Hindu texts as a sacred complex associated with Lord Shiva. The Bhilangana River drainage — also the source of the Khatling Glacier — is a significant part of the sacred Himalayan landscape described in the Skanda Purana. The extreme remoteness of the area has preserved it from the commercialisation affecting more popular Garhwal treks, making it one of the last truly wild, under-visited destinations in the region.
overview.length: 55–65 km over 7–9 days from Ghuttu village. Total elevation gain approximately 2,580m. The trail is not well-marked beyond the lower valley — a guide is essential. Very limited facilities beyond Ghuttu; full camping provisions must be carried from town.
overview.temperature: May–Jul: 5°C–18°C at lower camps; –5°C to 5°C near the lake complex. Sep–Oct: 0°C to 10°C; clearest skies. Monsoon (Jul–Aug) brings rain but the lower valley is still accessible. The high lake complex may be partially frozen into July.
overview.fitness: Hard. Remote and unmarked trail requiring a guide and full wilderness camping capability. High altitude approach to 3,780m. Prior experience on multi-day Himalayan treks is essential. Self-sufficiency in camping, navigation, and emergency response is the primary requirement for this route.

permitInfo.type: Forest Entry Permit (Uttarkashi Forest Division)
permitInfo.where: Uttarkashi DFO office or Reeh village check-post
permitInfo.fee: ₹150/day Indian; ₹600/day foreigner
permitInfo.note: Uttarkashi division forest permit required. Uttarkashi district practice: insurance and medical fitness mandatory on this route due to remoteness and 4,700m altitude. No rescue infrastructure beyond Uttarkashi — carry a personal GPS or PLB device. Guide with knowledge of this specific route essential (few operators run this trek). No facilities beyond Reeh trailhead village.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to all nationalities. No ILP required on this route.

itinerary.title: Rishikesh to Uttarkashi to Reeh Village
itinerary.desc: Drive from Rishikesh via the Bhilangna Valley road to Reeh — the small trailhead village for Sahastra Tal. Collect permits. Very limited facilities — carry all supplies.

itinerary.title: Reeh to Kush Kalyani
itinerary.desc: Steep forest climb from Reeh through deodar and oak. The trail is less travelled than Uttarkashi's popular routes — you may need to route-find with a local guide.

itinerary.title: Kush Kalyani to Gangar
itinerary.desc: Above the treeline into open high-altitude pasture. Gangar is a summer herder camp with stone shelters. The peaks above begin to reveal themselves.

itinerary.title: Gangar to Sahastra Tal Base Camp
itinerary.desc: Gain the high rocky basin below Sahastra Tal. Scattered lakes and tarns appear. The main lake complex is just above, ringed by unnamed 5,000m peaks.

itinerary.title: Sahastra Tal Lake Exploration
itinerary.distance: Up to 5 km around lake complex
itinerary.desc: Explore the lake complex — a series of interconnected high-altitude tarns in a glacial bowl. Complete solitude. This lake sees perhaps a few hundred trekkers in a good year.

itinerary.title: Sahastra Tal to Reeh — Return to Rishikesh
itinerary.desc: Return over 2 days to Reeh village, then drive back to Rishikesh via the Bhilangna Valley and Tehri. Total return journey approximately 7 hours by road.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Siddhartha Sen on Pexels

name: Bagji Bugyal
description: A lesser-known counterpart to the famous Roopkund meadows, Bagji Bugyal offers an expansive alpine grassland at 3,800m with unobstructed views of the Nanda Ghunti, Trishul, and Kedarnath group — with virtually none of the crowds of Roopkund or Bedni. The route from Lohajung passes through the same forest approach but diverges westward into quieter terrain.

overview.location: Bagji Bugyal (3,650m) is a pristine alpine meadow in Chamoli district above the Wan valley in the Nanda Devi buffer zone. Less visited than the nearby Ali-Bedni meadows, Bagji offers an authentic high-altitude grassland experience with clear views of Nanda Ghunti (6,309m) and the Trishul group. The approach is from Lohajung or Wan village, branching from the standard Roopkund trail.
overview.history: Bagji Bugyal is part of the broader pastoral circuit of the Garhwali shepherd communities and is named in the Uttarakhand High Court's bugyal protection order (WPPIL 123/2014) — the landmark ruling that banned overnight camping on all alpine meadows statewide. The meadow has been part of the extended Nanda Devi Raj Jat Yatra pilgrimage circuit for centuries, lying on the approach routes to the sacred bugyals above Wan.
overview.length: 40–45 km over 5–6 days from Lohajung village. Total elevation gain approximately 1,380m to the bugyal. Can be combined with the Ali-Bedni circuit for an extended 8-day meadow traverse of the Nanda Devi buffer zone.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: Wildflower bloom; 0°C–15°C. Sep–Oct: 0°C–10°C; excellent weather. Monsoon: Green and rainy. The bugyal camping ban means no overnight stays on the meadow surface — camps staged below or above.
overview.fitness: Moderate. Similar requirements to the Ali-Bedni Bugyal trek. The forest approach trail is well-maintained. Suitable for trekkers with 1+ prior multi-day treks. A local guide is recommended for the Bagji branch-off from the main Roopkund trail.

permitInfo.type: Nanda Devi Biosphere Reserve Buffer Zone Forest Entry Permit
permitInfo.where: Lohajung check-post (Chamoli Forest Division)
permitInfo.fee: ₹150/day Indian; ₹600/day foreigner
permitInfo.note: Same permit zone as Roopkund/Bedni Bugyal (Chamoli Forest Division, Lohajung check-post). Bugyal camping ban (HC order WPPIL 123/2014) applies — overnight camps on open meadow are prohibited. Use designated off-meadow sites. Chamoli district medical fitness + insurance practice applies. Route is less structured — local guide strongly advised.
permitInfo.foreigners: Open to all nationalities with standard forest permit.

itinerary.title: Kathgodam to Lohajung
itinerary.desc: Drive from Kathgodam through Almora and Gwaldam to Lohajung. Collect permits. Same base village as Roopkund and Brahmatal.

itinerary.title: Lohajung to Wan to Forest Camp
itinerary.desc: Drive to Wan village and begin trekking. The Bagji route diverges westward from the main Roopkund trail into quieter forest.

itinerary.title: Forest Camp to Bagji Bugyal
itinerary.desc: Gain the Bagji plateau — a wide meadow with 360° views. Trishul and Nanda Ghunti are the dominant peaks. The complete absence of other trekkers is the defining quality of this route.

itinerary.title: Bugyal Exploration and Return to Wan
itinerary.desc: A morning in the meadow followed by a descent back to Wan village through the same forest. Evening in the village.

itinerary.title: Wan to Kathgodam — Return Drive
itinerary.desc: Drive back to Kathgodam from Wan via Gwaldam and Almora. Approximately 8 hours by road.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Satyabrata Maiti on Pexels

name: Ronti Saddle
