permitInfo: No formal permit needed for the main pilgrimage trail. Forest entry registration at local range post (Rudraprayag district). Trek insurance recommended. Medical certificate for 50+. Religious site — no alcohol or non-vegetarian food near the temple.

itinerary.title: Rishikesh to Ukhimath — Drive to Ransi Village
itinerary.distance: 190 km Rishikesh to Ukhimath + 24 km to Ransi
itinerary.desc: Drive from Rishikesh (190 km, 7 hrs) via Devprayag, Rudraprayag, and Kund to Ukhimath. Drive 24 km further on the Mansuna-Ukhimath road to Ransi village (2,200m) — last motorable point. Ukhimath's Omkareshwar temple houses Kedarnath and Madmaheshwar deities in winter. Madmaheshwar is 16 km from Ransi (32 km round trip).

itinerary.title: Ransi to Lower Bantoli (Chhoti Bantoli)
itinerary.desc: 7 km mostly DOWNHILL trek on paved stone path from Ransi above the Madmaheshwar Ganga, passing Gaundhar village. Lower Bantoli (Chhoti Bantoli, 2,634m) at the confluence of Madmaheshwar Ganga and Martyenda Ganga. NOTE: the trail is downhill going in but uphill on return — factor extra time for return day. From Bantoli, the trail is continuously steep to the temple.

itinerary.title: Lower Bantoli to Madmaheshwar Temple + Buda Madmaheshwar
itinerary.distance: 6.5 km to temple + 2 km to Buda (optional)
itinerary.time: 4-5 hrs to temple + 1.5 hrs to Buda
itinerary.desc: 6.5 km continuous steep ascent from Bantoli through Khatara and Nanu to Madmaheshwar (3,497m) — 2nd Panch Kedar where Shiva is worshipped as the Navel (Nabhi / Madhya). Altitude gain: 863m in 6.5 km. Chaukhamba massif (7,138m) appears dramatically as you approach. Optional: 2 km further to Buda Madmaheshwar (3,600m) — ancient shrine on high meadow with the most sweeping Chaukhamba panorama. Sunrise from Buda Madmaheshwar is the highlight of the trek.

itinerary.title: Madmaheshwar to Ransi Return
itinerary.desc: Descend 6.5 km from Madmaheshwar to Bantoli (3-3.5 hrs — steep, poles essential), then 7 km Bantoli to Ransi (mostly uphill on return, allow extra time). Total: 13.5 km, 6-7 hrs.

itinerary.title: Ransi to Rishikesh Return Drive
itinerary.distance: 24 km to Ukhimath + 190 km to Rishikesh
itinerary.desc: Drive from Ransi (24 km) to Ukhimath, then 190 km to Rishikesh via Rudraprayag and Devprayag.

name: Kedarnath Yatra

reviews.name: Ramesh S. ★ Google Maps
reviews.text: The most powerful place I have ever stood. The temple at dawn with the peak above, in the pre-monsoon mist — I have never felt anything like it. India's greatest pilgrimage.

reviews.name: Anna L. ★ TripAdvisor
reviews.text: Even as a non-Hindu, the energy at Kedarnath is extraordinary. The landscape is dramatic and the devotion of the pilgrims is deeply moving. Go in October for the best weather and fewer crowds.

description: India's most famous high-altitude pilgrimage, Kedarnath temple sits at 3,583m beneath the towering Kedarnath peak (6,940m). The 16 km trail from Gaurikund passes through dramatic canyon terrain along the Mandakini River. One of the Char Dhams and one of the twelve Jyotirlingas — the spiritual energy at the temple is overwhelming. Equally compelling as a trekking destination.

overview.location: Kedarnath temple (3,583m) sits beneath the towering Kedarnath peak (6,940m) in Rudraprayag district, Uttarakhand — one of the twelve Jyotirlingas and the holiest Shiva shrine in the Himalayas. The 16 km trail from Gaurikund (1,982m) follows the Mandakini River through a dramatic canyon carved by glacial meltwater. The first sight of the temple with the peak filling the sky above it is one of the most powerful arrivals in Indian pilgrimage.
overview.history: Kedarnath temple is believed to have been built in the 8th century by Adi Shankaracharya, who is also said to have attained moksha (liberation) here. The site is one of the oldest continuously worshipped Shiva shrines in the Himalayas. The 2013 Kedarnath disaster — a cloudburst and flash flood on 16–17 June 2013 — devastated the town and killed over 5,000 people. The temple itself was protected by a giant boulder that deflected the flood — an event widely regarded in India as a divine miracle. Reconstruction is ongoing.
overview.length: Standard trek: 16 km each way (32 km round-trip) over 3–4 days. Total elevation gain from Gaurikund: 1,601m. Helicopter service from Phata, Guptkashi, and Sirsi is available (book well in advance). Biometric registration at Gaurikund is mandatory. Temple open May–October (Diwali closure for winter).
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–18°C; high season for pilgrimage. Sep–Oct: 0°C–12°C; fewer crowds; clearest views of Kedarnath peak. Jul–Aug: Monsoon; rain on the trail but manageable. Winter: Temple closes; trail under snow. October is the finest month for trekkers seeking both darshan and peak views.
overview.fitness: Moderate. The 16 km trail has 1,601m of elevation gain — manageable for most healthy adults at a steady pace. Pony and doli (palanquin) services are available for those who need them. The altitude of 3,583m requires normal precautions. The emotional and spiritual intensity of the arrival at the temple is a component of the experience that visitors consistently describe as overwhelming.

permitInfo: No forest permit required. Registration at Gaurikund (biometric registration for pilgrims). State government ID required. Pony and doli (palanquin) services available. Helicopter service from Phata/Guptkashi (book well in advance). VIP darshan passes available online. Temple open May–Oct (Diwali closure).

itinerary.title: Rishikesh to Sonprayag — Drive to Gaurikund
itinerary.distance: 210 km Rishikesh to Sonprayag + 5 km shared jeep
itinerary.desc: Drive from Rishikesh (210 km, 8-9 hrs) via Devprayag, Rudraprayag, Augustmuni, and Guptkashi to Sonprayag (1,840m) — last point for private vehicles. Shared government jeep (Rs 25/person) for the final 5 km to Gaurikund (1,982m). Register mandatory biometric Char Dham Yatra pass at Gaurikund. Hot sulphur springs at Gaurikund. IMPORTANT: Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary closes trail to new departures at 1:30 PM — trek must start at 4:00 AM. Sleep by 8 PM.

itinerary.title: Gaurikund to Kedarnath Temple — Evening Darshan
itinerary.distance: 16 km (post-2013 rebuilt route via Mandakini valley)
itinerary.camp: Kedarnath — GMVN tent city / temple trust lodge
itinerary.desc: Start 4:00-5:00 AM. The 16 km route rebuilt after 2013 floods: Gaurikund (1,982m) → Jungle Chatti (6 km, first rest stop with medical facility) → Bhimbali (10 km, GMVN tents, medical camp) → Linchauli (13 km, steepest section) → Base Camp (15 km) → Kedarnath Temple (16 km, 3,583m). Total ascent: 1,601m. Pony/dandi/kandi available from Gaurikund at govt-regulated rates (pony Rs 4,100, dandi Rs 4,450, kandi Rs 3,300). Evening aarti and darshan at the 8th-century temple — Lord Shiva worshipped here as the hump of the divine bull (1st Panch Kedar). Overnight at Kedarnath.

itinerary.title: Kedarnath to Gaurikund — Drive to Rishikesh
itinerary.desc: Descend 16 km from Kedarnath (3,583m) to Gaurikund (1,982m) — 4-5 hours. Last descent departure from Kedarnath: 6:30 PM. Shared jeep 5 km back to Sonprayag. Drive 210 km to Rishikesh (8-9 hrs). Helicopter: Phata helipad 15.3 km from Gaurikund, 5-7 min flight. Also from Sirsi, Guptkashi, Agastyamuni. Advance booking essential in peak season (May-June).

name: Yamunotri Trek

reviews.name: Preethi N. ★ Google Maps
reviews.text: The Surya Kund at Yamunotri where you cook rice in the thermal waters is a completely unique experience. The setting — a narrow gorge with the peaks above — is spectacular.

reviews.name: James K. ★ TripAdvisor
reviews.text: Less crowded than Kedarnath, more intimate. The hot spring bath at Janki Chatti before the trek is a highlight. The trail along the Yamuna gorge is beautiful.

description: The source of the Yamuna River and the first of the four Char Dhams, Yamunotri temple at 3,293m is approached by a scenic 6 km trail from Janki Chatti. The trail follows the Yamuna gorge through forests with hot spring at Janki Chatti and a sacred kund (pool) of scalding thermal water at the temple itself where pilgrims cook rice as prasad.

overview.location: Yamunotri temple (3,293m) — the source of the Yamuna River and the first of the four Char Dhams — is approached by a 6 km trail from Janki Chatti (2,650m) in Uttarkashi district. The trail follows the Yamuna gorge through a narrow canyon past natural hot springs, emerging at the temple where a scalding thermal pool (Surya Kund) allows pilgrims to cook rice as prasad — a unique sacred tradition.
overview.history: Yamunotri is the most westerly of the four Char Dhams — the sacred pilgrimage circuit of Badrinath, Kedarnath, Gangotri, and Yamunotri that represents one of Hinduism's most important religious journeys. The temple is dedicated to Goddess Yamuna, daughter of the sun god Surya. The present temple was built in the 19th century by Maharani Guleria of Jaipur. Janki Chatti's natural hot springs have been used for bathing by pilgrims for centuries.
overview.length: 12 km round-trip (6 km each way) from Janki Chatti over 2–3 days. Total elevation gain: approximately 643m. The drive from Rishikesh to Janki Chatti is 220 km (7 hours). Pony and doli services available for those who need them. Temple open May–October.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–18°C; peak pilgrimage season. Sep–Oct: 0°C–12°C; clearer and less crowded. Jul–Aug: Monsoon; trail can be slippery. Winter: Temple closes after Diwali; trail under snow. The hot spring bath at Janki Chatti is enjoyable year-round.
overview.fitness: Easy. The most physically accessible of the Char Dhams. Suitable for all adults including older pilgrims and those with limited mobility (pony and doli available). The 6 km trail has only 643m of elevation gain over a gentle incline. The thermal spring experience at the temple, the gorge scenery, and the sacred atmosphere make this a complete pilgrimage experience.

permitInfo: No formal trek permit. Biometric registration at Janki Chatti encouraged. Temple open May–Oct. Pony and doli services available. No camping inside temple complex. State ID required.

itinerary.title: Dehradun/Rishikesh to Janki Chatti
itinerary.desc: Drive via Barkot and Hanuman Chatti to Janki Chatti — the trailhead for Yamunotri. Natural hot springs at Janki Chatti are open for bathing.

itinerary.title: Janki Chatti to Yamunotri Temple and Return
itinerary.desc: Trek 6 km along the Yamuna gorge to Yamunotri temple. The Divya Shila (sacred rock pillar) and Surya Kund (thermal pool) are at the temple. Cook rice in the pool as prasad — a unique pilgrimage tradition. Return to Janki Chatti.

itinerary.title: Janki Chatti to Rishikesh — Return
itinerary.desc: Drive back to Rishikesh via Barkot and Uttarkashi. ~7 hours total.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Raj Pritam on Pexels

name: Hemkund Sahib Trek

reviews.name: Gurpreet S. ★ Google Maps
reviews.text: The gurdwara at the lakeside at 4,633m is humbling. The langar in that setting — volunteers serving food at the world's highest Sikh shrine — brings tears to the eyes.

reviews.name: Caroline F. ★ TripAdvisor
reviews.text: Pairing Hemkund Sahib with Valley of Flowers is the ideal combination. Two completely different experiences — the wildflower meadow and the icy sacred lake — both extraordinary.

description: The highest Sikh shrine in the world, Hemkund Sahib sits beside a glacial lake at 4,633m ringed by seven snow peaks. The 6 km trail from Ghangaria climbs steeply through wildflower meadows to the star-shaped white gurdwara on the lakeside. Combining it with the Valley of Flowers (2 km away from Ghangaria) is one of the great double treks of the Himalayas.

overview.location: Hemkund Sahib gurdwara (4,633m) — the highest Sikh shrine in the world — sits beside a glacial lake ringed by seven snow peaks in Chamoli district, Uttarakhand. The 6 km trail from Ghangaria (3,048m) climbs steeply through wildflower meadows to the lakeside. It shares Ghangaria as a base with the Valley of Flowers National Park, just 2 km away, making the combination of both sites one of the great double-feature treks of the Himalayas.
overview.history: The site was identified in the 1930s by Sikh scholar Havildar Sohan Singh, who matched the description in the Sikh scripture Dasam Granth — Guru Gobind Singh wrote of meditating at a lake ringed by seven peaks in a previous life. Hemkund (Sanskrit: hemkund = golden lake) became a major Sikh pilgrimage destination and the star-shaped white gurdwara was constructed from the 1960s onwards. Today it receives over 50,000 pilgrims annually during its June–October season. Volunteers operate a free langar (community kitchen) at 4,633m — one of the highest community kitchens in the world.
overview.length: 12 km round-trip from Ghangaria (6 km each way). Elevation gain from Ghangaria to Hemkund: 1,585m — steep and sustained. The approach from Govindghat to Ghangaria is 14 km additional on each side. The gurdwara is accessible only June–October when the lake is ice-free.
overview.temperature: Jun–Jul: 5°C–15°C at Ghangaria; 0°C–5°C at the lake; wildflower display on the lower slopes. Aug: Similar; the lake is fully ice-free. Sep–Oct: 0°C–10°C; clearest skies; snow patches on the upper trail. Snow can fall even in August at 4,633m.
overview.fitness: Moderate to hard. The 1,585m climb from Ghangaria is steep and relentless — this is the most physically demanding section of any standard Uttarakhand pilgrimage trail. However, the motivation of reaching the gurdwara and the extraordinary lakeside setting drive most pilgrims forward. Good cardiovascular fitness and experience at altitude are recommended. Acclimatisation at Ghangaria for one night before ascending is strongly advised.

permitInfo: Ghangaria/Valley of Flowers park gate entry fee (same base as VoF — ₹150 Indian, ₹600 foreigner). Hemkund itself is a Sikh religious site — free entry to the gurdwara. No camping inside the sacred lake area. Temple open Jun–Oct only (snow closes it other months). Joshimath district medical check practice applies to Ghangaria approaches.

itinerary.title: Rishikesh to Govindghat via Joshimath
itinerary.desc: Drive to Govindghat — the trailhead on the Badrinath highway where the Lakshman Ganga valley opens. Register and pay park entry fees here.

itinerary.title: Govindghat to Ghangaria
itinerary.desc: Trek along the rushing Lakshman Ganga through forest with waterfalls. Ghangaria is the base village at 3,048m with accommodation and food. Gateway to both Hemkund Sahib and Valley of Flowers.

itinerary.title: Ghangaria to Hemkund Sahib
itinerary.desc: A steep but well-constructed trail climbs 6 km to the Hemkund lake and gurdwara at 4,633m. Snow patches are possible even in August. The gurdwara's langar (community kitchen) serves hot food to all visitors. The lake, ringed by seven peaks, is one of the most sacred places in Sikhism.

itinerary.title: Ghangaria to Govindghat — Return Drive
itinerary.desc: Trek back down to Govindghat, then drive to Rishikesh (9 hours). Optionally spend the previous day doing Valley of Flowers instead of returning immediately.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Ex Route Adventures on Pexels

name: Khaliya Top Trek

reviews.name: Ritika P. ★ Google Maps
reviews.text: The Panchachuli view from Khaliya Top in November is breathtaking — five glaciated peaks in a single frame above Munsiyari. The most dramatic peak view in Kumaon.

reviews.name: Henrik B. ★ AllTrails
reviews.text: Perfect short trek from Munsiyari. Easy enough for beginners but the reward is world-class. Come in February for the snow version.

description: An easy ridge walk above Munsiyari in Kumaon, Khaliya Top (3,500m) is famous for its direct view of the Panchachuli massif — five summits rising above the Munsiyari valley in a single unbroken sweep. The meadow is covered in snow from December to March and wildflowers in spring. One of Kumaon's most rewarding short treks.

overview.location: Khaliya Top (3,500m) is a high ridge above Munsiyari town in Pithoragarh district, Kumaon Himalayas. The summit meadow faces the Panchachuli massif (five peaks; highest 6,904m) directly across the Munsiyari valley in what many consider the finest single-point mountain panorama in Kumaon. The trail climbs through rhododendron and oak forest from Munsiyari town (2,200m). Khaliya is also the start of the Milam and Ralam glacier approach routes.
overview.history: Khaliya Top has been a traditional grazing ground and lookout point for the Munsiyari community for generations. Munsiyari itself was founded as a permanent settlement by Bhotiya (Shauka/Rang) trading families who were displaced from the high Milam and Ralam valleys after the 1962 border closure. The town became a trekking base in the 1990s after permits were liberalised for the Milam and Ralam glacier routes. Khaliya has been a popular day walk for visitors since Munsiyari's development as a hill station.
overview.length: 16 km round-trip from Munsiyari town over 2 days (8 km each way). Total elevation gain approximately 1,300m. Day 1: trek to Khaliya Top (5–6 hours). Day 2: rest and exploration, return to Munsiyari. Can be done as a single long day walk (9–10 hours) by fit trekkers.
overview.temperature: Mar–May: 0°C–15°C; rhododendron bloom; trail muddy from snowmelt. Oct–Nov: 2°C–15°C; finest Panchachuli views; recommended season. Dec–Mar: –5°C to 5°C; summit under snow; magnificent winter ridge — popular with snowshoe groups. Monsoon (Jul–Aug): Lush but overcast.
overview.fitness: Easy to moderate. The 1,300m gain over 8 km through forest is steady but not technical. Suitable for trekkers with basic fitness. The extraordinary Panchachuli panorama from the top — five glaciated summits rising directly above Munsiyari — is a reward disproportionate to the effort invested.

permitInfo: No formal permit. Register at Munsiyari forest range office. No overnight bugyal camping (HC order applies). Stay in Munsiyari town or forest rest house at base. Trek insurance recommended. Guide suggested in snow conditions.

itinerary.title: Kathgodam to Munsiyari
itinerary.desc: Drive from Kathgodam through Almora and Birthi Falls to Munsiyari. The first view of Panchachuli from Munsiyari town is a proper arrival moment — five summits rising directly above the rooftops.

itinerary.title: Munsiyari to Khaliya Top and Return
itinerary.desc: Climb through rhododendron and oak forest above the town to the Khaliya Top meadow. The Panchachuli group (5 peaks, highest 6,904m) towers above. In December–March the entire ridge is a snowfield. Return to Munsiyari.

itinerary.title: Munsiyari to Kathgodam — Return
itinerary.desc: Drive back to Kathgodam for trains or onward journeys to Delhi.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Sajal Niraula on Pexels

name: Darma Valley Trek
description: A scenic road-trip and short glacier trek into Darma Valley, Pithoragarh. Since 2024, the road is motorable all the way to Duktu village (3,048m). The trek is now a 4km walk each way along the Yuli River to the Panchachuli Glacier zero point (4,620m), with the five Panchachuli summits rising dramatically overhead. An Inner Line Permit (ILP) is required for this border-area valley.

overview.location: Darma Valley is in Pithoragarh district, Kumaon, Uttarakhand — a high-altitude gorge carved by the Dhauli Ganga river near the India–Nepal–Tibet border. The trek starts from Sobla village (1,670m), 42 km from Dharchula by road. The valley is home to 12 villages of the Rung (Rang/Shauka) community and is a base for Panchachuli (6,904m) expeditions. Dharchula town (895m) is the gateway, 330 km from Kathgodam.
overview.history: The Darma Valley is one of the historic Himalayan trade corridors once used by Rang/Bhotiya traders for wool-salt trade with Tibet across the Himalayan passes. The Rung community, also called Darmi, maintained these routes for centuries before the 1962 India-China war sealed the border. The five peaks of Panchachuli ('five cooking fires') are sacred in Hindu tradition — the Pandavas are believed to have cooked their last meal here before ascending to heaven. The valley retains one of the most intact examples of traditional Himalayan stone-and-wood architecture in Kumaon.
overview.length: Approximately 60 km from Sobla to Panchachuli Glacier base and back via Bungling. The route through the valley visits 6–7 villages over 8–9 days of trekking. Daily distances: 5–12 km. Maximum altitude: Panchachuli Glacier base at approximately 4,620m. The valley floor sits between 1,670m (Sobla) and 3,048m (Duktu/Dantu).
overview.temperature: May–June: Best season — trails clear of snow, rhododendrons in bloom at lower elevations, 10–25°C in valley. September–October: Second window, clear skies, 5–18°C. Monsoon (July–August): Heavy rain, slippery trails, landslide risk on the Dharchula–Tawaghat road — not recommended. December–April: Valley villages evacuated as Rung community winters in the plains.
overview.fitness: Moderate with some hard sections. Daily walking 5–12 km on forest and mountain trails. No extreme altitude (max 4,620m at glacier base). The Dar–Sela section (12 km) is the most demanding — long, steep, and at times narrow. ITBP inner line permit required — check at Baling checkpost. Suitable for trekkers with multi-day experience.

permitInfo.type: Inner Line Permit (ILP) — Pithoragarh District, Uttarakhand
permitInfo.cost: Nominal fee. Obtainable at SDM office, Dharchula. Also available online via Uttarakhand government ILP portal.
permitInfo.process: Apply at the SDM office in Dharchula with passport-sized photo, route map, and ID proof. Process takes 1–2 hours. Carry multiple copies — permit is checked at the ITBP camp at Baling village. Indian nationals only need ILP; no additional PAP required unless going to restricted border zones.
permitInfo.foreigners: Foreigners require both ILP and Protected Area Permit (PAP) for Pithoragarh border district. Apply well in advance through the Ministry of Home Affairs. Upper reaches near Panchachuli may require additional clearance.
permitInfo.note: The Rung community villages are inhabited only May–October — the entire population migrates to lower plains each winter. Homestays available in most villages (₹300–600/night). Carry sufficient cash — no ATMs beyond Dharchula. ITBP checkpost at Baling: register all trekkers. The plastic deposit system (₹100/item, refundable on return with wrapper) applies in the valley to reduce waste.

itinerary.title: Kathgodam to Dharchula
itinerary.desc: Drive from Kathgodam via Almora, Pithoragarh road through the scenic Kumaon hills. Cross Jauljibi — the confluence of Gori and Kali rivers — and follow the Kali River gorge to Dharchula, a border town where India faces Nepal across the river. Obtain the Inner Line Permit at the SDM office. Dharchula has good accommodation, ATMs, and a lively market — stock up on supplies.

itinerary.title: Dharchula to Sobla — Trek to Dar Village
itinerary.desc: Drive 42 km from Dharchula north through Tawaghat to Sobla (1,670m) — the last motorable point and entry to Darma Valley. The trek begins here: 5 km through rhododendron and mixed forest to Dar village at 2,134m. Dar is the first Rung community village — traditional stone houses with carved wooden windows. The Panchachuli summits appear for the first time above the valley.

itinerary.title: Dar to Sela Village
itinerary.desc: The longest and most demanding day — a 12 km trail through hillside pastoral fields and lush forests along the Dhauli Ganga. The path is narrow in sections and the gradient is unrelenting. Sela village at 2,438m is a beautiful Rung settlement with terraced fields and mountain views. Carcasses of mules on the trail are a reminder of how seriously the locals take this route.

itinerary.title: Sela to Baling Village
itinerary.desc: A relatively easier day — the trail undulates through dense conifer forest. The altitude gain is moderate and distant glacier views open up for the first time. Baling village at 2,743m has an ITBP (Indo-Tibetan Border Police) checkpost — register here. The forest department's Darma Valley sanctuary begins in this area.

itinerary.title: Baling to Duktu / Dantu
itinerary.desc: Short but spectacular day. Duktu and Dantu are the last two villages of Darma Valley and the highest permanently inhabited settlements in the region (3,048m). They sit on a broad meadow with an unobstructed full-frontal view of the Panchachuli massif — five summits rising to 6,904m in a single sweep. The Rung villages here have no grid electricity — solar lights only. Homestays are warm and welcoming.

itinerary.title: Duktu to Panchachuli Glacier Base and Back
itinerary.desc: The high point of the trek. A 4 km trail from Duktu heads east through alpine meadows and boulder fields to the snout of the Panchachuli Glacier at approximately 4,620m. The five Panchachuli peaks fill the horizon — an extraordinary view of one of Kumaon's greatest mountain massifs. Return to Duktu for the night.

itinerary.title: Duktu to Nagling
itinerary.desc: Begin the return journey. The trail from Duktu descends through the valley on the return route toward Nagling — a different Rung village offering a new perspective on the valley landscape.

itinerary.title: Nagling to Bungling — Drive to Dharchula
itinerary.desc: Final trekking day — 12 km from Nagling to Bungling village, the last settlement before the road begins. From Bungling, a jeep can be arranged back to Dharchula. Overnight in Dharchula.

itinerary.title: Dharchula to Kathgodam — Return Drive
itinerary.desc: Drive back through the Kumaon hills to Kathgodam for onward trains or buses to Delhi. The return drive through Pithoragarh, Almora, and Nainital region is scenic throughout.
