name: Rohini Bugyal Trek

reviews.name: Vibha K. ★ Google Maps
reviews.text: Rohini Bugyal after the Deoriatal lake is like discovering Garhwal's secret meadow. The flower display in May is extraordinary and there's almost no one else around.

reviews.name: Mark S. ★ AllTrails
reviews.text: Hidden gem above Chopta. The combination of Deoriatal, Rohini Bugyal, and Chandrashila in one trek is the best value for a week in Garhwal.

description: A hidden meadow trek in Rudraprayag district, Rohini Bugyal is a wide alpine plateau at 3,680m above the Okhimath valley. Often combined with Deoriatal and Chandrashila as a longer trek package, Rohini Bugyal itself is one of the finest flower meadows in Garhwal. Chaukhamba, Kedarnath Dome, and Neelkanth are clearly visible. Very few foreign visitors.

overview.location: Rohini Bugyal (3,680m) is a wide alpine plateau in Rudraprayag district above the Okhimath valley, one of the finest flower meadows in Garhwal with direct views of Chaukhamba (7,138m), Kedarnath Dome (6,831m), and Neelkanth (6,861m). It is often combined with Deoriatal lake and Chandrashila as part of a week-long Rudraprayag circuit trek, and remains one of the least-known of Garhwal's major bugyals.
overview.history: Rohini Bugyal is part of the traditional pastoral circuit above Okhimath and the Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary. The meadow has been a summer grazing ground for centuries and lies on the high ridge connecting the Kedarnath and Chopta belts. Its relative obscurity compared to Chopta and Deoriatal has protected it from commercialisation — no tea stalls, no crowds, and no vehicle access at the meadow level.
overview.length: 35 km over 4–5 days from Sari village (1,900m) near Ukhimath. Total elevation gain approximately 1,780m. The standard approach traverses Deoriatal lake (2.5 km from Sari) before continuing uphill to the bugyal. The Chaukhamba reflection at Deoriatal lake combined with the peak panorama at Rohini Bugyal makes a deeply satisfying combination trek.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 0°C–18°C; wildflower season; rhododendron forest on the approach. Sep–Oct: 0°C–12°C; best peak views; autumn colours below. Monsoon: Green but rainy. The bugyal camping ban restricts overnight stays on the meadow surface.
overview.fitness: Moderate. The forest and meadow approach is well-maintained and gradual. The altitude of 3,680m is manageable for trekkers with basic fitness who pace themselves. Suitable for those with 1 prior multi-day trek. The combination with Deoriatal and Chandrashila makes a complete 6–7 day Rudraprayag circuit.

permitInfo: Forest permit from local range office (Rudraprayag/Okhimath). No overnight bugyal camping under HC order. Stay at nearby forest rest houses. Trek insurance recommended. ID required.

itinerary.title: Rishikesh to Sari Village via Ukhimath
itinerary.desc: Drive through Rudraprayag and Ukhimath to Sari village — the main trailhead for the Deoriatal-Rohini Bugyal belt. Register at forest check-post.

itinerary.title: Sari to Deoriatal to Rohini Bugyal
itinerary.desc: Trek 2.5 km up to Deoriatal lake (2,438m) — the famous Chaukhamba reflection lake — then continue on the less-travelled trail up to the Rohini Bugyal plateau. Views of the Kedarnath group emerge above the treeline.

itinerary.title: Rohini Bugyal Exploration
itinerary.desc: Rest and explore the meadow. Wildflowers from April to June. Kedarnath Dome, Chaukhamba, and Neelkanth fill the north and northwest horizon.

itinerary.title: Rohini Bugyal to Sari — Return to Rishikesh
itinerary.desc: Descend to Sari, then drive back to Rishikesh.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Satyabrata Maiti on Pexels

name: Gidara Bugyal Trek

reviews.name: Tarun R. ★ Google Maps
reviews.text: We were alone on the Gidara plateau for two days. Bandarpoonch from here is closer than anywhere else I've seen it. The forest approach is magnificent.

reviews.name: Julia A. ★ AllTrails
reviews.text: Underrated in every guide. The meadow is as beautiful as Dayara Bugyal but without a single other trekker. The peak views are exceptional.

description: A secretive high meadow in Uttarkashi district, Gidara Bugyal sits at 3,700m with direct views of Bandarpoonch, Swargarohini, Black Peak (Kalanag), and the Tons valley. Far less visited than Dayara Bugyal which is just 15 km south, Gidara offers a genuine remote meadow experience. The approach from Morinda village is through dense mixed forest.

overview.location: Gidara Bugyal (3,700m) is a remote high meadow in Uttarkashi district with direct views of Bandarpoonch (6,316m), Swargarohini (6,252m), and Black Peak (Kalanag, 6,387m). The approach is from Morinda or Bansol village above Uttarkashi, following a far less-travelled path than the better-known Dayara Bugyal 15 km south. It is one of the most genuinely undiscovered bugyals in Garhwal.
overview.history: Gidara Bugyal is part of the ancient shepherd grazing territory above the Bhagirathi valley and takes its name from local pastoral tradition. Unlike the well-developed Dayara Bugyal circuit, Gidara has no commercial trekking infrastructure — no signboards, no rest houses, no organised campsites. The forest above Bansol through which the approach passes is ancient oak and silver birch, virtually unchanged by human activity.
overview.length: 35–40 km over 4–5 days from Uttarkashi via Morinda or Bansol. Total elevation gain approximately 2,300m. The trail is unmarked — a local guide is essential. Full camping provisions must be carried from Uttarkashi.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–18°C; the meadow at its most colourful with wildflowers. Sep–Oct: 0°C–12°C; Bandarpoonch and Black Peak at their most vivid. Winter: Deep snow. The bugyal camping ban restricts overnight stays on the meadow.
overview.fitness: Moderate. The approach is sustained uphill through beautiful forest with no technical terrain. Good basic fitness and comfort with basic camping self-sufficiency are the requirements. The extraordinary solitude — no other trekkers for the entire final 2 days — is the defining experience.

permitInfo: Forest permit from Uttarkashi Forest range office or Morinda/Bansol check-post. No overnight bugyal camping (HC order). Trek insurance and ID required.

itinerary.title: Dehradun to Uttarkashi to Morinda Village
itinerary.desc: Drive to Uttarkashi then continue on the less-travelled Bansol-Morinda road. Register at the local range post.

itinerary.title: Morinda to Bansol
itinerary.desc: Trek through oak and silver birch into the high forest zone. Bansol is a small shepherd settlement in a clearing with partial views of the Bandarpoonch group.

itinerary.title: Bansol to Gidara Bugyal
itinerary.desc: Emerge onto the Gidara Bugyal plateau. Bandarpoonch, Swargarohini, and Black Peak (Kalanag, 6,387m) dominate the north horizon. The meadow is a sweeping grassland of extraordinary beauty and solitude.

itinerary.title: Gidara Bugyal to Morinda — Return to Dehradun
itinerary.desc: Retrace to Morinda over 2 days, then drive back to Dehradun (195 km, ~6 hours).

coverImageCredit: Photo by Satyabrata Maiti on Pexels

name: Vasuki Tal Trek (Kedarnath)

permitInfo.type: Kedarnath Yatra Registration + Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary Permit
permitInfo.where: Yatra registration at Gaurikund counter (mandatory) or online; Wildlife Sanctuary permit from Range Officer Ukhimath
permitInfo.fee: Yatra registration ₹50 per person; Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary entry fee applicable
permitInfo.note: Vasuki Tal lies within Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary. Trek starts from Gaurikund (1,980m) — last motorable point, 232 km from Rishikesh via Rudraprayag–Guptkashi. Helicopter options: Phata/Sersi/Guptkashi to Kedarnath (₹3,500–5,000 one way). Kedarnath shrine opens on Akshay Tritiya (Apr/May) and closes on Bhai Dooj (Oct/Nov). Do NOT trek Jul–Aug monsoon (landslide risk). Important: do not confuse with the completely different Vasuki Tal (4,880m) in the Gangotri region — see trek ID 411. That lake is reached via Tapovan and Nandanvan in Uttarkashi district.

description: A sacred glacial lake at 4,135m (14,200 ft) set 8 km above the Kedarnath shrine — offering panoramic views of Chaukhamba (7,138m), Kedar Dome (6,831m), and the Mandakini Valley far below. The lake, shaped like a coiled snake, is named for Vasuki — the serpent around Lord Shiva's neck. Lord Vishnu is believed to have bathed here on Raksha Bandhan. Most trekkers do this as a day extension from Kedarnath, returning the same evening. Not to be confused with the higher Vasuki Tal (4,880m) in the Gangotri region, which requires a full 9-day expedition via Tapovan and Nandanvan.

overview.location: Vasuki Tal (4,135m / 14,200 ft) is a large glacial lake — roughly 0.5 km in radius — in Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary, Rudraprayag district. It lies 8 km above the Kedarnath temple (3,584m) and 24 km from the Gaurikund roadhead (1,980m). The route from Kedarnath climbs to Vasuki Top (c.4,500m) — a high ridge with sweeping views — then drops ~900 m to the lake. The Chaturangi Glacier flows nearby. Note: this is an entirely different lake from the Vasuki Tal (4,880m) in Uttarkashi district, reached via Gangotri–Tapovan–Nandanvan (Trek ID 411).
overview.history: Vasuki Tal is named for Vasuki — the great serpent king coiled around Lord Shiva's neck — and the lake itself is shaped like a coiled snake. Hindu mythology holds that Lord Vishnu bathed here on Raksha Bandhan, purifying the waters. Brahma Kamal, the sacred lotus of the Himalayas, blooms abundantly around the lake's edge. The surrounding Kedarnath Wildlife Sanctuary (975 sq km), established in 1972, protects snow leopard, Himalayan black bear, bharal, and musk deer. The 2013 Kedarnath disaster (flash flood from Chorabari Glacier) altered the valley terrain; the trail to Vasuki Tal was subsequently restored.
overview.length: 48 km total over 4 days from Gaurikund and back. Standard itinerary: Day 1 Gaurikund→Kedarnath (14 km, 6–7 hrs); Day 2 acclimatisation at Kedarnath; Day 3 Kedarnath→Vasuki Top→Vasuki Tal→Kedarnath (16 km round trip, 6–8 hrs); Day 4 Kedarnath→Gaurikund (14 km, 5–6 hrs). From Kedarnath temple to Vasuki Top (c.4,500m): continuous steep ascent of ~916m. From Vasuki Top to Vasuki Tal: ~900m downhill to the lake.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–18°C at Kedarnath; –2°C–8°C at Vasuki Tal; snow patches on approach — crampons may be needed in early May. Sep–Oct: 0°C–15°C at Kedarnath; –5°C to 5°C at lake; clearest skies and best views; the recommended season. Jul–Aug: Monsoon — dangerous landslide risk on the Gaurikund–Kedarnath trail; not recommended. Nov–Apr: Shrine closed; deep snow; inaccessible.
overview.fitness: Moderate to Hard. The Kedarnath–Vasuki Top climb involves a steep 916m ascent at high altitude after already trekking 14 km from Gaurikund. Good cardiovascular fitness and prior Himalayan trek experience recommended. Most trekkers hire a guide for the Vasuki Tal extension. Preparation: 6–8 weeks of cardio and hill walking.

itinerary.title: Rishikesh → Gaurikund → Kedarnath
itinerary.desc: Drive from Rishikesh via Rudraprayag and Guptkashi to Gaurikund (232 km, 7 hrs). Register yatra at Gaurikund counter. The 14 km trail to Kedarnath passes through Jungle Chatti and Rambara alongside the Mandakini gorge — India's busiest pilgrimage trail, shared with ponies, mules, and palanquins. Attend evening aarti at the ancient Kedarnath Jyotirlinga temple.

itinerary.title: Kedarnath — Acclimatisation Day
itinerary.desc: Crucial acclimatisation at Kedarnath before the 4,500m Vasuki Top the next day. Visit the Kedarnath temple (built by the Pandavas; restored by Adi Shankaracharya in the 8th century). Walk to Gandhi Sarovar lake (1.5 km) and observe the Chorabari Glacier. Rest well — the Vasuki Tal extension the next day is demanding.

itinerary.title: Kedarnath → Vasuki Top (4,500m) → Vasuki Tal (4,135m) → Kedarnath
itinerary.desc: Start by 5–6 AM. The trail climbs steeply from Kedarnath to Vasuki Top ridge (c.4,500m) — panoramic views of Chaukhamba (7,138m), Kedar Dome (6,831m), and the deep Mandakini Valley below. Then descend ~900m on the north face to Vasuki Tal itself: a large, clear glacial lake (~0.5 km radius) fringed with Brahma Kamal flowers. The Chaturangi Glacier is nearby. Spend an hour at the lake, then retrace back over Vasuki Top and return to Kedarnath before dark. A guide is strongly recommended for this section.

itinerary.title: Kedarnath → Gaurikund → Rishikesh
itinerary.desc: Early descent on the 14 km Kedarnath–Gaurikund trail. Drive back to Rishikesh via four sacred river confluences (Panch Prayag) of the Garhwal Himalayas.

coverImageCredit: Photo by sudhanshu sharma on Pexels

name: Alkapuri Glacier Trek

reviews.name: Venkat R. ★ Google Maps
reviews.text: The Satopanth triangular lake at 4,400m is one of India's sacred wonders. The Alkapuri glacier above it is a high-altitude wilderness that few trekkers ever reach. Spiritually profound and physically demanding.

reviews.name: Ingrid T. ★ AllTrails
reviews.text: Not to be taken lightly — serious altitude, serious terrain. But the Sacred Satopanth lake and the glacier above are extraordinary. Badrinath is a world-class base for high-altitude trekkers.

description: The source of the Alaknanda River, Alkapuri Glacier lies at 4,660m above Badrinath. The trek from Mana village approaches the glacier through the Satopanth basin — one of the most dramatic and sacred landscapes in the Himalayas, with the Satopanth lake (Hindu/Jain sacred triangular lake) en route. Swargarohini peak (6,252m) and the Badrinath ridge dominate the upper cirque.

overview.location: Alkapuri Glacier (4,660m) is the source of the Alaknanda River — one of the primary headwaters of the Ganges — above Badrinath in Chamoli district. The route approaches through the Satopanth basin via Mana village, the Laxmi Van campsite, and the sacred Satopanth Lake (4,402m), continuing to the glacier's snout. The Swargarohini group (6,252m) and the Badrinath peaks rise above the upper cirque.
overview.history: The Alaknanda is one of the main tributaries of the Ganga and its source at Alkapuri has deep sacred significance. The name 'Alkapuri' refers to the celestial city of Kubera (god of wealth) in Hindu cosmology, said to lie beyond the high Himalayan passes. The Satopanth Lake en route — the triangular sacred lake associated with the Hindu Trinity — is one of the most significant high-altitude pilgrimage sites in Garhwal.
overview.length: 60 km over 7–8 days from Badrinath. Total elevation gain approximately 1,527m from Badrinath. Shares the first section with the Satopanth Tal trek as far as Satopanth Lake, then continues to the glacier. Requires NP permit, ITBP registration at Mana, and Joshimath medical certificate.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 0°C–10°C at Satopanth Lake; glacier approach icy. Sep–Oct: –5°C to 8°C at Satopanth; best conditions. Badrinath NP closes by Diwali. Night temperatures at the glacier drop to –15°C even in September.
overview.fitness: Hard. High altitude approach to 4,660m requires proper multi-night acclimatisation at Badrinath. Boulder-field navigation and glacier moraine approach are physically demanding. Joshimath medical check and insurance mandatory. Prior experience on multi-day routes above 4,000m essential.

permitInfo: Forest/NP permit from Badrinath/Mana gate (DFO Chamoli). Medical certificate and trek insurance mandatory (Joshimath district practice for 4,660m+). ITBP registration at Mana village. Carry multiple permit copies.

itinerary.title: Rishikesh to Badrinath
itinerary.desc: Drive to Badrinath. Register permits. Badrinath Vishnu temple darshan in the evening is a memorable experience.

itinerary.title: Badrinath to Mana to Laxmi Van
itinerary.desc: Walk through Mana village (last Indian village) and up the Alaknanda to the Laxmi Van campsite.

itinerary.title: Laxmi Van to Satopanth Lake
itinerary.desc: Cross boulder fields and meadows to the triangular Satopanth Lake — one of Hinduism's most sacred high-altitude lakes, shaped like a triangle and associated with Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva.

itinerary.title: Satopanth to Alkapuri Glacier Base
itinerary.desc: Continue up the Satopanth glacier to the Alkapuri glacial basin — the true source of the Alaknanda. A high-altitude wilderness camp surrounded by ice and rock.

itinerary.title: Glacier Exploration and Return to Badrinath
itinerary.distance: Return 27 km over 2 days + 300 km road
itinerary.desc: Explore the glacier, then retrace to Badrinath over 2 days and drive back to Rishikesh.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Satyabrata Maiti on Pexels

name: Borasu Pass Trek

reviews.name: Gaurav B. ★ Google Maps
reviews.text: Borasu Pass into Kinnaur is the most dramatic border crossing in the Indian Himalayas. Ruinsara Tal before the pass is extraordinary — then Chitkul on the other side is like entering a completely different country.

reviews.name: Lena K. ★ AllTrails
reviews.text: Technical but magnificent. The Kinnaur Kailash range reveals itself on the descent into Chitkul. The red rice and apple orchards after weeks in the high Himalayas are very welcome.

description: A high trans-Himalayan pass (5,450m) connecting the Uttarkashi district to Kinnaur in Himachal Pradesh, Borasu Pass crosses from the Tons River watershed into the Baspa Valley. One of the oldest trade routes between Uttarakhand and the Tibetan plateau, the trail passes through remote Sangla Valley terrain with views of the Kinnaur Kailash range. Technical snow crossing at the pass.

overview.location: Borasu Pass (5,450m) connects the Uttarkashi district of Uttarakhand with Kinnaur district of Himachal Pradesh — one of the highest and most historically significant trans-Himalayan passes in the western Himalayas. The approach from Sankri passes through the Govind Sanctuary and the sacred Ruinsara Tal lake (4,025m). The descent into Kinnaur reaches Chitkul village — the last village in the Baspa Valley and one of the most beautifully sited villages in India.
overview.history: Borasu Pass has been used for centuries as a trade route between the Tons River valley communities and the Baspa Valley's Kinnauri culture. Salt, wool, and mountain goods moved across this pass as part of the broader trans-Himalayan trade network. The Kinnauri culture on the descent side has deep Tibetan Buddhist influences — ancient gompas, carved wood facades, and distinctive flat-roofed architecture define Chitkul and the Baspa Valley villages.
overview.length: 70 km over 9–10 days from Sankri to Chitkul (one-way crossing). Total elevation gain approximately 3,530m on the Uttarakhand approach. The pass crossing day involves technical snow climbing on the Uttarakhand side. Foreigners crossing into Kinnaur require a Protected Area Permit (PAP) from SDM Reckong Peo — apply 2+ weeks in advance.
overview.temperature: Jun: Snow on pass; technical crossing. Sep–Oct: –5°C to 5°C at the pass; best stable conditions. May: Very technical with maximum snow. Pass closes November–April.
overview.fitness: Hard. One of the highest standard trekking passes in the Indian Himalayas. Technical snow climbing on the Uttarakhand approach side. Prior experience on high-altitude pass treks is essential. Crampons and trekking poles required. Preparation: 12 weeks of intensive training. Guide is strongly recommended.

permitInfo: Uttarakhand side: Forest permit from Uttarkashi Forest Range (Harsil/Sankri area). Himachal exit: Kinnaur district forest entry. Foreigners: Kinnaur requires PAP (Protected Area Permit) from SDM/DC Reckong Peo — apply at least 2 weeks in advance. Indians: no PAP needed in Kinnaur open valleys. Trek insurance mandatory. Medical certificate required for the 5,450m crossing.

itinerary.title: Dehradun to Sankri or Harsil
itinerary.desc: Drive to either Sankri (Tons valley approach) or Harsil (Bhagirathi side) depending on chosen route variant. Collect forest permits.

itinerary.title: Osla / Taluka to Har Ki Dun Junction
itinerary.desc: Trek up the Supin valley through the Govind Sanctuary to the Har Ki Dun junction. The Swargarohini group stands above the valley head.

itinerary.title: Trek to Ruinsara Tal
itinerary.desc: Climb to the sacred Ruinsara Lake in its glacier basin. Bandarpoonch and Kalanag loom above.

itinerary.title: Ruinsara to Borasu Pass Base Camp
itinerary.desc: Approach the high camp below the Borasu Pass. Ice and snow may be encountered.

itinerary.title: Borasu Pass Crossing to Kinnaur Side
itinerary.desc: Cross Borasu Pass at 5,450m. Technical snow climbing on the Uttarakhand side. A long descent leads to Chitkul — the last village in the Baspa Valley — famous for its red rice and traditional architecture.

itinerary.title: Chitkul to Sangla to Reckong Peo — Return
itinerary.desc: Road return from Chitkul via Sangla, Reckong Peo, and Shimla to Delhi (520 km, 14–15 hrs or 2 days with stop in Shimla). Alternatively fly Shimla to Delhi.

coverImageCredit: Photo by UTkarsh on Pexels

name: Trishul Base Camp Trek

reviews.name: Neeraj K. ★ Google Maps
reviews.text: Trishul is one of the most beautiful peaks in India and seeing it from the base camp directly below the three prongs is an astonishing experience. Very remote — carry everything.

reviews.name: Anita S. ★ AllTrails
reviews.text: Harder than it looks. The glacier approach is serious. But the combination of Trishul, Nanda Devi, and Panchachuli from one campsite is extraordinary.

description: The three-pronged Trishul massif (main peak 7,120m) — Shiva's trident — dominates the skyline above Kausani and Munsiyari. The base camp approach from Munsiyari via the Trishul glacier offers extraordinary close views of Nanda Devi, Panchachuli, and the Trishul peaks in a remote cirque. One of the finest mountaineering base camp treks in Kumaon.

overview.location: The Trishul massif — 'Shiva's Trident' — consists of three peaks (main summit 7,120m) visible from across the Kumaon and Garhwal Himalayas. The base camp approach from Munsiyari (2,200m) via Thalkedar and Namik village in Pithoragarh district reaches the glacier cirque at 4,500m, directly beneath the three-pronged south face. Views of Nanda Devi (7,816m), Panchachuli (6,904m), and Trishul's three summits are visible simultaneously from the approach.
overview.history: Trishul — literally 'trident' — is Shiva's weapon and one of the most recognisable peak forms in the Himalayas. It was first climbed in 1907 by T. G. Longstaff and companions — the first ascent of a 7,000m+ peak anywhere in the world, a milestone in Himalayan mountaineering history. The Namik Valley approach to the base camp was documented by Longstaff's expedition and has served as the approach for subsequent mountaineering teams ever since.
overview.length: 58 km over 7–8 days from Munsiyari. Total elevation gain approximately 2,300m from Munsiyari. The forest section (Munsiyari to Thalkedar) is through dense rhododendron and oak. The upper section (Namik to base camp) crosses open moraine and high-altitude grassland.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–18°C at lower camps; –2°C to 5°C at base camp. Sep–Oct: 0°C–12°C; clearest conditions. Remote nature requires self-sufficiency in all weather. Night temperatures at base camp reach –10°C even in September.
overview.fitness: Hard. Remote route with no infrastructure beyond Namik village. Full camping self-sufficiency required in the upper valley. ITBP checkpost en route. Medical certificate and insurance mandatory. Prior multi-day Himalayan trek experience at 4,000m+ is essential.

permitInfo: Forest permit from Munsiyari range office (Pithoragarh Forest Division). Trek insurance and medical certificate mandatory for this altitude. ITBP checkpost en route. Remote route — limited facilities; carry all provisions.

itinerary.title: Kathgodam to Munsiyari
itinerary.desc: Drive to Munsiyari. Collect permits and prepare for the Trishul approach.

itinerary.title: Munsiyari to Thalkedar
itinerary.desc: Trek through dense rhododendron and oak forest above Munsiyari. Thalkedar is a clearing with first views of the Trishul peaks.

itinerary.title: Thalkedar to Namik Village
itinerary.desc: Continue up the Namik Gad valley. Namik is an upper village with exceptional views of Trishul, Nanda Ghunti, and Panchachuli.

itinerary.title: Namik to Trishul Base Camp
itinerary.desc: Approach the Trishul glacier base. The three peaks of Trishul rise directly overhead. Nanda Devi (7,816m) is visible to the south above the Nanda Devi sanctuary walls.

itinerary.title: Trishul Base Camp to Munsiyari — Return Drive
itinerary.desc: Retrace to Munsiyari over 3 days, then drive back to Kathgodam.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Rukia Sultana on Pexels

name: Kartik Swami Trek

reviews.name: Kavya S. ★ Google Maps
reviews.text: A completely underrated viewpoint. The panorama of peaks from Kartik Swami temple includes Kedarnath, Chaukhamba, Trishul, and even Nanda Devi. Worth every step for the view alone.

reviews.name: Peter H. ★ AllTrails
reviews.text: Short, beautiful forest trail leading to a magnificent viewpoint. Perfect half-day trek near Rudraprayag. The temple itself is charming.

description: A short but dramatic pilgrimage and viewpoint trek near Pokhri village in Rudraprayag district, Kartik Swami temple at 3,048m is dedicated to Kartikeya (Murugan) — the son of Shiva. The trek passes through oak and rhododendron forest and arrives at an extraordinary panoramic viewpoint with views of Kedarnath, Chaukhamba, Trishul, Nanda Devi, and Kamet on clear days.

overview.location: Kartik Swami temple (3,048m) — dedicated to Kartikeya/Murugan, the son of Shiva — sits on a compact summit 4 km above Kanakchauri village near Pokhri in Rudraprayag district. The summit commands a 270° panorama of Himalayan peaks: Kedarnath (6,940m), Chaukhamba (7,138m), Trishul (7,120m), Nanda Devi (7,816m), and Kamet (7,756m) are all visible on a clear day. Rudraprayag is the nearest major town (30 km).
overview.history: Kartik Swami is one of the rarer Hindu pilgrimage sites dedicated to Kartikeya (also called Skanda or Murugan) — the war god and son of Shiva and Parvati. The temple on this summit is ancient and is believed to be the site where Kartikeya meditated after his famous race with Ganesha around the world. Local tradition holds the summit as particularly sacred for prayers for sons and for military success.
overview.length: 8 km round-trip (4 km each way) from Kanakchauri village (1,640m). Total elevation gain approximately 1,408m. Trek typically done in a single long day (4–5 hours up, 2.5 hours down) from Rudraprayag area. Can be combined with a Chopta/Deoriatal visit as a 2–3 day Rudraprayag district loop.
overview.temperature: Mar–Jun: 5°C–20°C; forest in bloom; best combined with rhododendron season. Sep–Nov: 2°C–15°C; clearest peak views. Dec–Feb: –2°C to 8°C; possible snow at summit; worth the effort for winter peak panorama. Monsoon: Trail slippery but possible.
overview.fitness: Easy to moderate. The 1,408m elevation gain over 4 km is the most demanding aspect — a sustained but non-technical climb. Suitable for fit adults and older teenagers. The relatively short distance makes it achievable for those with moderate fitness. One of the most underrated panoramic viewpoints in Uttarakhand.

permitInfo: No formal permit required. Short religious trek. Forest range check-post at trailhead may require ID registration. No camping. Day visit only. Trek insurance voluntary.

itinerary.title: Rishikesh to Pokhri — Trek to Kartik Swami
itinerary.camp: Return to Pokhri or Rudraprayag guesthouses
itinerary.desc: Drive to Pokhri village near Rudraprayag. A 4 km forest trail climbs to the Kartik Swami temple at 3,048m — a compact shrine on a peak with a 270° panorama of Himalayan peaks. Return the same day.

itinerary.title: Return to Rishikesh
itinerary.desc: Drive back to Rishikesh from Pokhri/Rudraprayag.

coverImageCredit: Photo by dinesh verma on Pexels

name: Dokriani Glacier Trek

reviews.name: Sanjay K. ★ Google Maps
reviews.text: The Dokriani glacier is scientifically important and visually beautiful. The approach through the forest above Harsil is gorgeous. Not many other trekkers — highly recommended for those who want genuine peace.

reviews.name: Rachel B. ★ AllTrails
reviews.text: An underrated glacier approach. The Harsil valley is beautiful and the trek itself is challenging but very rewarding. Jogin peak from the snout is a stunning sight.

description: The Dokriani glacier is one of the most scientifically monitored glaciers in India — a 5-km-long glacier at 3,900m–5,000m in the upper Bhagirathi basin of Uttarkashi district. The trek from Harsil passes through the beautiful Jalandhari village and forests of the Bhagirathi catchment. The glacier's snout is dramatically accessible and the moraines offer excellent views of Jogin, Draupadi Ka Danda, and the Gangotri group.

overview.location: The Dokriani Glacier (3,900m–5,000m) is a 5-km-long glacier in the upper Bhagirathi basin of Uttarkashi district, one of the most scientifically monitored glaciers in India. The approach is from Harsil village (2,620m) — a beautiful apple-orchard settlement on the Bhagirathi River — via the Jalandhari Valley. The glacier sits beneath Jogin I (6,465m), Draupadi Ka Danda (5,716m), and Gangotri group peaks.
overview.history: Dokriani Glacier has been under continuous scientific monitoring by the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology since the 1990s and is one of India's primary reference points for measuring Himalayan glacier retreat. Harsil below has its own extraordinary history — it was the domain of Frederick 'Pahari' Wilson, a British-era adventurer who built a timber empire here in the 1860s–80s, married a local woman, and whose descendants still live in the valley. Wilson's story inspired Ruskin Bond's novel A Song of India.
overview.length: 40 km over 5–6 days from Harsil. Total elevation gain approximately 2,280m from Harsil to the glacier zone. The approach through the Dokriani Gad (stream valley) is through pristine forest that sees very few outside visitors. Forest permit from Harsil range office required.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–18°C; the glacier snout most accessible after snowmelt. Sep–Oct: 0°C–12°C; clear and stable. Remote nature requires complete self-sufficiency. The Harsil valley is also notable for its apple orchards — September is harvest season.
overview.fitness: Moderate. The approach is sustained uphill through forest with no technical terrain until the glacier moraines. Prior multi-day trek experience is recommended. The scientific interest of one of India's most closely observed glaciers, combined with the extraordinary solitude of the approach valley, makes this a deeply rewarding choice for experienced trekkers seeking something genuinely off the beaten path.

permitInfo: Forest permit from Harsil range office (Uttarkashi Forest Division). Uttarkashi district: trek insurance required, medical certificate for 50+. Carry permits for forest checkposts. ITBP presence in the area — ITBP registration advisable.

itinerary.title: Haridwar to Harsil
itinerary.desc: Drive through Uttarkashi to Harsil — a village famous for its apple orchards and Wilson's tragic 19th-century story. The Bhagirathi here is a cold, clear river flowing through pine forests.

itinerary.title: Harsil to Jalandhari / Dokriani Trek Entry
itinerary.desc: Trek up the Dokriani Gad valley through dense forest. The valley is lush and less-visited. Jogin and Draupadi Ka Danda peaks appear ahead.

itinerary.title: Dokriani Base to Glacier Snout
itinerary.desc: Approach the Dokriani glacier snout through boulder moraines. The glacier is a scientifically observed retreating body — ice structures and meltwater pools at the snout.

itinerary.title: Glacier Exploration — Return to Harsil
itinerary.desc: Explore the glacier on day 4, then return to Harsil and drive back to Haridwar over day 5.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Rishu Bhosale on Pexels

name: Bhrigu Lake

permitInfo.type: HP Trekking Management System Registration + Forest Permit
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in before departure; DFO Kullu Forest Division check-post at Gulaba
permitInfo.fee: ₹50–₹100 forest entry fee; HP TMS registration mandatory for all trekkers (Indian and foreign)
permitInfo.note: HP government mandates all trekkers register on the Trekking Management System (trekking.hp.gov.in) before entering any high-altitude trek in Himachal. Medical fitness certificate and valid ID required at registration. Gulaba check-post strictly enforces TMS receipts. Trek insurance mandatory; medical evacuation insurance recommended for treks above 4,000m.

description: The crown jewel of easy-moderate Manali treks. Bhrigu Lake (4,300m) is a stunning glacial tarn perched above the Rohtang Pass ridgeline east of Manali, offering sweeping views of the Kullu Valley, Rohtang, and the Lahaul peaks — all within 2–3 days from Manali town. Named for the sage Bhrigu who is said to have meditated here, the lake's deep blue waters and dramatic mountain backdrop make it one of Himachal's most photographed high-altitude lakes.

overview.location: Bhrigu Lake (4,300m) lies on the high ridge east of Manali town in Kullu district, immediately above the Solang Valley and Rohtang corridor. The approach starts from Vashisht village (2,050m) or Gulaba (2,900m) on the old Rohtang road — both reachable in 30 minutes from Manali bus stand. The lake sits in a glacial bowl with Rohtang Pass (3,978m) to the south, the Lahaul peaks to the north, and the entire Kullu Valley stretching west. Deo Tibba (6,001m) and Indrasan (6,221m) are visible on clear days.
overview.history: Bhrigu Lake takes its name from the sage Bhrigu — the celestial astronomer and one of the seven great rishis of Vedic tradition. The lake is considered sacred in Hindu tradition; Bhrigu is said to have meditated beside it and compiled his astronomical texts here. The surrounding meadows have been summer grazing grounds for the Gaddi shepherd community for centuries. The HP government's Trekking Management System lists Bhrigu Lake as one of Himachal's premier registered trekking destinations; the Gulaba check-post was established in the 2010s to enforce environmental regulations after overtrekking began damaging the high meadows.
overview.length: The standard route from Gulaba (2,900m) to the lake and back covers 22 km over 4–5 days, with a total elevation gain of 1,400m. Day 1: drive to Gulaba and trek to Rola Kholi meadow (3,500m) — 7 km, 4–5 hours. Day 2: ascend to Bhrigu Lake (4,300m) for sunrise, then descend to Rola Kholi — 7 km, 5–6 hours. Day 3: return to Gulaba and Manali — 8 km, 4 hours. An alternative 1-night approach can compress this to 3 days for fit trekkers.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–18°C at meadows; 0°C–5°C at lake. Snow patches near the lake in May; meadows turn lush green by June with wildflowers in bloom. July–Aug: Monsoon rarely affects this ridgeline heavily — it sits in a partial rain shadow. 8°C–20°C at meadows; cloud builds in afternoon. Sep–Oct: 0°C–15°C at meadows; –5°C at lake; the most spectacular season — crystal-clear blue skies and vivid autumn colours. Nov–Apr: Deep snow blocks the approach; trek closed.
overview.fitness: Moderate. Suitable for trekkers with basic fitness and prior experience of day hikes at altitude. The total elevation gain of 1,400m spread over 2 trek days is manageable for most healthy adults with a gradual approach. Altitude of 4,300m requires proper acclimatisation — spending at least 1 night in Manali (2,050m) before starting is essential. No technical terrain. Preparation: 4–6 weeks of cardio and hill walking with a light pack.

itinerary.title: Manali to Gulaba — Trek to Gulaba Meadows (Jonker Thatch)
itinerary.desc: Drive 22 km from Manali to Gulaba roadhead on the Manali–Leh highway. Register at the forest check-post. The trail immediately enters open oak and deodar forest, then opens onto vast alpine meadows. Jonker Thatch (also called Gulaba Meadows/Gulaba Bugyal) is the first campsite — a wide grassy shelf with first views of Hanuman Tibba and the Seven Sister peaks. Short day by design — the altitude gain to 3,135m in just 90 minutes of trekking requires a slow approach.

itinerary.title: Jonker Thatch — Rola Kholi
itinerary.desc: A steep but beautiful climb from the Jonker Thatch meadow through birch and rhododendron to Rola Kholi (3,800m) — a massive bowl-shaped grazing ground used by Gaddi shepherds. The treeline is left behind completely here. Views of Solang Valley, Manali, and the entire Pir Panjal range expanding with each metre of altitude. Rola Kholi is the base camp for the lake — the final push begins tomorrow.

itinerary.title: Rola Kholi — Bhrigu Lake — Return to Rola Kholi
itinerary.desc: Early start — by 6 AM. The trail climbs steeply from Rola Kholi on a rocky ridge path above the meadows. The lake often sits in cloud by early afternoon. Bhrigu Lake (4,300m) is a sacred glacial lake named after Maharishi Bhrigu — one of the Saptarishis — who is believed to have meditated on its shores. The lake is unusually deep and rarely freezes completely even in winter. Panoramic views: Deo Tibba (6,001m), Hanuman Tibba (5,982m), Indrasan (6,221m), the Pir Panjal and Dhauladhar ranges. Descend by the same route to Rola Kholi for the night.

itinerary.title: Rola Kholi — Gulaba — Drive to Manali
itinerary.desc: Descend 8 km through the meadows and forest back to Gulaba roadhead. The descent is easier on the legs than the ascent — allow 3 hours at a comfortable pace. Drive back to Manali (22 km). Typically back in Manali by 3–4 PM.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Winson Mathew on Pexels

name: Beas Kund Trek

permitInfo.type: HP Trekking Management System Registration + Solang Valley Forest Permit
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; Solang Nullah check-post at trek entry
permitInfo.fee: ₹50 forest entry; HP TMS online registration mandatory
permitInfo.note: HP TMS registration at trekking.hp.gov.in is mandatory for all trekkers. Solang Nullah check-post at the start of the trek verifies TMS registration receipt. Medical certificate and ID mandatory. This is one of Himachal's most-visited beginner treks and the check-post is strictly managed in season. Trek insurance is compulsory under HP trekking rules.

description: The sacred source of the Beas River, reached on one of Manali's best beginner treks. Beas Kund (3,700m) is a glacial lake tucked beneath the snowfields of Solang Nullah valley — the same valley famous for skiing in winter. The trek weaves through meadows of wildflowers and glacial streams to a sacred pool that Hindus revere as the bathing place of the sage Vyas (Beas), who wrote the Mahabharata.

overview.location: Beas Kund (3,700m) is the glacial source of the Beas River, situated in the upper Solang Nullah valley northwest of Manali, Kullu district. The trek starts from Solang Nullah (2,480m) — the famous ski resort village 14 km from Manali — and ascends through meadows beneath Friendship Peak (5,289m) and Hanuman Tibba (5,982m). The Beas River flows 470 km south to the Punjab plains from this single glacial pool.
overview.history: Beas Kund is named for the sage Vyas (Beas in Punjabi/Hindi) — the legendary author who dictated the Mahabharata to Ganesha. The lake is said to be where Vyas bathed after completing the great epic. The Beas River — one of the five sacred rivers of the Punjab — originates here. The site has been a pilgrimage destination for Hindu devotees for centuries. Solang Nullah below was developed as a ski resort in the 1970s under HPTDC. The HP government now uses Beas Kund as a model trek for TMS registration enforcement.
overview.length: 26 km round-trip over 3–4 days from Solang Nullah. Total elevation gain from Solang (2,480m) to Beas Kund (3,700m): 1,220m. Day 1: Solang to Dhundi (2,900m) — 8 km, 3–4 hours. Day 2: Dhundi to Beas Kund and back to Bakarthach (3,400m) — 10 km, 5–6 hours. Day 3: Bakarthach to Solang via Dhundi — 8 km, 3–4 hours.
overview.temperature: Jun–Jul: 5°C–20°C; excellent snowmelt streams; wildflowers peak. Aug: 8°C–22°C; the meadows are lush and green; best for families. Sep–Oct: 0°C–15°C; clear autumn skies; Friendship Peak and Hanuman Tibba perfectly visible. Nov–May: Closed under deep snow; Solang Nullah operates as a ski resort in this period.
overview.fitness: Easy. This is one of Himachal's most accessible glacier-approach treks. Suitable for beginners, families with children above 10, and older adults with basic fitness. The 1,220m elevation gain is spread comfortably over 2 days. No technical terrain anywhere on the route. Preparation: 3–4 weeks of regular walking is sufficient. The main physical challenge is altitude acclimatisation — 1 night in Manali before starting is recommended.

itinerary.title: Manali to Solang Nullah — Trek to Dhundi
itinerary.desc: Drive 22 km from Manali to Dhundi (via Solang Nullah ski resort) and register at the TMS check-post. The trail begins at Dhundi — just past the small hydro project — and follows the Beas River upstream through deodar and pine forest. Dhundi (2,840m) is a pleasant meadow clearing at the valley narrows, with Hanuman Tibba visible in the distance — a perfect first camp.

itinerary.title: Dhundi — Bakarthach — Beas Kund — Bakarthach
itinerary.desc: The most rewarding day. The trail leaves Dhundi and enters a wide upper valley of magnificent wildflower meadows at Bakarthach (3,400m). Leave your heavy pack at Bakarthach and day-hike the final 2.5 km to Beas Kund. The sacred glacial pool sits beneath snowfields with Hanuman Tibba and Friendship Peak towering above. Return to Bakarthach for camp.

itinerary.title: Bakarthach — Dhundi — Solang Nullah — Manali
itinerary.desc: A relaxed morning descent through the valley meadows and forest back to Solang Nullah. The entire valley with its glacier backdrop is visible on the return — ideally photographed in the clear morning light before the valley clouds build up around noon.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Rasikka  Patil on Pexels

name: Indrahar Pass Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Dhauladhar Wildlife Sanctuary Permit
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; Dharamkot/McLeod Ganj check-post at start
permitInfo.fee: ₹100–₹200 sanctuary entry; HP TMS mandatory
permitInfo.note: HP TMS registration mandatory at trekking.hp.gov.in. The Dhauladhar Wildlife Sanctuary check-post at Dharamkot (above McLeod Ganj) collects forest entry fees. The Chamba district descent requires a separate HP TMS registration update (trekkers crossing from Kangra to Chamba must notify both DFOs). Medical certificate and insurance mandatory. This is a serious mountain trek — the HRTC bus from Pathankot/Dharamshala takes 6–7 hours from Chandigarh.

description: The most dramatic one-day high pass crossing above Dharamshala — a rugged traverse of the Dhauladhar range from the Kangra Valley (McLeod Ganj / Dharamshala) to the remote Chamba district. Indrahar Pass (4,342m) towers above Triund meadow and involves a steep, exhilarating ascent through rock and scree to a narrow notch with views of both the Kangra Valley and the Ravi River watershed.

overview.location: Indrahar Pass (4,342m) is a high notch in the main Dhauladhar Range above McLeod Ganj, Kangra district — the range that forms the dramatic 5,000m + wall visible from Dharamshala. The trail starts at Dharamkot village (1,457m), 3 km above McLeod Ganj, and ascends through Triund meadow (2,828m) — one of Himachal's most popular short treks — before the serious climb to the pass. The descent into Chamba's Ravi watershed reaches Chatta village (2,400m) or Lahesh Cave (3,700m) as the first night camp after the crossing.
overview.history: The Dhauladhar Range has been a physical and cultural divide between the Kangra Valley's Hindu lowland culture and the more isolated Gaddi pastoral communities of Chamba for centuries. The Gaddi shepherd community has crossed Indrahar Pass seasonally for generations — driving their flocks of sheep and goats between the Kangra winter pastures and the Chamba summer grazing grounds. McLeod Ganj became the home of the Tibetan Government in Exile after the Dalai Lama fled Tibet in 1959. The Triund meadow approach became one of India's most popular weekend treks from the 2000s due to Dharamshala's growing tourism.
overview.length: 48 km one-way traverse, McLeod Ganj to Chamba, over 6–7 days. Total elevation gain from McLeod Ganj (1,457m) to pass (4,342m): approximately 2,885m. The pass crossing day (typically Day 3) is the hardest — a 7–8 hour effort gaining 1,514m from Lahesh Cave (2,828m) to the pass and descending to Chatta (2,400m). The route is typically walked McLeod Ganj → Triund → Lahesh Cave → Indrahar Pass → Chatta → Chamba, requiring vehicle logistics at both ends.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–18°C at Triund; –5°C to 5°C at pass; snow on and below the pass in May. Sep–Oct: 0°C–15°C at Triund; –10°C at pass; the most stable season — recommended. Monsoon (Jul–Aug): The Dhauladhar receives some of India's heaviest monsoon rainfall — Dharamshala averages 3,500mm annually; not recommended. Nov–Apr: Pass blocked by snow.
overview.fitness: Hard. The Indrahar Pass crossing is genuinely demanding — a 2,885m elevation gain to 4,342m with a steep, exposed final 500m on rock and scree. Prior experience on multi-day mountain treks is required. The descent into Chamba is also steep and hard on the knees. Triund alone (first 2 days) is easy and suitable for beginners, but the full traverse requires serious preparation. Preparation: 10–12 weeks of intensive cardio, hill walking, and stair training with a loaded pack.

itinerary.title: McLeod Ganj / Dharamkot — Trek to Triund
itinerary.distance: 9 km from McLeod Ganj / 7 km from Dharamkot
itinerary.desc: Register at the Dharamkot forest check-post and ascend through cedar, oak, and rhododendron forest via Gallu Devi temple. The famous 22 Curves section near the top is steep but brief. Triund meadow opens suddenly onto a wall of white Dhauladhar peaks to the north and the entire Kangra Valley spreading to the south horizon. This is one of the most dramatic camp locations in Himachal Pradesh. HPFD rest house available (advance booking required at Dharamshala).

itinerary.title: Triund — Snowline Café — Laka Got (Ilaqa Got)
itinerary.desc: The trail above Triund enters true alpine terrain. Pass Snowline Café (the last tea stall) at around 3,100m. Continue past to Ilaqa Got — a wide open grazing meadow at the snout of the Laka glacier. The boulder fields begin above here. Laka Got (3,250m) is the established base camp for the Indrahar Pass ascent — a spectacular setting with the sheer Dhauladhar headwall towering above. Lahesh Cave (3,500m) is a further 30–40 minutes — smaller groups sometimes camp there instead.

itinerary.title: Laka Got / Lahesh Cave — Indrahar Pass — Laka Got return
itinerary.camp: Laka Got or descend to Triund (3,250m or 2,825m)
itinerary.desc: Alpine start at 4–5 AM essential — the weather deteriorates by noon. From Lahesh Cave the cairn-marked trail climbs steeply through boulder fields and rock staircases built by Gaddi shepherds. Indrahar Pass (4,342m) offers one of the most extraordinary panoramas in the Indian Himalayas: Kangra Valley and the plains behind, the Chamba-Ravi watershed ahead, and peaks from Hanuman Tibba to Mani Mahesh Kailash in view. Return by the same route to Laka Got or push down to Triund.

itinerary.title: Laka Got / Triund — McLeod Ganj — Departure
itinerary.desc: Full descent from Laka Got or Triund through the forest to McLeod Ganj. The trail back through the oak and cedar forest with the Kangra Valley panorama unfolding below is one of Himachal's great mountain descents. Alternatively (advanced trekkers): cross the pass to Chamba district and descend to Chatta/Kuarsi village for a 5–6 day full traverse.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Anshuman Sharma on Pexels

name: Pin Parvati Pass Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Pin Valley National Park Entry Permit + Inner Line Permit (foreigners)
permitInfo.where: HP TMS: trekking.hp.gov.in; Pin Valley NP permit: DFO Kaza or Mudh check-post; Inner Line Permit for foreigners: SDM Kaza
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory; Pin Valley NP entry: ₹200/day Indian, ₹1000/day foreigner; Foreigners require Inner Line Permit for Spiti (PIN: 172114)
permitInfo.note: This is one of India's most technically demanding standard treks. HP TMS registration mandatory. The Pin Valley descent requires Pin Valley National Park permit from the Mudh check-post. Foreigners entering Spiti need an Inner Line Permit (ILP) from the SDM Kaza — apply before departure (2–3 days processing). A licensed guide is strongly recommended. Trek insurance with high-altitude evacuation coverage is mandatory. The Parvati Valley check-post at Barshaini requires ID and TMS receipt. Kullu DFO forest fee applies for the Parvati Valley ascent section.

description: The ultimate Himachal crossover — a 110 km odyssey from the lush cannabis-scented Parvati Valley to the lunar Tibetan plateau of Spiti via the Pin Parvati Pass (5,320m). The dramatic landscape transition — green forested canyon to stark Tibetan desert — is one of the greatest single-trek contrasts in the Indian Himalayas. A gruelling glacier crossing, multiple river fords, and 5+ days of true wilderness make this the most demanding 'standard' trek in Himachal Pradesh.

overview.location: Pin Parvati Pass (5,320m) breaches the Kullu-Spiti watershed between the Parvati River valley (Kullu district, Himachal Pradesh) and the Pin Valley (Lahaul and Spiti district). The approach starts from Barshaini village (2,200m) in the Parvati Valley, 35 km from Bhuntar airport via Manikaran hot springs. The descent reaches Mudh village (3,760m) in Pin Valley National Park — the first human settlement after the wilderness crossing. The Spiti River eventually drains to the Indus.
overview.history: The Pin Parvati watershed has been significant in the religious geography of both Kullu and Spiti. Manikaran hot springs at the valley entrance is one of the holiest Sikh and Hindu pilgrimage sites in Himachal — legend holds that Guru Nanak meditated here and the springs opened to provide food. The Parvati Valley became a destination for Western travellers and spiritual seekers in the 1970s–80s. The Pin Valley National Park on the Spiti side protects one of the last viable snow leopard populations in the Indian Himalayas.
overview.length: 110 km one-way, Barshaini to Mudh, over 10–12 days. Total elevation gain from Barshaini (2,200m) to pass (5,320m): approximately 3,120m. The glacier crossing section above Mantalai Lake (4,100m) involves 2 days of technical glacier travel. The pass crossing day is 10–12 hours. Vehicle logistics at both ends are essential.
overview.temperature: July: –5°C to 15°C at glacier camps; 5°C–20°C in Parvati Valley; glacier technically soft but manageable. August: Similar; peak of the season; most teams on this route. September: –10°C at the pass; 0°C–12°C at glacier camps; most stable conditions. Pass may close with early October snowfall. Outside Jul–Sep: Completely inaccessible; glacier too dangerous or buried under snow.
overview.fitness: Expert/very hard. This is not a recreational trek — it is a 10-12 day wilderness expedition with glacier travel, high-altitude river crossings (dangerous during monsoon), and a 5,320m pass that requires crampons and possibly ice axe. Prior experience on multi-day high-altitude treks is essential. A guide experienced on this route is strongly recommended. Preparation: 12+ weeks of intensive fitness training. Only attempt with experienced companions or a licensed guide.

itinerary.title: Bhuntar/Bhuntar — Barshaini — Kheerganga
itinerary.desc: Drive via Bhuntar and Manikaran (visiting the sacred hot springs) to Barshaini roadhead. Register at the TMS/forest check-post. The trail ascends through the Parvati Valley's famous canyon — a dramatic gorge of waterfalls and dense forests — to Kheerganga, where natural hot springs offer a magnificent camp experience.

itinerary.title: Kheerganga — Tunda Bhuj
itinerary.desc: Above Kheerganga the valley narrows and the forest gives way to high-altitude meadows. Tunda Bhuj is the last treeline camp — a wide meadow with views up the valley toward the permanent snowfields. Wildlife (Himalayan brown bear) occasionally seen in this section.

itinerary.title: Tunda Bhuj — Mantalai Lake
itinerary.desc: A long approach day through increasingly barren terrain. Mantalai Lake (4,100m) is a stunning glacial lake — the main feeder of the Parvati River — in a dramatic high-altitude bowl. From here the glacier and the pass headwall are visible. This is the last reliable water source before the glacier.

itinerary.title: Acclimatisation at Mantalai — Glacier reconnaissance
itinerary.desc: Rest day at Mantalai Lake for essential acclimatisation. The guide will lead a glacier reconnaissance walk to identify the safest route through the lower icefield. Check crampons, rope, and ice axe — these will be needed from tomorrow. Weather assessment is critical at this point.

itinerary.title: Mantalai — Glacier High Camp
itinerary.desc: The most technically serious day. The Parvati glacier is crossed with crampons and rope — the guide sets the line. Crevasses are present in the upper section; stay roped. The high camp at 4,800m is a flat snow platform with an extraordinary 360° view of the surrounding peaks.

itinerary.title: Glacier High Camp — Pin Parvati Pass — Descent to Spiti side
itinerary.camp: First camp below pass, Spiti side (4,600m)
itinerary.desc: Alpine start at 4 AM. The final 520m to the pass is steep snow/ice — fixed rope in sections. The summit of the pass offers one of the most dramatic vistas in the Indian Himalayas: the green Parvati Valley behind, the brown Tibetan desert of Spiti ahead. The descent on the Spiti side is steep on scree and loose rock — take time, use poles.

itinerary.title: Spiti side descent — Pin Valley — Mudh village
itinerary.desc: The full descent to Mudh through the Pin Valley. The landscape is completely transformed — bare brown rock, brilliant blue sky, and the geometric terraced fields of Pin Valley coming into view. Mudh is the last village before the wilderness — a warm meal and a roof feel magnificent.

itinerary.title: Mudh — Kaza — Departure
itinerary.desc: Jeep or bus from Mudh to Kaza, the administrative headquarters of Spiti district. Kaza at 3,800m — ancient monasteries, whitewashed Tibetan-style buildings, and extraordinary stargazing. Foreigners process ILP documentation here if not already obtained. Return to Manali (210 km) via Rohtang Pass or Kunzum Pass.

coverImageCredit: Photo by INDU BIKASH SARKER on Pexels

name: Chandrakhani Pass Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Kullu DFO Forest Permit
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; Naggar check-post at trek start
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory; ₹50 forest entry; camera fee ₹25
permitInfo.note: HP TMS registration at trekking.hp.gov.in is mandatory. The Naggar check-post above Naggar Castle collects fees. The Malana village destination at trek end is in a Protected Area — separate Malana entry fee (₹200–₹500 per person) may be charged by the village council. Photography strictly restricted in Malana village. HP trek insurance mandatory.

description: A beautiful ridge walk from the historic Naggar Castle above Kullu Valley to the mysterious isolated village of Malana — one of India's most enigmatic communities — via a 3,660m pass with sweeping views of Deo Tibba, the Pir Panjal, and the Kullu Valley. The cultural contrast between the medieval Rajput heritage of Naggar and the ancient, fiercely independent culture of Malana makes this one of Himachal's most rewarding short treks.

overview.location: Chandrakhani Pass (3,660m) sits on the ridge separating the Kullu Valley's Beas River drainage from the secluded Malana Nullah. Naggar village (1,768m) — home to Naggar Castle, the old Kullu royal summer capital — is the starting point, 23 km from Kullu town. The pass commands views of Deo Tibba (6,001m), Indrasan (6,221m), and the full Kullu Valley breadth. Malana village (2,652m) on the descent is one of India's most archaeologically and culturally distinct communities.
overview.history: Naggar Castle, the 500-year-old seat of the Kullu rajas, anchors the beginning of this route in medieval Himachali history. The castle now houses an art gallery featuring works by the Russian painter Nicholas Roerich, who lived nearby from 1928 to 1947 and painted extensively in the Kullu Valley. Malana village at the end is one of the oldest surviving direct democracies in the world — its population claims descent from Alexandrian soldiers or from Aryans, follows a unique legal system administered by the god Jamlu Devta, and maintains strict rules around outsider contact. The culture is under increasing pressure from cannabis tourism.
overview.length: 35 km over 4–5 days, Naggar to Malana (one-way, requiring transport from Malana to Bhuntar/Kullu). Total elevation gain from Naggar (1,768m) to pass (3,660m): 1,892m — the most sustained climb of any standard Kullu trek. Descent from pass to Malana: 1,008m over 6 km. Most operators run this one-way with a vehicle waiting at Malana roadhead.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–18°C at pass; snow possible in May; rhododendron bloom spectacular on lower approaches. Jul–Aug: 10°C–22°C; the Kullu side is relatively monsoon-sheltered but Malana receives some rainfall. Sep–Oct: 0°C–12°C at pass; best views; recommended season. Nov–Apr: Pass closed; Naggar accessible year-round by road.
overview.fitness: Moderate. The sustained 1,892m climb from Naggar to the pass over 2 days is the defining physical challenge. No technical terrain. Good cardiovascular fitness and hill-walking experience are the requirements. Preparation: 6–8 weeks of regular cardio and hill walking. The descent to Malana is steep — trekking poles strongly recommended.

itinerary.title: Manali — Naggar — Rumsu — Naya Tapru / Ghan Kuradi
itinerary.desc: Drive 23 km from Manali to Rumsu (2,100m) via Naggar — visit Naggar Castle and the Roerich Gallery en route. Register at the check-post. The trek begins at Rumsu village and climbs steeply through dense forests of deodar, walnut, chestnut, and oak. Pass through the open clearing of Stiling and the forest meadow of Ghan Kuradi. Naya Tapru (2,950m) is a vast open meadow — the first camp with sweeping views of Kullu Valley and the Pir Panjal range.

itinerary.title: Naya Tapru — Chaklani Meadows
itinerary.desc: A steady climb from Naya Tapru through rhododendron and high-altitude shrub to the magnificent open meadows of Chaklani (3,463m). The Pir Panjal range — Hanuman Tibba, Friendship Peak, Indrasan (6,221m), Deo Tibba (6,001m) — fills the northern skyline. Chaklani is one of the finest meadow camps in the Kullu valley. From here a 2 km ridge walk tomorrow reaches the pass.

itinerary.title: Chaklani — Chandrakhani Pass — Nagruni — Malana Village
itinerary.desc: Early start for the 2 km ridge walk from Chaklani to Chandrakhani Pass (3,660m) — a superb 360° panorama of the Kullu, Parvati, Malana, and Dhauladhar ranges. From the pass the trail descends steeply to Nagruni (3,395m) and then through Magic Valley to Malana village (2,652m). Approach Malana with full respect — do not touch any village structure, deity, or resident; outsiders must stay on designated paths. The Jamlu Devta temple is architecturally extraordinary.

itinerary.title: Malana — Malana Dam Road — Bhuntar/Manali
itinerary.desc: Descend from Malana to the Malana Dam road (7 km, ~2 hrs). Pre-arranged vehicle to Bhuntar and onwards to Kullu or Manali. The Malana canyon drive is dramatic. Back in Manali by mid-afternoon.

name: Buran Ghati Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Shimla DFO Forest Permit
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; Janglik check-post at start; Baspa Valley (Kinnaur) check-post at end
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory; ₹50–₹100 Shimla Forest Division entry; Kinnaur side: ₹100 Baspa Valley forest fee
permitInfo.note: HP TMS registration at trekking.hp.gov.in is mandatory. Janglik is reached via Rohru, Shimla district. The trek crosses from Shimla district to Kinnaur district — both district forest departments must be notified via TMS. The descent into Baspa Valley (Chitkul/Sangla) area requires prior Kinnaur forest department TMS registration. Trek insurance with high-altitude evacuation coverage mandatory. Snow conditions near the pass are unpredictable even in June — check with local guides before departure.

description: A stunningly varied Himachal classic — from the lush Pabbar River valley near Rohru (Shimla district) to the spectacularly beautiful Baspa Valley of Kinnaur via the 4,572m Buran Ghati pass, with an iconic snow-wall descent on a fixed rope that is unlike anything else in Indian trekking. The 2-day ridge walk above treeline through pristine alpine meadows, followed by the dramatic snow rappel descent, makes this one of the most talked-about treks in Himachal Pradesh.

overview.location: Buran Ghati (4,572m) is a high mountain pass in the Shimla-Kinnaur watershed, connecting the Pabbar River valley (Shimla district) with the Baspa River valley of Kinnaur. The trek starts from Janglik village (2,400m) in the Pabbar valley, 140 km from Shimla via Rohru. The descent ends at Barua village (3,175m) in the Baspa Valley — the same valley that contains the beautiful villages of Sangla and Chitkul. Kinnaur Kailash (6,050m) is visible from the pass approach.
overview.history: The Pabbar Valley communities of Shimla district have used Buran Ghati as a high-altitude crossing to Kinnaur for centuries — the pass connects two culturally and geographically distinct worlds. The Pabbar Valley is Hindu Himachali; the Baspa Valley has deep Tibetan Buddhist influences, with ancient gompas and traditional flat-roofed stone architecture. The dramatic snow-wall below the pass (typically 40–60m of near-vertical snow in May–June) creates the iconic rappel descent that defines the modern trekking experience here.
overview.length: 50 km over 7–8 days, Janglik to Barua (one-way crossing). Total elevation gain approximately 2,172m. The pass crossing day involves a 2-hour steep snow ascent and a 40–60m fixed-rope rappel descent on the Kinnaur side — one of Indian trekking's most memorable single moments. Vehicle logistics at both ends are essential (Janglik from Shimla; Barua/Sangla to Shimla or Manali via NH5).
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 0°C–15°C; heavy snow at pass creates the dramatic wall — the most popular season for the rappel experience; crampons required. Sep–Oct: –2°C to 12°C; pass is snow-free or lightly covered; most stable conditions; no rappel but still beautiful. Jul–Aug: Monsoon; lower sections receive rain; pass approach wet. Nov–Apr: Pass completely blocked.
overview.fitness: Hard. The snow rappel descent requires physical confidence, upper body strength, and the ability to control a rope under the guide's instruction. No prior technical climbing experience needed but vertigo is a disqualifying factor. The 7–8 days of sustained uphill with a loaded pack at 4,000m+ demands good cardiovascular fitness. Prior experience on multi-day high-altitude treks strongly recommended. Preparation: 10–12 weeks of training.

itinerary.title: Shimla to Janglik
itinerary.desc: Drive from Shimla via Rohru and Chirgaon to Janglik village (2,804m / 9,200ft) in the Pabbar Valley. The last stretch follows the turquoise Pabbar River. Janglik is a traditional Himachali village of carved wooden houses, terraced wheat fields, and fruit orchards. Collect TMS registration and meet your guide. Evening walk through the village.

itinerary.title: Janglik to Dayara Thatch
itinerary.desc: The first trekking day begins with a steep climb from Janglik's wheat fields through dense pine, oak, and rhododendron forest. The trail enters and exits the forest several times before bursting suddenly into the vast Dayara Thatch meadows (11,050ft) — sweeping alpine grasslands with views of the Dhauladhar range and grazing horses in season. One of the finest first-day campsites in Himachal Pradesh.

itinerary.title: Dayara Thatch to Litham
itinerary.desc: A shorter, scenic day through forests, meadows, and gushing mountain streams. The trail crosses the Chandranahan stream before reaching Litham (3,533m / 11,590ft) — a beautiful campsite at the confluence of two valleys with waterfalls on both sides.

itinerary.title: Litham — Acclimatisation Hike to Chandranahan Lake — Return
itinerary.desc: A vital acclimatisation day with a day-hike to the sacred Chandranahan Lake (4,260m / 13,975ft) — a glacial tarn considered the source of the Pabbar River and sacred to Janglik villagers. Steep ascent through wildflowers and rocky terrain; extraordinary views from the lake. Return to Litham to sleep lower.

itinerary.title: Litham to Dhunda High Camp
itinerary.desc: Push into the true alpine zone. The trail follows the Pabbar stream — now a small torrent — through rocky terrain as the valley narrows. Dhunda (4,000m / 13,123ft) is the last camp before the pass: exposed, often snow-covered, with the Buran Ghati ridge directly visible above. Prepare gear for the early start tomorrow.

itinerary.title: Dhunda — Buran Ghati Pass — Munirang River Camp
itinerary.desc: Very early start (4–5 AM). Steep ascent to Buran Ghati Pass (4,572m / 14,993ft). In early season a 40–70m near-vertical ice wall requires fixed ropes and a rappel descent — the most memorable single moment in Indian trekking. Even in later season the descent is steep scree. Views from the pass span the Dhauladhar, Pir Panjal, and the Pabbar Valley. Descend to Munirang River Camp.

itinerary.title: Munirang to Barua Village — Drive to Shimla / Sangla
itinerary.camp: Return to Shimla or overnight Sangla
itinerary.desc: Final descent to Barua village (2,900m) in the Baspa Valley on the Kinnaur side — fruit orchards, traditional wooden architecture, and Buddhist prayer flags. Pre-arranged vehicle drives back to Shimla via the Sutlej gorge, or continue to explore Sangla and Chitkul in the Baspa Valley.

itinerary.title: Barua — Sangla — Chitkul (Optional Extension)
itinerary.desc: Explore the stunning Baspa Valley — Sangla (2,680m) with its ancient Kamru Fort and Buddhist temple, and Chitkul (3,450m), the last village in the Baspa Valley and one of India's most beautiful mountain villages. The valley is a destination in itself.

itinerary.title: Sangla/Chitkul — Shimla or Manali — Return
itinerary.desc: Return journey via NH5 through Reckong Peo and Rampur to Shimla. Alternatively, continue on NH5 to Karcham and then north to Manali via Sangla-Karcham-Wangtu road — extraordinary scenery through the deep Sutlej gorge.

name: Kinnaur Kailash Yatra

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Kinnaur Protected Area Permit (foreigners) + Inner Line Permit
permitInfo.where: HP TMS: trekking.hp.gov.in; PAP for foreigners: SDM Recong Peo; ILP check-posts at Puh/Spillo
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory; Indian trekkers: ₹100–₹200 DFO Kinnaur; Foreigners: Protected Area Permit from SDM Recong Peo — apply minimum 3 days before; free but requires passport copies and ID
permitInfo.note: Kinnaur is a Protected Area (PA) under the Inner Line Permit (ILP) system. Indian nationals do not require ILP but must register with ITBP at checkpoints and obtain DFO Kinnaur forest permit. Foreign nationals require a Protected Area Permit from SDM Recong Peo — groups of minimum 4 with registered guide required; individual foreigners cannot trek independently. HP TMS mandatory for all. Medical certificate and high-altitude trek insurance required. The Kinnaur Kailash Parikrama is a challenging pilgrimage route with significant altitude — altitude sickness is common.

description: The sacred circumambulation of Kinnaur Kailash (6,050m) — the winter abode of Lord Shiva in Kinnauri tradition, and site of the 79-foot Shivling rock formation visible from across the Kinnaur valley. This high-altitude pilgrimage trek through the remote Kinnaur range combines extraordinary mountain scenery — the steep rock walls of the Kailash range, ancient Buddhist monasteries, apple orchards and terraced barley fields — with one of Hinduism's most revered pilgrimage circuits.

overview.location: Kinnaur Kailash (6,050m) is the sacred peak of Kinnaur district, rising above the Sutlej River gorge in the eastern Himachal Pradesh. The parikrama (circumambulation) circuit passes through the villages of Kalpa (2,759m) and Tangling, ascending to the Charang La pass (5,241m) area before completing the high-altitude loop. Recong Peo is the district headquarters (2,290m). The trailhead villages of Kalpa and Morang are spectacular — apricot and apple orchards beneath the Kailash rock face.
overview.history: Kinner Kailash is identified in Hindu scripture as Shiva's winter domain — where he retreats when Kedarnath closes in winter. The 79-foot Shivling (natural rock formation) on the mountain's northwest face glows different colours at sunrise and sunset and is visible from Kalpa village. The Kinnauri people have maintained a unique syncretic Hindu-Buddhist culture for centuries — the same households contain both shrines. The Kinnaur Kailash Yatra (pilgrimage) traditionally coincides with Janamashthami (August) and brings thousands of pilgrims on the parikrama route annually.
overview.length: 40 km circuit over 5–6 days. The Charang La pass crossing (5,241m) is the high point. Total elevation gain approximately 2,482m from Kalpa. The route passes through Charang village — a remote Kinnauri settlement at 3,450m — before the high pass section. Return is via Tangling village to Kalpa.
overview.temperature: Jun: 0°C–15°C; snow on Charang La reducing. Jul–Aug: 5°C–18°C; pilgrimage season peak; trail busiest. Sep: –2°C to 12°C; most stable and clear conditions; recommended for trekkers. Oct: –10°C to 5°C; pass may have early snowfall. Nov–May: Route closed.
overview.fitness: Hard. Charang La at 5,241m is very serious altitude. ITBP check-posts require medical fitness — carry a doctor's certificate. Prior experience at 4,500m+ is strongly recommended. The combined pilgrimage and trekking atmosphere means many physically unfit pilgrims attempt this route and require rescue — do not underestimate the demands. Preparation: 10–12 weeks of intensive training with prior altitude experience.

itinerary.title: Chandigarh / Shimla to Reckong Peo — Kalpa Overnight
itinerary.distance: 320 km from Chandigarh / 235 km from Shimla
itinerary.time: 10-12 hrs from Chandigarh / 7-8 hrs from Shimla
itinerary.desc: Drive from Chandigarh (320 km) or Shimla (235 km) to Reckong Peo via Narkanda, Rampur Bushahr along the Old Hindustan-Tibet Highway (NH-5/21) beside the Sutlej River — apple orchards, deep gorges. Reckong Peo (2,290m) is the district HQ of Kinnaur. Stay in Kalpa village (6 km above Reckong Peo, 2,960m) for stunning sunset views of Kinner Kailash range and the Shivling rock changing colour in the evening light. Obtain Inner Line Permit from the DC Office, Reckong Peo (mandatory). Trek list must be submitted to local police station per Himachal Pradesh Adventure Activity Rules 2017.

itinerary.title: Kalpa / Reckong Peo to Tangling — Trek to Ganesh Park
itinerary.distance: 7 km drive to Tangling + 8-10 km steep trek to Ganesh Park
itinerary.camp: Ganesh Park (Ashiqui Park / Kailash Darr) — tents
itinerary.desc: Drive 7 km from Reckong Peo to Tangling village (2,149m) on the left bank of the Sutlej — cross via suspension bridge near Powari (11 km before Reckong Peo on NH-21). Fill water bottles at Tangling; no water for next 6-7 km. The 8-10 km trek is almost PERPENDICULAR immediately after Tangling — unlike other Kailash yatras. Trail: Tangling → stream crossing (2.5 km, 1.5 hrs; last water before Ganesh Park) → steep 6-7 km vertical climb through Bara Pathar (big rock resting point) → Kailash Darr/Dwaar (the entrance gate to Kinner Kailash) → Ganesh Park meadow (8-9 hrs total). Ganesh Park (also Ashiqui Park) is the camp with 270-degree Himalayan views. The 79-ft Shivling is visible from here, changing colour from white to gold to red through the day.

itinerary.title: Ganesh Park to Bheem Dwar — Night Camp
itinerary.desc: Trek 3-4 km from Ganesh Park to Bheem Dwar (12,400 ft): first 2 km is a steep ascent, then descent to cross a glacial stream (usually frozen), then reach Bheem Dwar. Bheem Dwar is a natural cave under large boulders — shelter for 10-15 people. Stream nearby for water. This is your last overnight camp before the summit. Fill every water bottle here — NO water between Bheem Dwar and Parvati Kund (3 km ahead). Rest well; 4 AM start tomorrow.

itinerary.title: Bheem Dwar to Kinner Kailash Shivling — Summit Day — Return to Ganesh Park
itinerary.distance: 8-9 km round trip: Bheem Dwar → Parvati Kund (3 km) → Shivling (2-3 km more) → return same
itinerary.time: 12-15 hrs total round trip from Bheem Dwar
itinerary.desc: EARLIEST START 4:00 AM from Bheem Dwar. (1) Bheem Dwar to Parvati Kund: 3 km, 2.5-3 hrs — first 1.5 km is a near-vertical cliff, then boulder and snowfield sections; follow stone pillars. Parvati Kund is a small frozen glacial lake — worship Mata Parvati before proceeding. Carry all water from here. (2) Parvati Kund to Kinner Kailash Shivling: 2-3 km, 3-4 hrs — moraines, stone tunnels/caves, stone pillars mark the only route. The 79-ft natural Shivling (Swayambhu) faces Reckong Peo and changes colour through the day — worshipped as Lord Shiva's self-manifested lingam. Views of Mt Jorkandan and Mt Rangrik Rang. Descend same route back to Ganesh Park. Total: 16-18 km round trip from Ganesh Park. VERY LONG and difficult day.

itinerary.title: Ganesh Park to Tangling — Drive to Reckong Peo / Shimla
itinerary.distance: 8-10 km descent + 7 km drive + 235 km road to Shimla
itinerary.desc: Descend 8-10 km from Ganesh Park to Tangling (steep descent; poles essential). Drive 7 km to Reckong Peo. Then 235 km drive to Shimla (7-8 hrs) via Rampur and Narkanda. Yatra concludes.
