name: Deo Tibba Base Camp

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Great Himalayan National Park Buffer Zone Permit
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; Jagatsukh/Khanol check-post at trek entry
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory; ₹100 GHNP buffer zone daily entry; camera fee ₹100
permitInfo.note: HP TMS mandatory at trekking.hp.gov.in. The Deo Tibba approach passes through the buffer zone of Great Himalayan National Park (UNESCO World Heritage Site) — GHNP buffer zone entry permit required from the Jagatsukh check-post. The inner core of GHNP is not entered on this route but buffer regulations apply. Guide recommended for route navigation above Seri meadow. Trek insurance mandatory.

description: A remote and rewarding approach to the base of Deo Tibba (6,001m) — the 'god's peak' that dominates the Manali skyline — through some of the finest alpine meadow country in the Kullu Himalayas. The route passes through the extraordinary Tenta meadow (4,000m) with its direct views of the ice-capped summit, and the lush camps at Seri and Chikka through dense birch and rhododendron forests. One of Manali's finest multi-day treks.

overview.location: Deo Tibba (6,001m) — 'Peak of the God' — is the most prominent summit visible from Manali town, towering above the Jagatsukh Nullah drainage north of the Beas River. The trek begins from Jagatsukh village (2,050m) or Khanol (1,900m) — ancient settlements 7–10 km south of Manali on the Kullu Valley floor. The base camp approach reaches Tenta meadow (4,000m) directly below the peak's south face, with Indrasan (6,221m) visible to the northeast.
overview.history: Deo Tibba — 'Peak of the Gods' in the local Kullu vernacular — has been sacred in the religious landscape of the Kullu Valley for centuries. The Kullu Valley's ancient tradition of the Dussehra festival, when all local deities are carried in procession, includes Deo Tibba in the pantheon of peak-deities. The peak was first climbed by a British expedition in 1952. The adjacent Indrasan was first summited in 1961. The surrounding area falls within the buffer zone of Great Himalayan National Park, declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014.
overview.length: 55 km over 6–7 days from Jagatsukh, round-trip. Total elevation gain approximately 2,220m. The route passes through Khanol (base village), the beautiful Chikka and Seri meadows, before the sustained climb to Tenta (4,000m) and the final approach to base camp (4,270m). The return follows the same route.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–20°C at Seri; 0°C–8°C at Tenta; wildflower peak at the meadows. Jul–Aug: 8°C–22°C; lush and green; the valley floor is dry despite the broader monsoon. Sep–Oct: 0°C–15°C; best views of Deo Tibba and Indrasan; outstanding photography. Nov–Apr: Closed under snow.
overview.fitness: Moderate. The approach through Chikka and Seri is well-maintained and suitable for trekkers with basic multi-day experience. The climb from Seri to Tenta (1,200m in 2 days) demands sustained cardiovascular fitness. No technical terrain on the standard base camp route. Preparation: 6–8 weeks of cardio and loaded hiking. GHNP buffer zone regulations require trekkers to remain on established trails.

itinerary.title: Manali — Jagatsukh — Khanol — Chikka
itinerary.desc: Drive or walk to Jagatsukh and register at the check-post. The trail ascends through dense deodar and horse chestnut forest. Chikka is a wide forest clearing with a gurgling stream — a perfect first camp with views of the ridge above.

itinerary.title: Chikka — Seri Meadow
itinerary.desc: Above Chikka the forest thins to give way to open rhododendron and birch. Seri meadow is a breathtaking open alpine plateau with the first direct view of Deo Tibba's ice-capped summit. Camp here on the flat meadow grass.

itinerary.title: Seri — Tenta Meadow
itinerary.desc: From Seri the trail climbs steeply through rocky terrain into the high-alpine zone. Tenta meadow at 4,000m is directly beneath the south face of Deo Tibba — the peak towers above and the glacier is visible clearly. An extraordinary camp on the edge of the permanent snow zone.

itinerary.title: Tenta — Deo Tibba Base Camp — Return to Tenta
itinerary.desc: Day hike to the base camp proper at 4,270m — a morainic platform with close views of the Deo Tibba glacier and the seracs of the south face above. The ascent route for the peak (non-technical as far as the glacier, then technical) is visible. Return to Tenta for the night.

itinerary.title: Tenta — Seri — Chikka
itinerary.desc: Relaxed descent through familiar terrain — the meadows are beautiful in the afternoon light heading south. Many trekkers stop for a long rest at Seri before the final descent to Chikka.

itinerary.title: Chikka — Jagatsukh — Manali
itinerary.desc: Final morning descent through the deodar forest to Jagatsukh and back to Manali. The valley floor's warmth after days at altitude is immediately noticeable.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Harsh  Kukadiya on Pexels

name: Bara Bhangal Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Dhauladhar Wildlife Sanctuary + Kullu DFO Forest Permit
permitInfo.where: HP TMS: trekking.hp.gov.in; Manali DFO/Dharamshala DFO check-posts at both ends; Bara Bhangal village registration with ITBP
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory; Dhauladhar WLS permit: ₹100–₹200; Kullu Forest Div: ₹50–₹100
permitInfo.note: One of Himachal's most remote and serious treks. HP TMS mandatory and enforced. ITBP registration at Bara Bhangal village. The trek crosses two major passes — Thamsar (4,715m) and Kalihani (4,877m) — both requiring crampons and a guide with the route. Medical certificate mandatory. Emergency evacuation from Bara Bhangal is by helicopter only in case of serious injury — the village has no road connection. Trek insurance with helicopter evacuation coverage is essential. This trek is not suitable for independent travel without an experienced Himachali guide.

description: The most remote and demanding trek in the Kangra-Kullu wilderness — a 95 km expedition crossing two high passes (Thamsar 4,715m and Kalihani 4,877m) to reach Bara Bhangal village, a completely isolated community of Gaddi shepherds that has no road connection to the outside world. This is a true wilderness traverse through the back of the Dhauladhar range — forests, glaciers, ancient shepherd paths, and complete solitude.

overview.location: Bara Bhangal village (2,194m) is one of the most isolated permanently inhabited settlements in the Indian Himalayas — a small community of Gaddi shepherd families in the deep Ravi watershed of Kangra district, reachable only on foot over high passes. The trek typically starts from Manali (Kullu) and crosses Kalihani Pass (4,877m) and Thamsar Pass (4,715m) on the Dhauladhar range to arrive at Bara Bhangal before descending via Billing (Kangra) — the paragliding launch site famous worldwide.
overview.history: Bara Bhangal ('Big Bhangal' — likely from a Gaddi word for altitude or camp) has been home to the Gaddi shepherd community for generations. The Gaddis are a transhumant community who migrate seasonally between the Kangra Valley's winter pastures and the high summer grazing grounds of Lahaul and Spiti, crossing passes like Kalihani and Thamsar on foot with their sheep and goat flocks. This is their ancient migration route. The British Survey of India mapped the area in the 1860s–80s. Billing, the descent destination, is world-famous for paragliding and hosted the Paragliding World Cup in 2015.
overview.length: 95 km over 10–12 days. Starting from Manali (via Lama Dugh approach): Manali → Lama Dugh → Kalihani Pass (4,877m) → Bara Bhangal → Thamsar Pass (4,715m) → Billing → Bir (Kangra). Total elevation gain across both passes approximately 5,800m cumulatively. Vehicle logistics required at both Manali and Bir.
overview.temperature: Jun: 0°C–15°C at passes; snow on both; crampons essential. Jul–Aug: 5°C–18°C; passes accessible; some afternoon cloud and rain on the Kangra side. Sep: –2°C to 12°C; most stable season. Passes close by October. Bara Bhangal itself can be snowed in from November to May.
overview.fitness: Expert. Two serious high-altitude passes, extreme remoteness, and the near-total absence of any infrastructure beyond Bara Bhangal village make this one of Himachal's most demanding treks. A Himachali guide with prior Bara Bhangal experience is essential — this route is not for independent trekkers without mountain navigation skills. Prior experience on high-altitude crossover treks is mandatory. Preparation: 12+ weeks of intensive training.

itinerary.title: Manali — Lama Dugh Base
itinerary.desc: TMS check at Manali. Ascend through forest above the Beas River to the broad meadow of Lama Dugh — the traditional Gaddi grazing ground and first camp. Views of the Kullu Valley behind and the Dhauladhar wall ahead.

itinerary.title: Lama Dugh — Snowline Camp
itinerary.desc: Above Lama Dugh the trail steepens into boulder fields and the first permanent snow. The Kalihani headwall is visible ahead — a dramatic wall of rock and ice.

itinerary.title: Snowline — Kalihani Pass — Descent to Bara Bhangal valley
itinerary.desc: Alpine start. The Kalihani Pass (4,877m) is the highest point of the trek — a steep snow/rock ascent. From the top, the wild Bara Bhangal drainage opens below. The descent on the Kangra side is long and rocky.

itinerary.title: Valley camp — Bara Bhangal village
itinerary.desc: Reach Bara Bhangal — a magical settlement of stone houses and ancient wooden temples completely isolated from roads. The Gaddi families offer basic accommodation. Register with ITBP at the village post. Explore the ancient Shiva temples and experience the extraordinary isolation.

itinerary.title: Rest day at Bara Bhangal
itinerary.desc: Essential rest before the second pass crossing. The village has a primary school, a small ITBP post, and ancient temples. Witness the traditional Gaddi culture — the daily rhythms of a community that has lived without roads for generations.

itinerary.title: Bara Bhangal — Thamsar Lake camp
itinerary.desc: Ascend from Bara Bhangal up the spectacular gorge toward Thamsar Pass. The lake below the pass at 4,200m is one of the Himalayas' hidden gems — completely unknown to all but a few Gaddi shepherds and serious trekkers.

itinerary.title: Thamsar Lake — Thamsar Pass — Billing meadow
itinerary.desc: Cross Thamsar Pass (4,715m) — the exit from the wilderness. The long descent to the vast Billing meadow passes through dramatic mixed forest. Billing (world-famous for paragliding) has guesthouses and vehicle access to Bir in the Kangra Valley.

name: Manimahesh Kailash Yatra

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Chamba DFO Forest Permit + Manimahesh Yatra Registration (during festival)
permitInfo.where: HP TMS: trekking.hp.gov.in; Hadsar check-post at trail start (Bharmour); During Yatra: HRTC/HPTDC registration desks at Bharmour
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory; ₹50–₹100 DFO Chamba forest entry; During Yatra: free pilgrimage — HRTC registration for camping zones only
permitInfo.note: HP TMS registration mandatory for all trekkers. The Manimahesh Yatra (pilgrimage) falls between Janmashtami and Radha Ashtami (usually late August to mid-September) and draws hundreds of thousands of pilgrims — the trail is extremely crowded during this period. Outside the Yatra season, the trek is peaceful and the lake often has snow. Medical certificate and insurance required. Bharmour is reached from Chamba town (65 km, 2 hrs). Helicopter service from Bharmour to Gauri Kund during Yatra.

description: A sacred pilgrimage and an exceptional high-altitude lake trek in one — the Manimahesh Lake (4,080m) glitters in a high glacial bowl beneath the unclimbed Manimahesh Kailash (5,574m) in Chamba district. During the annual Manimahesh Yatra, hundreds of thousands of pilgrims walk this route from Bharmour. Outside the Yatra season, it's a tranquil mountain lake surrounded by extraordinary scenery with almost no crowds.

overview.location: Manimahesh Lake (4,080m) lies in the Budhil River watershed in Chamba district, below the sheer northwest face of Manimahesh Kailash peak (5,574m). The approach is from Hadsar village (2,286m), 13 km from Bharmour — the ancient Chamba hill capital 65 km from Chamba town. Bharmour itself is one of Himachal's most architecturally remarkable small towns — an 84-temple complex (Chaurasi Temple) dating to the 7th–10th centuries CE dominates the town centre.
overview.history: Manimahesh Kailash is Shiva's sacred abode in the Chamba tradition — the peak is called 'Mani' (jewel) after a legendary gem Shiva left on its summit. The annual Manimahesh Yatra is one of the largest pilgrimage gatherings in North India — the HP government estimates 400,000–800,000 pilgrims completing the trek in the fortnight of the festival. The circuit predates the current Chamba kingdom (estimated to have existed since the 6th century CE). The Chaurasi temples at Bharmour are a UNESCO-nominated site of extraordinary historic significance.
overview.length: 35 km over 4–5 days from Hadsar return. Total elevation gain from Hadsar (2,286m) to lake (4,080m): 1,794m. Standard itinerary: Day 1 Hadsar to Dhancho (2,946m) — 7 km. Day 2 Dhancho to Gauri Kund (3,700m) — 8 km. Day 3 Gauri Kund to Manimahesh Lake (4,080m) and return to Gauri Kund — 8 km. Day 4 Return to Hadsar — 15 km. During Yatra: helicopter service available Bharmour–Gauri Kund.
overview.temperature: Jul–Aug (Yatra season): 5°C–18°C; the pilgrimage atmosphere is extraordinary but crowded. Sep: 0°C–12°C; the clearest and most peaceful month after the Yatra concludes; lake partially frozen. Oct: –5°C to 8°C; deep snow near the lake; magical but cold. Jun: Lake under snow; trail icy. Nov–May: Closed.
overview.fitness: Moderate. The 1,794m elevation gain is spread over 2–3 approach days, making it manageable for reasonably fit adults. The trail during the Yatra season is a paved/stepped path most of the way to Gauri Kund — suitable for older pilgrims. Outside the Yatra the path is a rougher mountain trail. The lake itself at 4,080m will cause altitude effects in unprepared trekkers — pace carefully. Preparation: 4–6 weeks of regular hill walking.

itinerary.title: Pathankot / Chandigarh to Bharmour via Chamba
itinerary.distance: 165 km from Pathankot / 250 km from Chandigarh
itinerary.time: 6 hrs from Pathankot / 8 hrs from Chandigarh
itinerary.desc: Drive from Pathankot (165 km, 6 hrs) or Chandigarh (250 km, 8 hrs) via Chamba to Bharmour (2,195m). Chamba is a historic town with royal palaces and Lakshmi Narayan temple complex. Bharmour is the ancient capital of the Gaddi tribe — explore the famous Chaurasi Temple Complex (84 temples dating to the 7th century AD, built around the Manimahesh Kailash temple). Visit Brahmani Mata temple — a holy dip in the Brahmani kund is considered mandatory before proceeding to Manimahesh Lake. Overnight in Bharmour.

itinerary.title: Bharmour to Hadsar — Trek to Dhancho
itinerary.distance: 13 km road to Hadsar + 6-7 km trek to Dhancho
itinerary.desc: Drive 13 km from Bharmour to Hadsar (2,280m) — the last motorable point and official trek start. Ponies, palanquins, and porter services available from Hadsar. The 6-7 km trek to Dhancho follows the Budhil River valley: cross suspension bridges, pass Dibri (water point), Tos ka Goth (rest under fir trees), Dunali, then steep climb to Dhancho (2,900m) where the treeline ends. A spectacular waterfall marks Dhancho. GOVT SOURCE (hpchamba.nic.in): Dhancho is the standard overnight halt between Hadsar and the lake. Overnight in tents (govt + voluntary org tented camps available).

itinerary.title: Dhancho to Manimahesh Lake — Holy Darshan
itinerary.distance: 7 km trek (Dhancho to Lake via Sundarasi and Gauri Kund)
itinerary.desc: 7 km from Dhancho to Manimahesh Lake via: Sundarasi (meadow, scenic viewpoint), Shiv ke Gharat (water mill area), then ~1.5 km before the lake: Gauri Kund (sacred pond — women pilgrims take holy dip here) and Shiva Karotri / Shiv Krotri (men pilgrims take holy dip here). Manimahesh Lake (4,080m / 13,390 ft) is a high-altitude glacial lake at the base of Manimahesh Kailash peak (5,775m / 18,564 ft — a virgin peak, never summited). Take holy dip in the lake (Shiv Kund). Pray at the marble Shiva image on the lakeshore. Circumambulate the lake three times (parikrama). Manimahesh Kailash is the 3rd of Panch Kailash. Overnight in tents at the lake.

itinerary.title: Manimahesh Lake to Hadsar — Return to Bharmour
itinerary.desc: Morning holy dip and final prayers at the lake. Trek 13 km back to Hadsar (Dhancho → Hadsar: 7 km, then Hadsar reachable in 6-7 hrs total). Note: ponies and palanquins are NOT available for the descent — too steep. Drive 13 km from Hadsar back to Bharmour. Helicopter option (Yatra season only): Hadsar helipad to lake ~Rs 8,000 return. Last bus from Hadsar at 5 PM.

itinerary.title: Bharmour to Pathankot / Chandigarh — Return Drive
itinerary.distance: 165 km to Pathankot / 250 km to Chandigarh
itinerary.desc: Drive from Bharmour via Chamba to Pathankot (165 km, 6 hrs) or Chandigarh (250 km, 8 hrs). Optional: visit Khajjiar (Switzerland of India) and Dalhousie en route.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Senthilkumar Sivasamy on Pexels

name: Triund Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Dhauladhar Wildlife Sanctuary Day Entry Permit
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in (mandatory pre-registration); Gallu Devi check-post above Dharamkot
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS: free registration but mandatory; ₹100 sanctuary day entry; overnight camping fee: ₹200–₹500 at authorised camping zones only
permitInfo.note: HP TMS registration at trekking.hp.gov.in is mandatory — without this your check-post entry will be refused. Daily visitor numbers at Triund are capped under the NGT/HP Forest Department sustainable tourism order (2022) due to severe overtrekking damage — pre-register and pre-book. Only authorised camping zones above Gallu Devi are permitted; random camping is banned and fined. Plastic carry bags banned; carry all waste out. Medical certificate for treks above 3,000m. Photography of snow leopards or wildlife requires Wildlife Institute of India permission.

description: Himachal Pradesh's most-visited trek and one of India's most dramatic overnight destinations — a meadow ridge at 2,828m directly above McLeod Ganj (Dharamshala) offering a wall-to-wall view of the Dhauladhar snow peaks and the entire Kangra Valley below. The steep 2,828m ridge is only 9 km from the Dharamkot trailhead, making it achievable as a day trek but most rewarding as an overnight stay for the spectacular sunset and starlit night beneath the peaks.

overview.location: Triund meadow (2,828m) sits on the main Dhauladhar ridgeline above McLeod Ganj and Dharamkot village (1,457m), Kangra district. The Dhauladhar peaks — some rising to over 5,000m — form a white wall directly behind Triund when viewed from Kangra Valley. The 9 km approach from Dharamkot/McLeod Ganj ascends through Dhauladhar Wildlife Sanctuary's cedar and oak forest. McLeod Ganj below is the seat of the Tibetan Government in Exile and home to the Dalai Lama.
overview.history: Triund's name likely derives from a Gaddi word for a ridge camping ground used by shepherd communities. The meadow has been a seasonal Gaddi grazing area for centuries. McLeod Ganj was established as a British hill station in the 1850s and became famous worldwide after the Dalai Lama established his residence there in 1960. Triund became one of India's most popular short treks from the 2000s, driven by Dharamshala's growing international profile. Severe environmental degradation from mass tourism led the HP Forest Department to impose a visitor cap and TMS mandatory registration from 2022.
overview.length: 18 km round-trip (9 km each way) over 2 days. Total elevation gain from Dharamkot (1,457m) to Triund (2,828m): 1,371m. Day 1: Dharamkot to Triund (4–5 hours, steep in places). Day 2: Sunrise views, then return to Dharamkot (2–3 hours). Magic View Café at 2,600m is a mid-point landmark with panoramic views.
overview.temperature: Mar–Apr: 5°C–18°C at Triund; snow at the meadow edges; Kangra Valley green and hazy; rhododendron flowering on approach. May–Jun: 10°C–22°C; hot lower section; ideal season. Sep–Nov: 0°C–15°C; clearest skies; most dramatic Dhauladhar views — recommended season. Dec–Feb: –5°C to 5°C; Triund under snow; strikingly beautiful but cold; crampons needed above Magic View Café. Monsoon (Jul–Aug): Heavy rain and poor visibility — not recommended.
overview.fitness: Easy. The 1,371m ascent over 9 km is moderately steep but entirely non-technical and on well-maintained trails. Suitable for fit beginners and teenagers. The altitude of 2,828m poses minimal acclimatisation risk for most visitors. The main physical challenge is the sustained uphill gradient — take your time, stay hydrated, and the views are a constant reward.

itinerary.title: Dharamshala / McLeod Ganj to Triund
itinerary.distance: 9 km trek from McLeod Ganj / 7 km from Dharamkot
itinerary.desc: Trek from McLeod Ganj (1,457m) or Dharamkot (1,614m) through the Triund Forest (Kangra Forest Dept trail). 9 km from McLeod Ganj, 7 km from Dharamkot. The trail climbs through oak and rhododendron forest past Magic View Cafe, then enters open grassland for the last 2 km to Triund ridge (2,828m). Snow line ridge and Dhauladhar massif dominate the north. The Kangra Valley spread below to the south.

itinerary.title: Triund — Return to McLeod Ganj
itinerary.desc: Sunrise from Triund ridge over the Kangra valley is spectacular. Descend 9 km back to McLeod Ganj via Dharamkot. The entire round trip is 18 km. Many do this as a single-day trek from Dharamshala.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Stran Music on Pexels

name: Kareri Lake Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Dhauladhar Wildlife Sanctuary Permit
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; Kareri village check-post
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory; ₹100 sanctuary entry; camping fee: ₹200
permitInfo.note: HP TMS registration mandatory. Kareri village (starting point) is 25 km from Dharamshala — local guides available from the village. Dhauladhar WLS regulations prohibit open fires within the sanctuary; carry a stove. Trek insurance mandatory. The lake surface may be frozen from November to April.

description: A serene and less-crowded alternative to Triund — Kareri Lake (2,934m) is a beautiful glacial lake in the Dhauladhar foothills above Dharamshala, backed by the sheer rock walls of the range. The approach through the Gaj Khad valley is exceptionally beautiful — lush forests, meadows, and a river trail — and the lake's setting beneath the mountain wall is one of the finest in the lower Dhauladhar.

overview.location: Kareri Lake (2,934m) lies in the upper Gaj Khad valley in the Dhauladhar Wildlife Sanctuary, Kangra district, north of Dharamshala. The lake drains into the Gaj River, a tributary of the Ravi. Kareri village (1,500m) is the trailhead — 25 km from Dharamshala town via Ghera village on the Sidhbari road. The Dhauladhar peaks above the lake rise steeply to 4,500m+.
overview.history: Kareri village has been part of the settled agricultural landscape of Kangra district for centuries. The lake above it is sacred to local Gaddi and Kangri communities and appears in local folk traditions. The Dhauladhar Wildlife Sanctuary protecting this watershed was established to protect the watershed ecology of the Kangra Valley. The trek gained popularity from the 1990s as an alternative to the heavily trafficked Triund route.
overview.length: 32 km round-trip over 4–5 days from Kareri village. Total elevation gain approximately 1,434m. Day 1: Dharamshala/drive to Kareri village, then trek 7 km to Reoti Gad campsite. Day 2: Reoti Gad to Kareri Lake (9 km). Day 3: Lake exploration and return to Reoti Gad. Day 4: Return to Kareri village and Dharamshala.
overview.temperature: Apr–Jun: 5°C–20°C; the lake defrosts in April; wildflowers in May–June. Sep–Oct: 0°C–15°C; the clearest views; recommended season. Nov–Mar: Lake fully frozen; trail icy; not recommended without winter gear. Monsoon (Jul–Aug): Heavy rain in this zone; not recommended.
overview.fitness: Moderate. Suitable for trekkers with basic fitness and comfort on mountain trails. The 1,434m elevation gain over 2 trek days is manageable at a steady pace. The Gaj Khad river trail requires some boulder hopping. Preparation: 4–6 weeks of regular walking and cardiovascular exercise.

itinerary.title: Dharamshala — Kareri Village — Reoti Gad
itinerary.desc: Drive from Dharamshala to Kareri village. Register TMS at the check-post. The trail follows the Gaj Khad river through beautiful mixed forest — cedar, walnut, and horse chestnut — above the stream. Reoti Gad is a pleasant streamside camp.

itinerary.title: Reoti Gad — Kareri Lake
itinerary.desc: Above Reoti Gad the forest opens to meadows and the Dhauladhar wall begins to appear. The lake occupies a wide flat bowl — the glacier feeding it is visible above, and the sheer rockface of the Dhauladhar peaks rises directly behind.

itinerary.title: Kareri Lake exploration — Return to Reoti Gad
itinerary.desc: Morning at the lake for wildlife and bird watching — the lake is an important waterbird stopover; Himalayan golden eagles are regularly seen soaring the updrafts above the cliff face. Return descent to Reoti Gad.

itinerary.title: Reoti Gad — Kareri Village — Dharamshala
itinerary.desc: Final easy descent through the forest valley to Kareri village, then the drive back to Dharamshala. The Kangra Valley panorama on the drive is beautiful.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Veer Rajpoot on Pexels

name: Spiti Homestay Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Spiti Protected Area Permit (Foreigners only) + Inner Line Permit (Foreigners)
permitInfo.where: HP TMS: trekking.hp.gov.in (mandatory all); Foreign PAP/ILP: SDM Kaza — apply minimum 3 days before; apply at Recong Peo or Kaza
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS free registration mandatory; Indian nationals: no ILP; Foreigners: PAP from SDM Kaza — free, but groups of 4+ required with registered guide; single foreigners cannot trek Spiti independently
permitInfo.note: Spiti is a Protected Area — foreigners require an Inner Line Permit from the District Magistrate Kaza. Indian nationals do not need ILP but must register at ITBP check-posts. HP TMS mandatory for all. This trek uses local village homestays exclusively — no camping — making it an excellent community-based tourism experience. Kaza is accessible by road from Shimla (10 hrs) or Manali (10 hrs via Rohtang). Air access via Kullu/Bhuntar airport (230 km). Altitude sickness is common in Spiti — 1–2 nights in Kaza for acclimatisation mandatory before starting.

description: An extraordinary cultural and landscape immersion through the ancient monasteries, high-altitude villages, and moonscape valleys of Spiti — the 'Little Tibet' of India. This homebased trek visits Ki Monastery, Kibber village (one of the world's highest inhabited villages with a road), the Chicham bridge crossing, and Pin Valley National Park on a route that stays in traditional Spiti homestays each night — a deeply rewarding community tourism experience in one of India's most remote inhabited landscapes.

overview.location: The Spiti Valley (average elevation 3,800–4,200m) is an arid Trans-Himalayan plateau in Lahaul and Spiti district — geographically and culturally closer to Tibet than to the Indian plains. Kaza (3,800m) is the administrative headquarters. The trek circuits through villages above the Spiti River: Ki (3,950m), Kibber (4,205m), Langza (4,400m), Hikkim (4,400m), and Komic (4,587m — one of the world's highest inhabited villages with a road). Pin Valley and Mudh village (3,760m) round out the circuit.
overview.history: Spiti Valley has been Tibetan Buddhist territory for over 1,000 years — its monasteries (Ki, Tabo, Dhankar) date from the 11th–14th centuries and contain extraordinary wall paintings and thangkas. The valley was part of the Kingdom of Guge (western Tibet) before coming under Ladakh and then Kullu rule. The 1962 Indo-China war led to Inner Line restrictions that kept Spiti closed to outsiders until 1992. The removal of the ILP requirement for Indians (while maintaining it for foreigners) spurred a rapid rise in domestic tourism since 2010.
overview.length: 45 km over 6 days from Kaza to Mudh, with a vehicle return from Mudh. This is a moderate daily walking distance of 6–10 km per day — the high altitude means shorter distances feel more challenging. Total elevation change is relatively modest (the plateau is already at 3,800–4,500m throughout) but altitude demands a measured pace.
overview.temperature: Jun–Jul: 10°C–25°C daytime; –2°C to 5°C night. The valley is arid so rainfall is minimal even during monsoon. Aug–Sep: 5°C–20°C; excellent clear skies; most comfortable. Oct: 0°C–12°C; brilliant autumn light; early snow at village level possible. Nov–May: Road from Manali via Rohtang closed; Shimla route may remain open but harsh conditions.
overview.fitness: Moderate. The altitude (3,800–4,500m throughout) is the primary challenge rather than the distance or gradient. Acclimatisation days in Kaza before starting are essential and must not be skipped — acute mountain sickness affects many visitors to Spiti who arrive too quickly. The daily walking distances are gentle. Suitable for trekkers with prior experience of 4,000m altitude. Preparation: 6–8 weeks of cardio training.

itinerary.title: Kaza — Acclimatisation — Ki Monastery visit
itinerary.desc: Rest in Kaza (3,800m) for the first day — essential acclimatisation. Visit Ki Monastery (12th century), spectacularly perched on a rocky outcrop above the Spiti River — one of the most photographed Buddhist monasteries in India. Walk to Ki village for the first homestay experience.

itinerary.title: Ki — Kibber — Chicham
itinerary.desc: Trek to Kibber (4,205m) — a high-altitude village whose houses are painted turquoise and white in traditional Spiti style. Cross the Chicham bridge — a dramatic suspension bridge above a 150m deep gorge. Views of the snow leopard habitat zones above.

itinerary.title: Kibber — Langza — Hikkim
itinerary.desc: Walk the high ridge from Kibber to Langza — famous for its Buddhist stupa and excellent fossil hunting (marine fossils at 4,400m prove this was once ocean floor). Langza offers sweeping views of Manerang (6,593m). Hikkim houses the world's highest functioning post office — post a card.

itinerary.title: Hikkim — Komic — Demul
itinerary.desc: Komic (4,587m) is one of the world's highest motorable villages — the view from its ancient gompa across the barren plateau to the 6,000m peaks of Lahaul is incomparable. Descend to the quieter Demul village for a memorable homestay.

itinerary.title: Demul — Lara — Pin Valley — Mudh
itinerary.desc: Cross to the Pin Valley National Park boundary and descend to Mudh — the last village in the Pin Valley. The Pin Valley's landscape of brown rock walls and bright turquoise river is extraordinarily dramatic. Snow leopard habitat — look carefully at the scree slopes above.

itinerary.title: Mudh — Kaza — Return
itinerary.desc: Vehicle from Mudh back to Kaza on the Pin Valley road. Departure from Kaza by bus or jeep to Shimla (430 km, 10 hrs), Manali (210 km via Kunzum, 8 hrs in summer), or Chandigarh.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Yogendra  Singh on Pexels

name: Churdhar Peak Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Sirmaur DFO Forest Permit
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; Nauradhar check-post at trail start
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory; ₹50 DFO Sirmaur forest entry; temple entry: free (offerings welcome)
permitInfo.note: HP TMS mandatory registration. Nauradhar is 50 km from Solan or Nahan in Sirmaur district. Churdhar is the highest peak in the outer Himalayan range — the Shiwalik — outside the main Greater Himalayan chain. The Shirgul Maharaj temple at the summit is an active Hindu shrine with resident priests year-round. Trek insurance mandatory. The ridge can be very cold and windswept even in October — carry warm layers.

description: The highest peak of the Sirmaur-Shimla outer Himalayas — Churdhar (3,647m) is a striking summit crowned by the ancient Shirgul Maharaj temple, revered across Himachal Pradesh. The approach from Nauradhar (Sirmaur district) is through exceptional mixed Himalayan oak and rhododendron forest, emerging above treeline to a panoramic summit ridge. The view from Churdhar extends from the plains to the Greater Himalayan peaks — remarkably, both the Punjab plains and the 7,000m peaks are visible simultaneously.

overview.location: Churdhar (3,647m) is the highest summit of the Churdhardhar Range — the outermost ridge of the Himachal Himalayas, rising above Sirmaur and Shimla districts in the sub-Himalayan zone. The peak is 50–70 km from Nahan (Sirmaur HQ) or Solan. At 3,647m it stands isolated from the main Great Himalayan chain and thus offers an extraordinary 360° panorama — the Punjab/Haryana plains to the south and the Greater Himalayan peaks including Swargarohini and Bandarpoonch to the north.
overview.history: Churdhar is the abode of Shirgul Maharaj — the god of Sirmaur and Shimla districts — whose temple at the summit is one of the most important sacred sites in Himachal's outer hills. The deity Shirgul (also called Churdhar Maharaj) is worshipped across a wide belt of Sirmaur and Shimla hill communities. The annual Shirgul Mela brings thousands of pilgrims to Churdhar each summer. The temple complex at the summit includes a shrine that remains staffed year-round. The British Survey of India established a triangulation point on Churdhar — one of their outer Himalayan reference peaks.
overview.length: 30 km round-trip over 3–4 days from Nauradhar (2,238m). Total elevation gain approximately 1,409m. Day 1: Nauradhar to Teel (2,700m) — 7 km, 3 hours. Day 2: Teel to Churdhar summit (3,647m) and back to Teel — 16 km, 7–8 hours. Day 3: Teel to Nauradhar return. Forest rest houses at Teel and Sankri (HPFD) provide basic accommodation.
overview.temperature: Apr–May: 5°C–18°C; rhododendron bloom in April — the forests below are spectacular. Jun: 10°C–22°C; warmest; plains haze reduces summit view. Sep–Oct: 0°C–15°C; clearest summit views; best season. Nov–Mar: –5°C to 5°C; snow on the summit ridge; cold but possible with proper gear. Summit wind-chill can be brutal year-round.
overview.fitness: Moderate. The sustained forest trail to the summit involves significant elevation gain on Day 2 (1,000m+ in a single day). No technical terrain. Suitable for trekkers with basic multi-day experience. The summit wind and temperature can be extreme — carry more warm layers than you think necessary. Preparation: 6–8 weeks of hill walking and cardiovascular training.

itinerary.title: Solan/Nahan — Nauradhar — Teel
itinerary.desc: Drive from Solan or Nahan to Nauradhar check-post. Register at TMS post. The trail ascends immediately through beautiful mixed forest — oaks, deodars, and spectacular rhododendron. Teel forest rest house is a comfortable overnight base at the treeline edge.

itinerary.title: Teel — Churdhar Summit — Return to Teel
itinerary.desc: The summit day — an alpine start recommended to catch clear views before afternoon haze. The trail climbs above treeline onto the open ridge before the final steep push to the summit temple. Shirgul Maharaj temple at the top — priests provide prasad to pilgrims. The plains-to-peaks panorama is extraordinary. Return to Teel carefully in afternoon.

itinerary.title: Teel — Nauradhar — Return
itinerary.desc: Final leisurely descent through the forest. The birding on this section is outstanding — Himalayan monal, Koklas pheasant, and various laughing thrushes inhabit the forest. Return to Nauradhar and drive to Solan or Nahan.

coverImageCredit: Photo by ASHISH SHARMA on Pexels

name: Jalori Pass & Serolsar Lake Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; Jalori Pass roadhead check-post
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory (free); ₹50 forest entry at Jalori; camping at Serolsar: ₹200
permitInfo.note: HP TMS mandatory pre-registration. Jalori Pass (3,120m) is drive-accessible — the road from Aut/Kullu via Banjar and Shoja reaches the pass, making this one of the few high-altitude treks where you start directly at 3,000m. The short approach to Serolsar Lake (7.5 km) makes it excellent for families and beginners. HP Forest permit issued at the Jalori check-post. No camping on the Jalori Pass meadow surface.

description: A perfectly accessible beginner alpine trek starting directly from the motor road at Jalori Pass (3,120m) — one of Himachal's most beautiful and least-known high passes in the Great Himalayan National Park buffer zone. The short walk to the sacred Serolsar Lake (3,120m) passes through pristine oak-rhododendron forest with brilliant views of the Kullu-Shimla divide peaks. The combination of drive-up high altitude and a rewarding walk makes this one of HP's finest easy mountain experiences.

overview.location: Jalori Pass (3,120m) is a motorable pass on the divide between the Kullu and Shimla districts, connected by road from Aut (NH3) via Banjar and Shoja. The pass lies within the buffer zone of Great Himalayan National Park (UNESCO WHS). Serolsar Lake (7.5 km from the pass) is a sacred glacial lake under a dense oak forest canopy. The Banjar Valley below is one of Himachal's most beautiful — the traditional Kullu wooden-frame villages, apple orchards, and the deep Tirthan River gorge are all visible.
overview.history: Jalori Pass has been a trade and movement route between the Kullu Valley and the Shimla hills for centuries. The surrounding Great Himalayan National Park protects the last continuous tract of temperate Himalayan forest in Himachal Pradesh. Serolsar Lake is sacred to Buddhni Mata (the 'Old Woman Goddess') — a local deity of the Banjar Valley whose temple sits beside the lake. The 2014 UNESCO World Heritage inscription of GHNP included the Jalori buffer zone.
overview.length: 15 km round-trip from Jalori Pass to Serolsar Lake and back. Total elevation gain from pass to lake: minimal — the trail stays close to 3,120m throughout. Best combined with a side climb to Raghupur Fort (3,165m) — an ancient hilltop fortification 1.5 km from the pass with 360° views. Total combined: 20 km.
overview.temperature: Apr–May: 5°C–18°C; rhododendron bloom spectacular; some snow at lake level in April. Jun–Aug: 10°C–20°C; green and lush; Tirthan Valley below in monsoon. Sep–Oct: 0°C–12°C; brilliant clear skies; best panoramic views. Nov: –2°C to 8°C; pass may close under snow by late November. Dec–Mar: Pass road closed; trek inaccessible.
overview.fitness: Easy. The flat/gradual trail to Serolsar Lake at constant 3,120m requires minimal physical fitness. Ideal for families with young children, older adults, and complete beginners at Himalayan altitude. The Raghupur Fort side trip adds a brief 45m climb. Altitude of 3,120m may cause mild symptoms in those arriving from sea level — 1–2 hours at Jalori before the lake walk is a natural acclimatisation.

itinerary.title: Kullu/Manali or Shimla — Aut/Banjar — Jalori Pass
itinerary.desc: Drive from Kullu via Aut and up the spectacular Banjar Valley road to Jalori Pass. Register TMS and collect forest entry receipt. Evening walk to the Jalori meadow for sunset views of the Kullu Valley peaks. The road itself is an adventure — hairpin bends through apple orchards above the Tirthan gorge.

itinerary.title: Jalori Pass — Serolsar Lake — Raghupur Fort — Return
itinerary.camp: Jalori Pass or return to Banjar/Shoja
itinerary.desc: Morning walk through enchanting dense oak and rhododendron forest to Serolsar Lake. The Buddhni Mata shrine at the lakeside is ancient and beautifully maintained. Afternoon: climb to Raghupur Fort for the panoramic 360° view — Dhauladhar behind, Spiti peaks ahead, and Kullu Valley below. Return to Jalori for the drive down.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Amjad ali on Pexels

name: Kheerganga Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Kullu DFO Forest Permit
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; Barshaini check-post at trail start
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory; ₹50 forest entry; ₹50 camping fee per night at authorised Kheerganga zone
permitInfo.note: HP TMS pre-registration mandatory. Barshaini check-post at the trailhead is 35 km from Bhuntar airport via Manikaran. The Kheerganga hot spring area has been severely impacted by overtourism — the NGT has issued orders restricting camping and plastic use. Only authorised camping zones are permitted; camping in the meadow itself is banned. Open fires banned. All waste must be carried out. The hot spring pools are communal — segregated pools are available. Entry to Kheerganga natural area: ₹100 charged by village committee.

description: The most famous easy trek in the Parvati Valley — Kheerganga (2,960m) is a stunning mountain meadow at the end of a scenic Parvati River gorge trail, crowned by a famous outdoor natural hot spring pool. The walk through the dramatic canyon to these thermal pools — set in a meadow with mountain views — has made Kheerganga one of North India's most popular trekking destinations. The combination of beautiful forest trail, dramatic river gorge, and the reward of a hot spring soak makes this Himachal's perfect introductory trek.

overview.location: Kheerganga (2,960m) is in the upper Parvati Valley, Kullu district, at the confluence of the Parvati River tributaries draining from the Mantalai glacier above. The valley is renowned for its dramatic narrow gorge walls, dense forest, and the Parvati River's intense turquoise colour. Manikaran hot springs (1,760m) — one of Himachal's holiest Sikh and Hindu sites — lies 22 km downstream. The trek begins from Barshaini roadhead, 35 km from Bhuntar (Kullu) via Manikaran.
overview.history: The Parvati Valley has been sacred since ancient times — Manikaran's hot springs are mentioned in Sikh scripture (Guru Nanak's meditation site) and Hindu scripture (the legend of Shiva's earring falling into the Parvati River). Kheerganga itself is named for the 'milk-white river' (kheer = milk) that flows from the glacial area above. The valley became a significant destination for Western travellers, yoga practitioners, and spiritual seekers from the 1970s onwards. The Kheerganga natural hot spring has been in continuous use for generations by sadhus, pilgrims, and local Gaddi communities.
overview.length: 24 km round-trip (12 km each way) over 2 days from Barshaini. The trail alternates between two sides of the Parvati River via suspension bridges, offering different perspectives on the gorge. Total elevation gain from Barshaini (1,920m) to Kheerganga (2,960m): 1,040m over 12 km — steady but not steep. Return by the same route or the alternative ridge path (more strenuous).
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–22°C; lush and green; rhododendron in bloom; the hot spring most enjoyed when air is cooler. Jul–Aug: 10°C–22°C; monsoon brings waterfalls and lush jungle atmosphere; trail occasionally slippery. Sep–Oct: 5°C–18°C; most stable; golden autumn foliage on the approach forest. Nov: 0°C–12°C; few people; magical snow at Kheerganga. Dec–Apr: Closed; heavy snow blocks trail above 2,500m.
overview.fitness: Easy. The most accessible high-altitude overnight trek in Himachal Pradesh. Suitable for complete beginners, families with children above 10, and anyone who can walk 12 km uphill at a gentle gradient. The hot spring at the top provides an unusual motivational endpoint. Preparation: No special fitness preparation required beyond regular walking.

itinerary.title: Bhuntar / Kasol to Barshaini — Trek to Kheerganga
itinerary.distance: 30 km road to Barshaini + 12 km trek
itinerary.camp: Kheerganga — open meadow with hot springs
itinerary.desc: Drive from Bhuntar via Kasol to Barshaini village (30 km, 1.5 hrs). Trek begins at Barshaini. 12 km one-way trek along the Parvati River valley via Nakthan, Rudra Nag waterfall, and dense forest to Kheerganga (2,950m). The trail climbs 1,150m. Kheerganga is famous for the natural hot sulphur spring pools. Lord Shiva and Kartikeya are believed to have meditated here.

itinerary.title: Kheerganga — Return to Barshaini
itinerary.desc: Morning soak in the hot springs, then 12 km descent from Kheerganga back to Barshaini. Drive to Kasol or Bhuntar for onward connections. Total trek: 24 km round trip.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Shreyas Kc on Pexels

name: Parang La Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS + Inner Line Permit (both Spiti and Ladakh sides) + Changthang Wildlife Sanctuary Permit
permitInfo.where: HP TMS: trekking.hp.gov.in; ILP Spiti side: SDM Kaza; ILP Ladakh side: DC Leh; Changthang WLS permit: DFO Leh
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory; Spiti ILP: free, SDM Kaza; Ladakh ILP/PAP: ₹200–₹400 DFO Leh; Changthang WLS: ₹200/day Indian, ₹1000/day foreigner; Foreigners require restricted area permit (group of 2+ minimum with guide)
permitInfo.note: One of the most serious trans-Himalayan treks. Both Spiti (HP) and Changthang (Ladakh) border zone permits required — apply minimum 1 week before in Kaza and Leh respectively. The trail crosses the Tibetan Plateau's edge and is within the sensitive border zone — ITBP registration at Korzok. A registered and experienced guide is mandatory — this trek has caused multiple casualties of unprepared teams. Medical certificate, full expedition first-aid kit, and helicopter evacuation insurance are essential.

description: A legendary trans-Himalayan expedition crossing from the high-altitude desert of Spiti (Himachal Pradesh) to the remote Changthang plateau of Ladakh over the Parang La (5,590m) — one of India's highest regularly crossed trekking passes. The 140 km route traverses one of the most remote and scenically extreme landscapes on Earth: the Tibetan plateau edge, with vast uninhabited plains, enormous glacial lakes, and encounters with the Changpa nomadic herders who tend their yak and pashmina goat flocks in this desolate high-altitude borderland.

overview.location: Parang La (5,590m) is a high Tibetan plateau pass crossing from the Spiti River watershed (Himachal Pradesh) to the Pare Chu drainage of the Changthang plateau (Ladakh), near Tso Moriri lake. The trek begins from Kaza (3,800m) in Spiti and ends at Korzok village (4,522m) beside Tso Moriri lake — a UNESCO-designated biosphere reserve. The crossing takes 4–5 days of completely uninhabited wilderness above 4,500m with no escape route in case of emergency.
overview.history: The Parang La has been used for centuries by Changpa nomadic herders moving between their summer grazing grounds (Changthang plateau) and their winter pastures in Spiti and the Kulu Valley. The route was part of the ancient Trans-Himalayan trade network that connected the Indian plains with Central Asia via Ladakh, Spiti, and Tibet. The Changpa people who live on the Changthang plateau are some of the world's highest-altitude permanent inhabitants — their pashmina goat herding culture has been maintained largely unchanged for centuries.
overview.length: 140 km over 12 days, Kaza to Korzok. Total elevation gain approximately 5,500m cumulatively across the route. The Parang La crossing itself (Day 7–8) involves 2 days above 5,000m with a 5,590m high point. The Tso Moriri lakeshore approach on the Ladakh side is one of the world's great wilderness walks.
overview.temperature: June: –5°C to 15°C in valleys; –15°C to 0°C at passes; considerable snow. Jul–Aug: 5°C–20°C in valleys; –5°C to 5°C at passes; most stable season. Sep: 0°C–15°C; drier and clearer; recommended for experienced parties. Oct: –10°C to 5°C; early snowfall possible on pass; for expert teams only.
overview.fitness: Expert only. 12 days of sustained wilderness trekking above 4,500m, a 5,590m pass, multiple days with no water sources, and no rescue infrastructure for 6 straight days. Only for highly experienced high-altitude trekkers with prior expedition experience. A Spiti/Ladakh-experienced guide is mandatory. Emergency medical first-aid expertise within the group is strongly recommended.

itinerary.title: Kaza — Acclimatisation at Kaza (3,800m)
itinerary.desc: Mandatory rest and acclimatisation in Kaza. Collect permits from SDM Kaza. Study the route with your guide. Evening: Kaza market for last supply purchases.

itinerary.title: Kaza — Kibber — Tashigang
itinerary.desc: Trek above Kibber village through the high Spiti plateau. The landscape shifts from the village zone to pure high-desert terrain. First wild camp of the expedition.

itinerary.title: Tashigang — Phorse
itinerary.desc: Increasingly remote terrain. The last traces of vegetation disappear. Navigation requires a guide — the trail is unclear in places. First view of the Gyama Range ahead.

itinerary.title: Phorse — Gyama Valley high camp
itinerary.desc: Enter the high-altitude wilderness properly. At 5,050m the altitude is serious — any symptoms of AMS require immediate descent. The scenery is extraordinary: brown rock, blue sky, distant snow peaks, and complete silence.

itinerary.title: High camp — Parang La Pass — Descent to Ladakh side
itinerary.desc: The high point of the entire trek. Parang La at 5,590m requires crampons and a headtorch start at 4 AM. The narrow snow/ice notch of the pass opens to the vast brown sweep of the Changthang plateau. The descent to Ladakh is long and slow at altitude.

itinerary.title: Ladakh camp — Puga hot springs — Korzok
itinerary.desc: Two days of walking across the extraordinary Changthang plateau — encounter Changpa nomads with their yak and pashmina herds. Puga hot springs (unusual volcanic activity) en route. Arrive at Korzok village beside the stunning Tso Moriri lake — register with ITBP.

itinerary.title: Korzok — Manali or Leh by road
itinerary.desc: Vehicle from Korzok to Leh (220 km via Chumathang, 7 hrs) or Manali (475 km via Pang and Rohtang, 12 hrs). After 12 days in the wilderness, the luxury of a proper meal and a shower feels extraordinary.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Ankush Bhatia on Pexels

name: Kalihani Pass Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Kullu DFO Forest Permit + Lahaul Forest Permit
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; Manali/Kullu check-post at start; Lahaul DFO Keylong at end
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory; Kullu Forest Div: ₹50–₹100; Lahaul Forest Div: ₹50–₹100
permitInfo.note: HP TMS mandatory. The trek crosses from Kullu to Lahaul district — both district forest permits required. Manali-based guides are familiar with this route. The Kullu side is approached from Solang Nullah. The Lahaul side descends to Jobri or Shuru in the Chandra Valley. Trek insurance mandatory. Crampons required in July–early August.

description: A demanding and supremely rewarding crossover trek from the Kullu Valley to Lahaul over the Kalihani Pass (4,800m) — a route beloved by experienced Himachal trekkers for its extraordinary variety: from Manali's forest and meadows up through glacial landscapes to the stark, treeless Lahaul Valley in a continuous 8-day arc. The final view from Kalihani Pass — the Lahaul peaks stretching north to the Zanskar range — is one of Himachal's great mountain panoramas.

overview.location: Kalihani Pass (4,800m) sits on the watershed between the Kullu Valley's Solang Nullah drainage and the Chandra River valley of Lahaul. The approach starts from Solang Nullah (2,480m) above Manali and crosses through high-alpine meadows and glacial terrain before the pass. The descent into Lahaul reaches Jobri or Shuru in the upper Chandra Valley — the same valley that Chandratal Lake drains from further east. The Lahaul side is characterized by the stark brown-and-white landscape of the Lahaul Himalayas.
overview.history: The Kalihani crossing has been used by Gaddi shepherds for centuries as a seasonal route from the Kullu Valley grazing grounds to the summer pastures of Lahaul. The Solang Nullah approach is the same valley used for skiing in winter — developed as a ski resort from the 1970s. The Lahaul Valley was opened to foreign trekkers from 1989 after restrictions were lifted. The Kalihani Pass trek gained popularity in the 1990s–2000s as an extension of the Beas Kund circuit.
overview.length: 58 km over 8 days from Solang Nullah to Jobri (Lahaul). Total elevation gain from Solang (2,480m) to pass (4,800m): 2,320m. The pass crossing day is the crux — 7–8 hours from the glacier high camp. Vehicle logistics required at both ends (Manali and Keylong/Lahaul).
overview.temperature: Jul: 0°C–18°C; pass accessible; crampons on the upper glacier section. Aug–Sep: 5°C–20°C; best season; most stable. Oct: –5°C to 10°C; pass may have new snowfall; experienced teams only. Nov–Jun: Pass closed.
overview.fitness: Hard. 8 days of sustained mountain trekking with a 4,800m pass crossing requiring crampons. Prior experience on multi-day high-altitude treks is required. Good cardiovascular fitness and comfort on snow terrain are essential. Preparation: 10–12 weeks of intensive training. Guide recommended.

itinerary.title: Manali — Solang Nullah — Dhundi
itinerary.desc: Register TMS at Solang Nullah check-post. The approach follows the Beas Kund trail up the Solang valley through forest and meadow. Dhundi is the established campsite at the valley's first narrows.

itinerary.title: Dhundi — Bakarthach Meadow
itinerary.desc: Above Dhundi the trail opens to the magnificent Bakarthach meadow — the same camp as the Beas Kund approach. Excellent views of Hanuman Tibba and Friendship Peak. The route branches here: Beas Kund goes left, Kalihani ascends right.

itinerary.title: Bakarthach — Kalihani High Camp
itinerary.desc: The route diverges from the Beas Kund trail and ascends the Kalihani glacier moraine. The upper glacier is visible ahead — crampons packed and ready. The high camp at 4,300m is on the glacier edge with extraordinary peak panoramas.

itinerary.title: High Camp — Kalihani Pass — Shuru (Lahaul)
itinerary.desc: Alpine start at 4 AM. Crampons on for the glacier ascent to the pass. Kalihani Pass (4,800m) is a wide snow saddle — the Lahaul peaks suddenly appear to the north and the Zanskar range is visible beyond. The descent on the Lahaul side is long — steep snow then rocky moraine to the valley floor.

itinerary.title: Lahaul valley — Keylong or vehicle to Manali
itinerary.desc: The final walk to the Lahaul road at Jobri. Vehicle arranged to Keylong (district HQ of Lahaul and Spiti) or directly back to Manali via the Lahaul Highway and Rohtang Pass.

coverImageCredit: Photo by UTkarsh on Pexels

name: Miyar Valley Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Lahaul DFO Forest Permit
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; Udaipur (Lahaul) check-post; Shukto village registration
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory; Lahaul DFO forest permit: ₹50–₹100; no national park entry fees
permitInfo.note: HP TMS mandatory. The Miyar Valley is in Lahaul district — accessible from Manali via Rohtang Pass (open Jun–Oct) or the Atal Tunnel (open year-round). Udaipur in Lahaul is the district's cultural centre (Triloknath temple). The valley beyond Shukto is very remote — full camping self-sufficiency required for the upper valley. ITBP check-post at Shukto village registration. Trek insurance mandatory.

description: Called the 'Valley of Flowers of Himachal' by those who know it, Miyar Valley (Lahaul) is a secluded side-valley of extraordinary beauty and remoteness — less visited than the better-known Spiti Valley circuits but arguably more dramatic. The 80 km approach to the Miyar Glacier passes through ancient Lahauli Buddhist villages of remarkable architectural beauty, vast wildflower meadows at 3,500–3,900m, and terminates at the glacier base beneath the extraordinary Kang Sapo and Miyar peaks.

overview.location: The Miyar Valley is a major side-valley of the Chandrabhaga (Chenab) River in Lahaul district, branching north from Udaipur town (2,743m). The valley extends 60 km into the Zanskar Range, culminating at the Miyar Glacier (3,962m) beneath a ring of impressive peaks: Kang Sapo (6,020m), Tipling (6,000m), and the CB (Chandrabhaga) peaks. The Miyar Nullah is exceptionally wide and flat-floored compared to most Lahaul valleys, allowing cultivation up to 3,600m.
overview.history: The Miyar Valley is home to a series of ancient Lahauli Buddhist villages — Khanjar, Tholang, Urgos, and Shukto — with gompas and chortens dating from the 10th–14th centuries. The valley is part of the broader Zanskar Buddhist cultural sphere and shares architectural and religious traditions with Zanskar and Ladakh. European mountaineers first explored the Miyar glacier in the 1930s–40s seeking routes onto the Zanskar peaks. The valley remained essentially unknown to trekkers until the 1990s.
overview.length: 80 km over 9 days from Udaipur to glacier base and return. Total elevation gain approximately 1,219m from Udaipur (2,743m) to glacier base (3,962m) — a very gradual ascent profile. The wide flat valley allows comfortable daily walking of 10–12 km despite the altitude.
overview.temperature: Jun: 5°C–20°C; some snowmelt; wildflowers beginning. Jul–Aug: 8°C–22°C; peak wildflower season — the valley is famous for its blanket of alpine flowers. Sep: 0°C–18°C; clearest skies; autumn colours on the lower sections. Oct: –5°C to 10°C; Rohtang may close; cold but beautiful. Nov–May: Inaccessible.
overview.fitness: Hard — due to remoteness and self-sufficiency requirements rather than technical difficulty. The terrain and gradient are actually moderate, but the 9 days of full camping self-sufficiency in a remote valley with no infrastructure beyond the villages requires strong logistics capability and experience. Prior multi-day camping trek experience is essential. Preparation: 10 weeks of training.

itinerary.title: Manali — Rohtang (or Atal Tunnel) — Udaipur (Lahaul)
itinerary.desc: Drive from Manali through the Atal Tunnel (bypassing Rohtang, open year-round) or over Rohtang Pass to Keylong, then to Udaipur — the cultural heart of Lahaul with its remarkable Triloknath temple (a shared Hindu-Buddhist shrine with a rare white marble Shiva-as-Avalokitesvara idol).

itinerary.title: Udaipur — Shukto village
itinerary.desc: Drive or walk the Miyar Valley road to its end at Shukto. ITBP registration at Shukto check-post. The ancient gompa above Shukto is worth visiting. Camp below the village at the valley meadows.

itinerary.title: Shukto — Khanjar — Tholang
itinerary.desc: The valley above Shukto is extraordinary — wide, green, and entirely enclosed by sheer rock walls of the Zanskar range. Ancient villages of flat-roofed stone with prayer flags and chortens at each turn. Wildflowers carpet the valley floor.

itinerary.title: Tholang — Urgos — Gumba Nullah
itinerary.desc: Above Tholang the settlements thin and the valley becomes more glacial. Gumba Nullah ('monastery stream') is named for an ancient ruined gompa high above the valley floor. The wildflower meadows here — at 3,600m — are remarkable.

itinerary.title: Gumba Nullah — Miyar Glacier Base
itinerary.desc: The final approach to the glacier across moraines and seasonal streams. The glacier base at 3,962m is ringed by the CB and Kang Sapo peaks. A rest day here allows extended glacier and high-camp explorations for fit trekkers.

itinerary.title: Rest / Exploration at Glacier Base
itinerary.desc: Exploration of the glacier snout and surrounding moraines. Views of Kang Sapo (6,020m) are exceptional from the glacier edge. The silence and remoteness here — 60 km from the nearest road — is complete.

itinerary.title: Glacier Base — Gumba Nullah — Tholang
itinerary.desc: Begin the return. The downhill walking is much faster — the same valley looks entirely different heading south, with new views of the CB peaks from behind.

itinerary.title: Tholang — Shukto — Udaipur — Manali
itinerary.desc: Complete the return to Shukto, then road to Udaipur. Celebrate with dinner at Udaipur's guesthouses (Lahauli food is excellent — Chha Gosht, locally grown barley flatbreads) before the final drive back to Manali through the Atal Tunnel.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Animesh Paul on Pexels

name: Tosh Glacier Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Kullu DFO Forest Permit
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; Barshaini check-post at Parvati Valley trail entry
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory; ₹50–₹100 Kullu forest entry
permitInfo.note: HP TMS mandatory. The trek starts from the village of Tosh (2,400m) — a charming traditional village above Barshaini accessible by jeep road from Barshaini. The approach to the glacier is through the Tosh Nullah above the famous Tosh village. White Sail peak (6,446m) and Dharamsura (6,446m) are the dominant peaks above the glacier. Trek insurance mandatory.

description: A beautiful and underrated glacier approach in the Parvati Valley above the famous Tosh village — offering a more peaceful alternative to the crowded Kheerganga route. The trail ascends the Tosh Nullah above the picturesque Tosh village to meadows and the glacier base beneath the massive White Sail (Dharamsura, 6,446m) peak. The combination of traditional Kullu village culture, wildflower meadows, and glacier scenery makes this one of the Parvati Valley's finest 4-day treks.

overview.location: The Tosh Glacier (4,050m) occupies the upper Tosh Nullah valley above Tosh village (2,400m) — a side valley of the main Parvati River valley in Kullu district. Tosh village is 6 km above Barshaini roadhead (the Parvati Valley motor road end) via a steep jeep track. The glacier drains beneath the south face of White Sail (Dharamsura, 6,446m) and Pyramid Peak. The Tosh Nullah joins the Parvati River at Barshaini — the same confluence where the Kheerganga trail begins.
overview.history: Tosh village is one of the most authentically preserved traditional villages in the Parvati Valley — its timber-frame houses, ancient wooden temples with elaborate carvings, and traditional terrace agriculture have been maintained by the Kullu Rajput community for centuries. The village has become a traveller destination from the 2000s due to its beauty and relative accessibility. The glacier above was first documented by Survey of India teams in the 19th century and has retreated significantly since.
overview.length: 35 km over 4–5 days from Barshaini, via Tosh village. Total elevation gain from Barshaini (1,920m) to glacier base (4,050m): 2,130m. Day 1: Barshaini to Tosh village (6 km, jeep or 2 hrs walk). Day 2: Tosh to Nudhar meadow (3,200m, 8 km). Day 3: Nudhar to glacier base (4,050m, 6 km). Day 4: Glacier exploration and return to Tosh. Day 5: Tosh to Barshaini.
overview.temperature: May–Jun: 5°C–18°C; wildflower peak; snow patches at glacier. Jul–Aug: 8°C–22°C; lush; some afternoon rain. Sep–Oct: 0°C–15°C; clearest skies; recommended season. Nov: –2°C to 8°C; cold but possible with proper gear. Glacier base can be cold even in August — nights reach –5°C.
overview.fitness: Moderate. The 2,130m elevation gain over 3 trek days is manageable for reasonably fit trekkers. The trail is well-maintained through the lower forest and village zone. The upper section above Nudhar meadow is on rougher mountain terrain. Prior multi-day trek experience is helpful. Preparation: 6–8 weeks of cardio and hill walking.

itinerary.title: Kullu/Bhuntar — Manikaran — Barshaini — Tosh Village
itinerary.desc: Drive to Barshaini. Register TMS. Walk or take shared jeep 6 km up to Tosh village. The village is extraordinarily beautiful — traditional timber houses with carved facades and slate roofs stacked on the steep hillside, with the glacier headwall visible far above. Explore the village and the ancient Sun Temple.

itinerary.title: Tosh Village — Nudhar Meadow
itinerary.desc: Above Tosh the trail enters a beautiful hanging valley with wide meadow benches. The White Sail peak becomes increasingly dominant as height is gained. Nudhar meadow is a broad pastoral ground with excellent camping — no facilities, full self-sufficiency required.

itinerary.title: Nudhar — Tosh Glacier Base
itinerary.desc: The approach to the glacier through rocky high-alpine terrain. The glacier base at 4,050m under the White Sail south face is a dramatic environment — large boulder fields, glacial streams, and the ice face above.

itinerary.title: Glacier Base — Tosh Village — Barshaini
itinerary.desc: Return descent to Tosh and down to Barshaini. The descent offers different perspectives on the Tosh Nullah — the valley opens dramatically on the way down. Final drive to Manikaran and Kullu/Bhuntar.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Rudra Gupta on Pexels

name: Jakhu Temple Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; forest entry checkpoint near Ridge Shimla
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory free registration; nominal forest entry fee; Ropeway (optional): ₹550 adults, ₹450 children return
permitInfo.note: HP TMS pre-registration mandatory even for this short trek (ID 111). Guide available: Himalyan Travels, Mall Road Shimla (9459619235). Indira Gandhi Medical College emergency: 01772-654713. Lakkar Bazar Police: 01772-655376. Nearest stations: Shimla Railway Station and Old Bus Stand. Jubber Hatti Airport 15 km. Open year-round per HP TMS. Monkeys are numerous near the temple — do not carry food visibly. Polythene banned in Himachal.

description: The most accessible mountain walk from Shimla's Mall Road — a 2.5 km forested climb through deodar cedar forest to Jakhu Temple (2,455m) and its 108-foot (33-metre) Hanuman statue (unveiled November 4, 2010; inaugurated by Abhishek Bachchan; built by HC Nanda Charitable Trust) — Guinness Record for tallest Hanuman statue at time of construction, visible from across Shimla. The HP government TMS (ID 111) describes it: 'The steep climb is rewarding for the fine views it offers over the surrounding valleys, out to the snow-capped peaks and over Shimla itself — the temple is only 2 km from the Ridge but it could be an hour walk.' Ponies available for the ride up.

overview.location: Jakhu Hill (2,455m) is the forested summit northeast of Shimla's Ridge and Mall Road, Shimla district. The trail starts from the Ridge (2,210m) — Shimla's central promenade near Christ Church — and ascends 2 km through Jakhu Forest Reserve. The HP TMS lists Scandal Point and the Ridge as key Points of Interest, describing the Ridge as 'the face of Shimla — a perfect spot to get photographed with spectacular views of the mountains.'
overview.history: According to the Ramayana, Hanuman rested on Jakhu Hill while searching for the Sanjeevani herb to save Lakshmana — making it one of the most ancient sacred sites in Shimla's history. The temple predates the British hill station (established 1864). The HP TMS notes the ropeway option and that 'there are many monkeys around the temple, but surprisingly they don't attack people.' The Jakhu Forest is a protected reserve dating from the colonial period.
overview.length: 4 km round-trip (2 km each way). Elevation gain from Ridge (2,210m) to summit (2,455m): 245m. Walking time: 30–45 minutes up, 20–30 minutes down. Ropeway alternative also available from town.
overview.temperature: Open year-round per HP TMS. Summer (Apr–Jun): 15°C–30°C; busy tourist season. Monsoon (Jul–Sep): 15°C–25°C; lush forest. Autumn (Oct–Nov): 8°C–20°C; clearest peak views. Winter (Dec–Feb): –2°C–10°C; possible snowfall; atmospheric.
overview.fitness: Easy. Suitable for all ages including children and elderly visitors. The 245m gain over 2 km is manageable at a slow pace. Main challenge: steep sections and monkeys near the temple — keep food in bags.

itinerary.title: Shimla Ridge → Jakhu Temple → Return
itinerary.desc: Start from the Ridge near Christ Church (near the State Library arrow sign pointing to Jakhoo). The 2.5km forested deodar path ascends steeply through Jakhu Reserve — ponies available for hire at the base. The 108-foot (33-metre) Hanuman statue appears dramatically as you emerge from the trees. Views of the entire Shimla town, surrounding valleys, and Himalayan peaks on clear days. Return by same path or take the ropeway down. Per official HP TMS Day 1: 'Start from Ridge Shimla, 30 minutes walk from Ridge to the Temple.'

coverImageCredit: Photo by Mohan Nannapaneni on Pexels

name: Prashar Lake Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Mandi DFO Forest Permit
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; Baggi village check-post (official HP TMS landmark: Baggi Bridge)
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory free registration; Mandi DFO forest entry fee at Baggi check-post; Prashar Lake Homestay: 9418047099
permitInfo.note: HP TMS registration mandatory (trek ID 153). Nearest hospital: PHC Kataula (01905-207287). Nearest fuel: Kamand. Police: Kamand (01905-269400). Forest guard, Kataula: 01905-235360. Baggi bridge is listed as the official landmark in the HP TMS. Prashar Lake Homestay available on arrival (9418047099). Open year-round per HP TMS (1 Jan–31 Dec). Baggi is 25 km from Mandi, 2 km from Kamand.

description: One of Mandi district's most beautiful destinations — Prashar Lake (2,730m) with its mysterious floating island and 13th-century pagoda temple on a high ridge above the Beas Valley. The HP TMS (ID 153) registers the Baggi–Prashar route as an official 1-day easy trek from Baggi Bridge landmark through oak forest to the lake. The extraordinary 360° panorama from the Prashar ridge takes in the Dhauladhar, Pir Panjal, and Kullu–Manali peaks simultaneously.

overview.location: Prashar Lake (2,730m) and the ancient Prashar Rishi pagoda temple sit on a prominent ridge in Mandi district, 49 km from Mandi town. Baggi village (the trailhead) is 25 km from Mandi near Kamand. The HP TMS lists Baggi Bridge as the official trek landmark, noting it connects 'Kamand, Baggi, Prashar' habitations. The lake has a legendary floating island (a mat of vegetation that moves position seasonally) protected as a sacred site.
overview.history: Prashar Rishi is the Vedic sage credited with composing portions of the Rigveda — the lake bears his name. The three-storeyed wooden pagoda temple is attributed to Bhima of the Pandavas and dates architecturally to the 13th century CE, representing one of Himachal's finest examples of traditional wooden pagoda architecture. The floating island has never been scientifically explained and is considered sacred. Registered as HP TMS trek ID 153.
overview.length: 14 km round-trip from Baggi (7 km each way). Elevation gain from Baggi (approximately 2,100m) to lake (2,730m): 630m. Walking time: 3–4 hours up, 2–3 hours down. Best combined with overnight at Prashar Lake Homestay for sunrise views.
overview.temperature: Apr–Jun: 8°C–22°C; meadows around lake lush; possibly icy in April. Sep–Nov: 5°C–18°C; clearest Himalayan panorama; recommended. Jul–Aug: 12°C–22°C; monsoon clouds often dramatic around the ridge. Dec–Mar: Snow possible; lake may freeze; cold but beautiful for experienced visitors.
overview.fitness: Easy. 630m elevation gain over 7 km on good forest trail. Suitable for families, beginners, and older adults. Preparation: regular walking is sufficient.

itinerary.title: Mandi → Baggi → Prashar Lake
itinerary.desc: Drive from Mandi to Baggi (27–30 km by road to the trailhead). Register TMS at Baggi check-post (official landmark: Baggi Bridge). The trail ascends through oak forest and meadows to the Prashar ridge. The 13th-century pagoda temple and floating island are extraordinary. Overnight at Prashar Lake Homestay for the sunset and Himalayan panorama.

itinerary.title: Prashar Lake sunrise → Return to Baggi → Mandi
itinerary.desc: Sunrise at Prashar Lake: the Kullu–Manali peaks and Dhauladhar chain glow gold at first light with the floating island in the foreground. Descent through the forest to Baggi. Drive back to Mandi.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Amaan Ali on Pexels

name: Bhagsu Nag to Karthani Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Dhauladhar Wildlife Sanctuary Permit
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; Bhagsu Bus Stand check-post above McLeod Ganj
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory free registration; Dhauladhar WLS sanctuary entry; self-tent required for overnight at Karthani
permitInfo.note: HP TMS registration mandatory (trek ID 57). Open 15 Mar–15 Oct per HP TMS. Hotel options in base area: The Club House, The Bhagsu McLeod Ganj (01892-224212). Police Dharamshala: 01892-224883. Hospital Dharamshala: 01892-224874. HP TMS itinerary: 'Bhagsu to Karthani and back; stay in Karthani (self tent).' Landmark: Leta forest — self camping zone.

description: A beautiful 2-day trek from the sacred Bhagsu Nag temple above McLeod Ganj through the Leta forest zone to the remote high-altitude camp at Karthani — a lesser-visited Dhauladhar route that escapes the crowds of the famous Triund trail. The HP government TMS (ID 57) registers this as a medium-difficulty 2-day trek through forest and mountain terrain. Bhagsu Nag is a revered Nag (serpent deity) temple with a famous waterfall beside it.

overview.location: The trek starts from Bhagsu Nag (2,290m) — a village and sacred temple 2 km above McLeod Ganj in Kangra district, served by the Bhagsu Bus Stand. The route ascends through the Dhauladhar Wildlife Sanctuary via the Leta forest zone to Karthani (approximately 2,676m). The HP TMS lists 'Leta–Karthani' as the key habitation chain on this route.
overview.history: Bhagsu Nag is one of the most important Nag (serpent deity) shrines in the Kangra district. The shrine is associated with water — a natural spring feeds the famous Bhagsu waterfall, and the tank at the temple is sacred for ritual bathing. The surrounding Dhauladhar Wildlife Sanctuary has been protected since the 1950s. The HP TMS registered this route to extend monitoring into the Bhagsu watershed beyond the crowded Triund approaches.
overview.length: 16 km over 2 days. Day 1: Bhagsu Nag to Karthani via Leta forest (8 km, 4–5 hours). Day 2: Karthani to Bhagsu Nag return (8 km, 3–4 hours). Total elevation gain approximately 386m.
overview.temperature: Mar–May: 5°C–20°C; excellent rhododendron bloom on approach; spring clarity. Sep–Oct: 0°C–15°C; the clearest skies and Dhauladhar peak views. Jun–Aug: Monsoon affects this exposed Dhauladhar slope; not ideal. Nov–Feb: Below 15 Oct HP TMS closing date; cold and potentially snowy.
overview.fitness: Moderate. A forest and mountain trek requiring basic multi-day fitness. Self-tent is required at Karthani — no infrastructure. Trail navigation through the Leta forest requires a guide or good route knowledge. Suitable for trekkers comfortable with overnight camping.

itinerary.title: McLeod Ganj → Bhagsu Nag → Leta Forest → Karthani
itinerary.desc: Register TMS at Bhagsu Bus Stand above McLeod Ganj. Visit the Bhagsu Nag temple and waterfall before ascending. The trail enters the Leta forest — dense Dhauladhar sanctuary zone with oak and rhododendron. Karthani is a forest clearing camp with Dhauladhar peak views — carry all supplies.

itinerary.title: Karthani → Leta Forest → Bhagsu Nag → McLeod Ganj
itinerary.desc: Morning in the forest clearing with bird calls and mountain air. Return descent through the Leta zone back to Bhagsu Nag. McLeod Ganj with its Tibetan restaurants and cafes awaits after the quiet of the forest.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Mohamed Regaieg on Pexels

name: Boh Valley–Khabru Waterfall Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; Boh village entry check-post
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory free registration; tented accommodation available at Boh Valley
permitInfo.note: HP TMS mandatory (trek ID 64). Open year-round per HP TMS (1 Jan–31 Dec). The HP TMS describes this as a 1-day hike 'Boh Valley to Khabru Waterfall and back' — 6 km each way. Hospital Shahpur: 01892-238038. Police Shahpur: 01892-238021. Boh Bus Stand is the nearest transit point. Hotels, homestays, and tent accommodation available in Boh Valley. 30 km from Shahpur town.

description: A refreshing day trek through the Boh Valley to the scenic Khabru Waterfall — a hidden gem in the Dhauladhar foothills of Kangra district. The HP government TMS (ID 64) describes the Boh Valley as 'located at the foothills of the Dhauladhar mountain range in Kangra district, 30 km from Shahpur town — offering Khabru Waterfall on one side and greenery of the valley on the other.' A perfect easy day out from Dharamshala or Kangra.

overview.location: Boh Valley is in the lower Dhauladhar foothills of Kangra district, 30 km from Shahpur town. The valley is a tributary drainage of the Baner River flowing south toward the Kangra Valley floor. The Khabru Waterfall, 6 km from Boh Village, is the scenic highlight — a natural cascade fed by the Dhauladhar snowmelt.
overview.history: The Boh Valley is part of the settled agricultural landscape of Kangra district, known for its rice paddy terraces and forest wildlife. The HP TMS registered this as a formal trek destination (ID 64) to extend monitoring to the foothill valleys of Kangra — previously little known to outsiders — and provide safety infrastructure for day visitors.
overview.length: 12 km round-trip (6 km each way) from Boh Village to Khabru Waterfall. The HP TMS notes 6 km as the one-way distance. Elevation gain approximately 300–400m. Walking time: 2–3 hours each way.
overview.temperature: Open year-round per HP TMS. Oct–Mar: Cool and clear; best for waterfall visits — strongest flow from winter snowmelt. Apr–Jun: Warm and pleasant; spring flowers. Jul–Sep: Monsoon; waterfall at maximum volume but trail may be slippery.
overview.fitness: Easy–Moderate. A 12 km round-trip on forest and valley trail with modest elevation gain. Suitable for most fit adults and families. Suitable for a half-day or full-day excursion.

itinerary.title: Boh Village → Khabru Waterfall → Return
itinerary.desc: Drive 30 km from Shahpur to Boh Village. Register TMS at Boh check-post. The trail follows the Boh Valley upstream through forest and meadow to the Khabru Waterfall — a scenic natural cascade with Dhauladhar peaks visible above. The valley has 'beautiful scenery and forest' per HP TMS. Return by the same route in the afternoon.

coverImageCredit: Photo by Simranpreet  Singh on Pexels

name: Bonthu–Gaj Pass Trek

permitInfo.type: HP TMS Registration + Dhauladhar Wildlife Sanctuary Permit
permitInfo.where: Online at trekking.hp.gov.in; Ghera/Rawa entry check-post
permitInfo.fee: HP TMS mandatory free registration; Dhauladhar WLS sanctuary permit; self-tent required at Rawa Bagga and Lamdal
permitInfo.note: HP TMS mandatory (trek ID 67). Open 15 Apr–15 Oct per HP TMS. Hotel options: The Dhauladhar HPTDC, The Kunal Hotel HPTDC, Kashmir House HPTDC (01892-224212); many homestays and hotels at Dharamshala base. Police Dharamshala: 01892-224883. Hospital Dharamshala: 01892-224874. Bus: Ghera Bus Stand. HP TMS itinerary: 'Rawa–Bagga night stay (self tent)–Lamdal stay (self tent) and back.' Landmark: Lamdal — Forest and Mountain.

description: A demanding Dhauladhar crossing from Kangra's Ghera valley through the Gaddi shepherd settlements of Rawa and Bonthu to the 4,164m Gag Pass and remote Lam Dal Lake zone — registered as a HARD trek on the HP government TMS (ID 67). The route passes through authentic Gaddi shepherd territory rarely visited by tourists, with self-tent camping at both Rawa–Bagga and Lamdal. The 4,164m pass sits above the treeline with sweeping views of the Kangra Valley and the wild Ravi watershed beyond.
